#3226. IEEE Program Schools Preuniversity Educators On Tech Topics

The TryEngineering workshops help teachers deliver engaging STEM lessons

An educator constructs a microchip model during the IEEE Making a Microchip lesson plan demonstration.

Now in their third year, the IEEE TryEngineering educator sessions continue to empower preuniversity teachers with specialized professional development programs on engineering topics and classroom-tested lessons.

This year’s sessions, held across the United States, have focused on educating teachers about artificial intelligence and semiconductor technology. One session was held in Egypt.

In all, 54 educators learned about the engineering design process this year. They received an overview of TryEngineering resources including the Making of a Microchip and Train Your Tree lesson plans.

Workshops are scheduled this year in Greece and Guatemala.

The TryEngineering program is administered by IEEE Educational Activities.

These teachers and guest speakers attended the two-day session held at the Florida Semiconductor Institute and SkyWater Technology chip manufacturing facility.IEEE Educational Activities

Central to the educator session program’s success is its university network. Host campuses welcome teachers into their facilities, where faculty provide background information about some of the technologies being taught, as well as possible engineering career paths and job opportunities for students.

This year’s sessions involved the educators in hands-on projects. Facilitators at each location were selected based on their experience in engineering education, and they worked with the TryEngineering staff on their presentations.

Sixteen teachers from nine schools participated in the session, held in Cairo. It was facilitated by Marwa Soudi, an IEEE member, and Senior Member Stamatis Dragoumanos. Both are past chairs of the IEEE preuniversity coordinating committee. GEMS provided outstanding STEM facilities for teachers, Saudi and Dragoumanos said. Participants received an overview of the Working With Wind Energy and Tall Tower Challenge lesson plans.

Another educator session is scheduled for later this year.

Educators from across the state gathered at the university’s Florida Semiconductor Institute, headquartered in Gainesville, and FSI’s NeoCity high-tech manufacturing campus near Orlando. The session was hosted by Roseanne Perez, an FSI workforce development program specialist, and Sophia Watson, FSI’s assistant director of workforce development. The two-day experience featured an inside look at microelectronics through a guided tour of a SkyWater Technology chip manufacturing facility.

Engineering instructor Mary Acken facilitated hands-on lesson demonstrations for the 15 attending teachers.

Reflecting on the workshop’s impact, one participant said the SkyWater tour was excellent, the instructors were great, and the teachers enjoyed learning from like-minded educators.

Michael Kozicki, an IEEE member, and Stefan Myhajlenko from the university’s engineering school welcomed 11 Arizona teachers to the Tempe campus.

The session was facilitated by Janet Hartkopf, an Arizona school leader and a former TryEngineering educator session participant. Hartkopf highlighted collaborative learning, the need for diverse perspectives in engineering education, and career paths.

The teachers received instruction on how to implement the hands-on lessons in their classrooms, and they toured the university’s NanoFab facility to observe microelectronics research.

“This training was amazing!” said a participant who leads an elementary after-school STEM club. “I loved the hands-on lessons and e-books, which I will definitely be using with my students. I am excited to explore all the resources on the TryEngineering website. The experts from ASU were great.”

Sixteen STEM educators attended this session, held at the university’s International Institute for Biosensing in Minneapolis. Its director, Patricia Khashayar, an IEEE member, introduced participants to the capabilities of the university’s Supercomputing Institute and Nano Center.

Under the guidance of Claire Dietz, an education and outreach coordinator, and Pam Schumacher, an instructor at St. Paul College, the teachers completed classroom-ready lessons including a photonics experiment using the Nano Center’s equipment. Schumacher attended last year’s TryEngineering educator session.

Nano Center Director Sarah Swisher, an IEEE senior member, provided an overview of semiconductor operations and highlighted growing job opportunities for the state’s young people.

The experience inspired all 16 teachers to plan student field trips to the Nano Center during the upcoming academic year, they said.

“Great class!” one participant said. “I’m excited to bring some of the TryEngineering materials back to our school.”

This year’s sessions built on the momentum from last year when, with financial support from Onsemi’s Giving Now program, nearly 80 teachers attended sessions across five U.S. states and Mexico.

Driven by that success and the demand for more, the IEEE Educational Activities Board continued its support. Upcoming global sessions are expected to expand the program’s international footprint.

“I appreciated the time to collaborate with peers on how to implement hands-on lessons,” one participating teacher this year said. Some participants said they planned follow-up visits with the experts and campus tours.

You can learn more about the sessions by emailing TryEngineering.

Debra Gulick is director of IEEE student and academic educational programs.

#3225. Real REMAX Group: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Management is budgeting for another drop in home sales, so the plan's debt reduction has a chance to hold up even if the slump deepens.

On its first-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 5, 2026, Real REMAX Group (REAX -6.17%) announced its first quarterly financial results after closing its acquisition of RE/MAX on Aug. 24, 2026. Combining proprietary technology with a massive global franchise network positions the business to maintain cash flow through industry slumps.

Three key takeaways from management's comments stand out for long-term investors.

Management is consolidating operations after closing the acquisition. It reduced headcount by 14% and closed underperforming mortgage offices to lower overhead. These structural cuts are designed to expand adjusted EBITDA (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization, a key measure of core operational cash profitability) despite broader market drag.

The company launched LEO Pro, an artificial intelligence (AI, software designed to automate complex tasks) platform featuring over 300 specialized tools to manage client communication and marketing. More than 3,000 agents signed up for paid subscriptions within one month of release.

Management is structuring its multiyear budget around a prolonged housing downturn rather than anticipating an immediate recovery. It projects existing home sales will decline another 5% to 10% in 2027, setting transaction volumes at 30-year lows while focusing on disciplined debt reduction.

Housing transaction volumes sit near historic troughs, but the combined platform expands operational cash flow regardless of market timing. Its automated software assets, capital-light franchise network, and focus on debt reduction protect earnings while leadership monitors regional listing trends and agent productivity.

By simplifying administrative overhead and integrating modern technology across all franchises, the company aims to expand market share throughout the current downturn.

#3222. Graphon Labs raises $35m to give AI agents a memory that lasts

Graphon Labs says its graph-based memory tops rival systems on three benchmarks. The 20-person company counts HP and the San Francisco 49ers among its users.

Graphon Labs co-founders, from left: Deepak Mishra, chief operating officer; Arbaaz Khan, chief executive; and Clark Zhang, chief technology officer.

Graphon Labs, a San Francisco startup that builds memory for AI agents, has raised $35m. RRE Ventures led the Series A. HP, Energy Impact Partners, Hitachi Ventures and Gaia VC also invested, Graphon said on Tuesday. The round brings its total funding to $43.3m, less than six months after it left stealth with an $8.3m seed round.

The 20-person company will spend the money mainly on engineers and researchers, plus some sales staff. Chief executive Arbaaz Khan gave those details to Shubhangi Goel of Business Insider, which reported the round first.

Khan compares common AI search to tearing the pages out of a book and digging through the scraps for an answer.

“You’ve basically lost all that information because each piece is living on its own,” he told Business Insider.

AI agents can write code and carry out tasks. But they can lose track of past conversations and changing company data. Graphon says common methods can lose context, relationships and timing as data grows. One example is retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), which feeds a model snippets of stored text.

Graphon’s system is built on graphons, a mathematical framework for very large graphs. Khan and co-founder Clark Zhang built graph-based memory for robots during their PhDs, Khan wrote in a blog post. The software maps the links between a company’s documents, videos and images, including where information came from and when it changed.

“You can basically point your Claude or GPT or whatever to Graphon,” Khan told Business Insider.

Graphon says it scored 93.9% on LoCoMo, a test of memory over long conversations. It used 58% fewer tokens than loading the whole conversation into the model. On ATM-Bench, a University of Cambridge benchmark across video, audio, images and text, it scored 81.7%. That is 5 points ahead of the next system on the public leaderboard.

Graphon says the San Francisco 49ers, Hitachi and other large companies use its software. HP also uses it, Business Insider reported. Costa Kladianos, the 49ers’ executive vice president of technology, said the team is exploring how to use it. One example is finding new sponsorship deals. Hitachi Rail said its evaluation “shows promise” in its industrial setting.

The company has three products: Graphon Enterprise, a developer platform, and on-device memory for phones, laptops, cameras and wearables. Khan told Business Insider that Graphon will stay focused on enterprise customers before moving further into devices and consumer products.

The biggest AI companies are also adding memory to their assistants. In August, Anthropic merged Claude’s memory across chat and Cowork. In October, Apple’s iOS 27.2 gave Siri memory.

#3220. How Do You Land on a Moon With Almost No Gravity?

Japan’s MMX mission aims to sample the Martian moon Phobos

Japan's MMX spacecraft will fire its engines to slow down and enter orbit around Mars.

Last August, looking up from the edge of an ancient river delta on Mars, the Perseverance rover’s electronic eye spied an oblong shadow crossing the distant, glowing Sun. Phobos, the Martian moon named for the Greek god of fear and panic, was transiting the solar disk. Too small to darken the pale, dust-tinged sky, but orbiting close enough to eclipse a significant fraction of the Sun, Phobos passed in less than a minute.

NASA’s Perseverance rover captured Phobos passing in front of the Sun from the surface of Mars.ASU/MSSS/SSI/JPL-Caltech/NASA

The tiny moon, with its murky origins, is an enigma, and one whose makeup and history could tell us much about Mars and the wider solar system. And now the international Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) mission, which successfully launched on 20 October, seeks to explore that mystery with an unprecedented series of landings on the unknown surface of Phobos.

This mission brings unusual challenges—for example, designing an orbit to study a microgravity moon orbiting a much larger planet. Engineers also had to figure out how to assess and land on this low-gravity pile of loosely assembled dirt and rock, how a rover might rove across it, and how the spacecraft might take samples and return them to Earth.

“I often say that landing on Phobos is like trying to land a balloon,” says Yasuhiro Kawakatsu, project manager of MMX at the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA). “It’s very difficult to drop a balloon to the ground and prevent it from tilting or bouncing.”

Phobos is one of two small Martian moons; the other is Deimos, named after the Greek god of dread and terror. Their cosmic origins are unknown, though there are two prevailing theories. One holds that the moons were once asteroids from the belt between Mars and Jupiter, captured by the smaller planet’s gravity. In the other theory, Phobos and Deimos formed when a large celestial body slammed into Mars, sending debris into orbit. Some models suggest the pair are the last survivors from a cluster of satellites.

The enormous Stickney crater, roughly 9 kilometers across, dominates this view of Phobos taken by NASA’s Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter.University of Arizona/JPL-Caltech/NASA

Scientifically speaking, Phobos is considered a rubble pile, a loosely consolidated aggregate of rock and dust. Far too small to become spherical under its own mass, it’s shaped like a lumpy potato, roughly 27 kilometers in length, with only 1/1,800th of Earth’s gravity. On Phobos, a typical adult would weigh about as much as a tennis ball does on Earth.

More than 10 years in the making, MMX launched on Japan’s flagship H3 rocket from Tanegashima spaceport on 20 October local time. It will arrive at Mars in 2027 carrying scientific payloads from several space agencies, including NASA, and a new rover called Idefix developed by the French and German space agencies (CNES and DLR) in collaboration with JAXA.

Engineers assembled MMX’s modules at Japan’s Tanegashima Space Center before the spacecraft’s October 2026 launch.JAXA

MMX consists of three modules: a propulsion module to power its journey to Mars and apply the brakes to enter orbit around the red planet; an exploration module carrying the rover, sampling gear, and other scientific instruments; and a return module, attached to the exploration module, that harbors the capsule destined for a high-speed reentry into Earth’s atmosphere. After collecting samples on Phobos, the exploration and return modules will lift off together. The exploration module will then be jettisoned while the return module sets a course back home.

If all goes according to plan, MMX will deliver a 10-gram sample to Earth in the second half of 2031. But the mission will face a series of daunting challenges to reach that end point, including navigating complex orbits around Phobos and landing on its surface while Mars periodically blocks communications with Earth.

The MMX’s modular design includes the propulsion module [left] and the exploration and return modules [right].Kyodo News/Getty Images

“It’s the most complex mission I have ever seen,” says Patrick Michel, director of research at CNRS (the French National Center for Scientific Research) and co-principal investigator on Idefix.

An H3 rocket carried MMX into space on 20 October 2026, beginning the mission’s five-year journey to Phobos and back.The Asahi Shimbun/Getty Images

Once MMX reached low Earth orbit, its propulsion module’s engine fired, kicking off a nearly year-long deep-space cruise to Mars. On arrival, the spacecraft will need to fire its engines in an extended, carefully timed burn to slow down enough to be captured by Mars gravity. The propulsion module will then be jettisoned, leaving the exploration and return modules to orbit Mars.

“If something doesn’t go according to plan, MMX will fly by Mars and get catapulted into the solar system,” says Nicola Baresi, an astrodynamicist who coauthored a paper on specially designed orbits for MMX.

From that initial orbit, MMX will transition into a specially designed quasi-satellite orbit that allows it to keep pace with the small moon but also move around it. Since Phobos is too small to orbit in the conventional sense, the spacecraft will orbit Mars alongside the moon, following a clever egg-shaped path that slings MMX alternately ahead of and behind the moon. “When you’re closer to Mars, you’re accelerating with respect to Phobos, and when you’re farther from Mars, you’re decelerating. So you essentially go back and forth,” explains Baresi.

Martian Maneuvers To reach Phobos, MMX will execute three major maneuvers: MOI-1 will put the spacecraft into orbit around Mars, MOI-2 will transfer it toward Phobos, and MOI-3 will place it into its final orbit alongside the moon.Chris Philpot

To reach Phobos, MMX will execute three major maneuvers: MOI-1 will put the spacecraft into orbit around Mars, MOI-2 will transfer it toward Phobos, and MOI-3 will place it into its final orbit alongside the moon.

The best existing images of Phobos, from spacecraft such as NASA’s Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter and ESA’s Mars Express, have resolutions of only a few meters per pixel. That’s larger than Idefix, the mission’s rover, itself about the size of a microwave oven. To map the surface in greater detail, MMX will loop in front of and behind Phobos at distances ranging from 200 kilometers to less than 20 km from the surface.

During its two-year remote sensing campaign, the exploration module will use several cameras and a laser altimeter to map the surface in high resolution and look for candidate landing sites. When Mars passes behind the Sun as seen from the Earth, causing a roughly two-week communications blackout, MMX will retreat into a larger, stable orbit. After communications resume, MMX will prepare to send its first visitor down to the surface.

Before the exploration and connected return modules attempt to land, Kawakatsu says, MMX will send a scout that in Japanese is called “the first penguin,” leaping into unknown waters. For this mission, the first to leap will be the Idefix rover, named for the canine companion to Obelix in the French comics series Asterix. The exploration module will release the rover during a low-altitude pass of between 40 and 100 meters above Phobos’s surface in 2028 or early 2029.

MMX will use its TENGOO camera [left] and LIDAR laser altimeter [right] to map Phobos’s terrain.JAXA

It will be a tense moment that calls back to 2005, during Japan’s Hayabusa mission to explore the asteroid Itokawa. In a similarly designed drop, the MINERVA rover was released from an orbiter, but erroneously at 200 meters instead of the intended 70 meters. The rover missed the asteroid and, without propulsion, drifted off into deep space.

Idefix will get a slight nudge out of the exploration module toward its negligible-gravity target, freefalling and likely tumbling as it goes. It’s expected to touch down with a velocity of less than 1 meter per second. Unlike rovers that have landed on other surfaces with airbags or dedicated landing legs, Idefix will land without protection, apart from some extra padding on the solar panels due to their critical nature. The barely-there gravity of Phobos should allow the 23-kilogram rover to land softly, though exactly how this landing will play out is hard to predict.

The Idefix rover will travel to Phobos with its wheels tucked in and solar panels folded.DLR

“It will bounce probably several times,” says Stephan Ulamec, Idefix’s co-principal investigator and project manager at DLR. “It will come to rest somehow in some position.” Once it’s still, four retracted legs will deploy to right the rover autonomously, regardless of its orientation. It will then unfold its solar panels to charge its batteries for exploration tasks ahead.

A simulation shows how Idefix is expected to tumble onto Phobos, right itself using its articulated legs, and begin exploring the moon’s surface. DLR

Once operational, Idefix will roll at a snail’s pace, topping out at one millimeter per second. Its metal wheels have protruding blades like a paddle wheel, designed to gain traction in Phobos’s microgravity. “If we were to drive our rover faster, then it would actually be more like we were swimming through instead of driving across the surface,” says Cecily Sunday, a doctoral student involved in testing Idefix’s WheelCams at the Institut Superieur de l’Aeronautique et de l’Espace (ISAE-Supaéro) in Toulouse, France.

The WheelCams, a pair of cameras placed on the underside of the rover, will observe the wheels and their tracks during Idefix’s planned 100-Earth-day primary mission. The images will help researchers study the size and distribution of grains in Phobos’s regolith and how cohesive they are. How much or how little the grains stick together will greatly impact how Idefix moves. Sunday likens this to the difference between driving on dry and wet sand. “Think of trying to build a sandcastle with dry sand,” she says. “You can’t. Add water, and suddenly you can.”

The Idefix rover was mounted between the MMX spacecraft’s landing legs for the journey to Phobos.DLR

The team tested the rover’s nine-bladed wheels on a variety of materials, including Phobos regolith simulants provided by JAXA and DLR, lunar simulants, glass beads, quartz sand, and clay pebbles. “We characterize the mechanical properties of each simulant precisely, then test across the full range, with varying grain size, angularity, and even color, so we can map what we see in the WheelCam images back to actual surface properties,” Sunday says.

Despite the microgravity and Phobos’s rubble-pile nature, Sunday says Earth-based tests can approximate the rover’s motion on the surface of the small moon fairly well. While Phobos’s reduced gravity lowers the rover’s effective weight, there is also reduced pressure between the grains beneath its wheels. “As long as you’re moving very, very slowly and using the same materials and the same weight of the system, they should be representative,” Sunday says.

With four paddle-like wheels and deployable solar panels, Idefix is designed to crawl across Phobos.Ardan Fuessmann/Imago/Alamy

Idefix’s interactions with its new home will offer “sub-millimeter resolution and information on porosity, on grain size, on surface strength, on how hard is the material,” Ulamec says. “It fills a gap between remote observations from orbit and detailed observations of the return samples back on Earth.”

What Idefix finds on this rocky, rugged world will help determine how and where JAXA attempts to land the main spacecraft. Michel says the touchdown will provide ground truth for understanding of Phobos. When NASA’s OSIRIS-REx spacecraft touched down on the asteroid Bennu to collect a sample, its sampling arm surprisingly sank nearly half a meter into the loose material. But Ulamec doesn’t think Idefix will sink deep into Phobos, noting that Bennu is very different and much smaller, with a diameter of 500 meters.

Once Idefix has investigated the surface, MMX will face an even greater challenge: landing its much larger exploration module on Phobos. The spacecraft will make a controlled descent to roughly 10 meters above the surface, then drop the remaining distance in free fall. With so little gravity to pull it downward, even a small sideways motion could cause the lander to tip or bounce away. A successful, upright landing would mark the start of up to two hours on Phobos for the crucial sampling phase.

The MMX mission draws on the experience and technologies of Japan’s two Hayabusa sample-return missions, which landed on the asteroids Itokawa and Ryugu. But this mission has many more moving parts. MMX’s exploration module will use two sampling devices—a coring sampler developed by JAXA and a pneumatic sampler provided by NASA and fabricated by Honeybee Robotics, a subsidiary of Blue Origin. Data from these tools, and those carried by the Idefix rover, could answer questions about the origin of Phobos and how the Mars system has evolved.

The coring sampler uses a robot arm and a cylindrical corer designed to reach at least 2 centimeters below the surface. The arm can maneuver to find the best site for digging. “That by itself is a challenge because we’ve never done it,” Michel says. “You never know what can happen at the very sampling site itself, where you might have a boulder and the arm cannot move.”

Probing beneath the top layer will be valuable because solar radiation, galactic cosmic rays, and micrometeorites have battered and weathered the surface. The material below should offer a better record of the moon’s origins, and JAXA aims to collect at least 10 grams of it.

MMX will carry both the Idefix rover [bottom] and a robotic coring sampler [top] designed to dig beneath Phobos’s weathered surface.JAXA

The pneumatic sampler takes a different approach. Mounted on one of the lander’s legs, it will inject pure, non-reactive nitrogen gas into the surface and capture the grains stirred up. This sample could illuminate the changes Mars and its moons have undergone over time. The dual system also adds redundancy in the face of Phobos’s unknowns. “If the surface of Phobos proves to be very hard, [the coring sampler] may struggle to penetrate the ground. [The pneumatic sampler] would not experience this issue and still be able to gather material,” Kawakatsu says.

One of the most intriguing aspects of MMX is the additional possibility of collecting material from the planet below. It’s likely that Phobos has been peppered by Martian ejecta thrown into space by meteor impacts, so MMX also provides an opportunity to return the first Martian samples to Earth. Michel estimates that the samples could contain “a few hundred grains coming from Mars.” Scientists can distinguish those grains from native Phobos material by analyzing their oxygen isotopes.

That possibility raises a planetary-protection question. A direct Mars sample-return mission would have to follow strict rules to ensure that potentially living biological material from Mars doesn’t contaminate Earth. But those protocols don’t apply to MMX, even if its sample does collect grains of Martian soil. A panel of experts concluded that any microbes blasted off Mars wouldn’t survive the violent impact and ejection or the intense radiation exposure on the way to Phobos. This saved MMX from implementing expensive and time-consuming quarantine and containment protocols for the returning sample.

After landing on Phobos, MMX will have roughly two hours to collect samples from the moon’s surface before lifting off again.JAXA

During the brief surface operation, the robotic arm will deposit the samples in a storage unit, from which they’ll be transferred into a capsule aboard the return module and sealed in a vacuum. After that, lift off.

Once back in Mars orbit, the exploration module will resume its observations of Phobos and make several flybys of Mars’s other diminutive moon, Deimos, to gather data on its surface, structure, and composition. In November 2030, during a favorable alignment of Mars and Earth, MMX will begin the homeward leg of its trip. The return module will separate from the exploration module and power the voyage home, its sole objective to bring the dust of Phobos to Earth.

MMX’s sample return capsule will carry material from Phobos through Earth’s atmosphere in 2031.JAXA

Finally, in 2031, the 60-centimeter-wide sample capsule will plunge into Earth’s atmosphere at roughly 12 kilometers per second. Assuming it survives the extreme heat of reentry and lands safely in Australia, scientists will begin to tease out clues about Phobos and the early solar system. JAXA’s Institute of Space and Astronautical Science will receive and curate the samples, which will also be shared with mission partners.

“We have macroscale measurements from the spacecraft, microscale measurements with the rover, and then sample analysis,” Michel says. “So we can relate the three kinds of scales together because we have all of them.” The insights gleaned from orbital images, close-up images of the regolith, and the chemical analysis of the samples could have wider implications for our understanding of our solar system.

“MMX is a mission to understand the Mars system and shed light onto how terrestrial planets like the Earth, and maybe Mars, develop a habitable environment,” Kawakatsu says. “We strongly suspect that our terrestrial planet region formed dry, and water and organics were scattered inwards from the icy-rich outer solar system.” Mars, he says, sits at the gateway between the inner and outer solar system, making its moons valuable witnesses to the processes that shaped potentially habitable worlds.

Andrew Jones is a freelance journalist based near Helsinki. He writes about the space industry and technology with a particular focus on China's activities.

#3219. Anthropic IPO: Here's What Betting Markets Are Predicting After the AI Correction

With AI stocks slumping, the Anthropic IPO.

In September, sentiment regarding a potential Anthropic IPO hit a fever pitch.

"The public sale, ​which could value it at more than $2 trillion, would capitalize on the rapid rise of the AI start-up lab that only came into existence five years ago, and establish it ​as a benchmark for how Wall Street values AI's leading companies, including rival OpenAI," a Reuters article reported. "Anthropic's ​expected valuation target is more than double its own estimated valuation of $965 billion in May."

The recent correction in artificial intelligence stocks, however, is throwing Anthropic's IPO valuation into question. Even a blue chip stock like Nvidia has fallen by more than 25% since its early October peak.

"Anthropic PBC's initial public offering plans ran into a punishing post-election sell-off, prompting a rethink among prospective investors of the company's expected valuation," a Bloomberg article noted on Nov. 6. Reports suggest that the company will now target a valuation between $1.2 trillion and $1.3 trillion. But some experts believe Anthropic will ultimately settle for a valuation closer to $1.1 trillion -- $900 billion short of the company's rumored target just over a month ago.

But it's not just Anthropic's valuation that is under fire. Betting markets are increasingly skeptical that Anthropic will even go public this year. Recent trading activity sheds light on what investors should expect next.

On Nov. 2, the day before the U.S. election, Kalshi betting markets gave Anthropic around an 87% chance of going public in 2026. The day of the election, Kalshi's implied odds of a 2026 IPO for Anthropic varied, but they ultimately settled closer to 87% again. The market's odds changed little over the next day, suggesting that bettors believed that the flip in control of Congress would minimally affect Anthropic's plans.

When AI stocks in general fell sharply on Nov. 5, however, betting markets reacted strongly. That day, Anthropic's odds of holding an IPO this year fell to just 64%. On Nov. 6, they fell as low as 53%, only to spike dramatically to around 85% by the end of the day.

Why the volatility? The drop in odds during the correction is self-explanatory. With AI company valuations falling across the board, Reuters reported that potential investors in Anthropic were growing skittish.

"Investors are pushing ‌for a more attractive valuation to commit to the offering, with some viewing the recently discussed $1.5 trillion valuation as being at the high end of expectations," the outlet revealed.

Why the spike in odds near the end of the day on Nov. 6? The exact cause isn't known, but there has been no indication from Anthropic management that its planned November IPO will be delayed. Perhaps the valuation will come under pressure, but going public soon still seems to be the plan.

Of course, if AI stocks continue to decline, Anthropic may shelve its offering in the hopes of attaining a higher valuation down the road. But for now, betting markets seem confident that we'll have another blockbuster AI IPO later this month.

Should investors trust the odds set by betting markets? I'm inclined to agree with the consensus here. The IPO preparation process typically takes between 12 and 24 months. And with an offering this large, Anthropic's management will be hesitant to institute a delay. That's especially true considering the company continues to lose money, making greater access to capital markets a priority. AI stocks have been volatile, but I'm fully expecting to see Anthropic go public before the end of the year.

#3218. Gritt and MasTec bring bolt-on construction robots to solar sites

MasTec will put Gritt's robot arms on its US solar farms, months after Burns & McDonnell signed up.

Infrastructure builder MasTec will deploy Gritt’s AI robotic attachments on its utility-scale solar projects across several US states, after testing them on live sites. It follows a similar deal with Burns & McDonnell in August. No financial terms were disclosed.

MasTec, one of North America’s largest infrastructure builders, will use Gritt’s AI-powered robots on its solar farms, the two companies said on Tuesday. Neither disclosed financial terms.

Gritt makes robotic arms that bolt onto equipment crews already use, such as skid steers and forklifts, to lift and place solar panels. MasTec tested the systems on live sites, where they helped install “megawatts” of panels. The companies now plan a pipeline of projects across several US states.

“We’ve evaluated Gritt systems on active construction sites, and we see an opportunity to pair our teams’ expertise with technology that supports them in the field,” said Rob Turner, vice president of construction at MasTec Renewables.

It is Gritt’s second named partner in three months. Burns & McDonnell signed a similar deal in August after a year of trials, Solar Power World reported.

When Gritt raised $32M in July, it said it worked with three of the top 10 US power construction firms but did not name them. It said its robots let crews place 3,000 to 4,000 panels a day instead of about 800.

At the time, Gritt had only two systems in the field. Its website now lists more than seven job sites.

Construction firms are turning to robots as skilled workers retire. Procore agreed to buy drone maker DroneDeploy for $845M in July, and welding startup Path Robotics raised $300M on Tuesday.

#3217. Report: Apple saved over $5 billion in taxes through Singapore and Ireland in 2026

A new Financial Times report reveals how Apple saved billions in taxes in 2026 by shifting profits through Singapore and Ireland. Here are the details.

A few days ago, Apple published its annual Form 10-K, as required by the SEC, containing detailed information about its financial performance and operations for its 2026 fiscal year.

Included in the form, as the FT noted, is information regarding how Apple reduced its tax bill by billions of dollars through its operations in Singapore and Ireland.

For years, Apple’s tax arrangements in Ireland were the subject of scrutiny, culminating in a 2024 ruling by the EU’s top court that required the company to pay €13 billion in back taxes. Apple completed the payment in 2025.

That came a few years after Apple announced plans to bring most of its $252 billion in overseas cash back to the US, following tax reforms introduced during Donald Trump’s first administration.

Since then, to discourage companies from shifting profits to countries with lower tax rates, more than 130 countries have agreed to introduce a minimum corporate tax rate of 15% for large multinational companies, as part of a 2021 initiative coordinated by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD).

Under the agreement, companies that pay less than 15% in a particular country may face additional taxes to make up the difference. The new rules also resulted in an additional $2.5 billion in taxes for Apple in Singapore in 2026, according to the company’s SEC filing.

Ireland adopted the new rules in 2024, followed by Singapore in 2025.

Back to the FT’s report, it notes that new US accounting rules now require publicly traded companies to disclose when their taxes on overseas profits differ significantly from the 21% US federal corporate tax rate.

These new requirements revealed that Apple saved $2.7 billion in taxes through Singapore in 2026, surpassing the $2.6 billion it saved through Ireland.

If Apple had been taxed on all of its global profits in 2026 at the US federal rate, it would have incurred a total bill of $33bn — demonstrating the scale of the $5bn tax reduction it received from booking profits in Ireland and Singapore. The company incurred corporation taxes totalling $27bn this year.

The FT also noted that Apple’s effective tax rate in Singapore fluctuated around 10% between 2023 and 2025, but is expected to approach 15% under the new rules. Singapore’s standard corporate tax rate is 17%.

#3214. Infinity Natural Resources: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Firm pipeline space on REX lets Infinity sell gas at regional prices instead of discounted local ones, a lever that matters if you hold for the long haul.

On its third quarter of 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 10, 2026, Infinity Natural Resources (INR -0.83%) announced record daily natural gas and oil production. Expanding ownership of gathering pipelines and optimizing well designs allow the business to cut operating costs and protect cash flows. Three things management said stand out.

Owned pipeline systems give the business a structural cost advantage as production volume expands. Higher pipeline utilization directly lowers gathering, processing, and transportation (GP&T) expenses per million cubic feet equivalent (Mcfe), a standard measure of gas volume.

Operational tweaks after acquiring Ohio acreage let management eliminate entire drill pads and pipeline connections. Re-engineering well paths with hairpin U-turns keeps drilling capital efficient without compromising reservoir access.

Securing firm transport capacity, or guaranteed pipeline space, on the Rockies Express Pipeline (REX) allows the business to bypass discounted local prices. Connecting local gas to higher-priced regional markets increases realized selling prices across major production volumes.

Production volumes are tracking toward the high end of full-year targets while capital spending stays at the low end. An integrated midstream network and disciplined hedging protect corporate cash flows against energy market swings.

Future growth hinges on capital allocation discipline and maintaining flexible project returns rather than chasing commodity price cycles.

#3213. AI Agents Are Testing the Limits of Zero-Trust Security

As autonomous AI agents work together, verifying their actions, enforcing security policies, and maintaining accountability becomes increasingly difficult

Vishal Sharma is a Reader in the School of Electronics, Electrical Engineering, and Computer Science at Queen's University Belfast, Northern Ireland, United Kingdom.

In a de-authentication attack on an aerial vehicle using a human- and agent-in-the-loop approach, an AI agent can quickly scan the active channel and autonomously intercept traffic, thus reducing the time to react and regain control.

This article is brought to you by Queen’s University Belfast.

Several teams around the globe are leveraging AI by creating a task force of agents managed by an orchestrator and creating applications to support risk assessment, client profiling, match making, and information yield with a slight overview of decision making. One of the important components for these agents is to ensure that the logs are managed and historic relevance is not being used to avoid skewing towards same decision making. Thus, the system is expected to keep checkpoints in place where agents are prompted to delete such historic relevance.

However, despite such methodology in place, a future prompt could make the agents bring forward the information that was supposed to be deleted and can be tricked into revealing more information, which is a classic case of context recovery attack. So, the question raised here is: How can we trust that our instructions have been followed? And where is the proof?

There is an element of utilizing zero-trust architectures (ZTA) for orchestrating and managing agentic activity, which simply means all agentic interactions use the core principle of “never trust,” “always verify.” ZTA components include a policy enforcement point (PEP) that has to be trusted to maintain trust across the system, so the question that remains is where is the component of zero-trust, and shall we trust the policies enforced by PEP?

Having a pro-agentic approach and utilizing agents could be helpful with the right guardrails in place. Opening our systems to random agents that are being trained on off-the-shelf models and blindly relying on them can pose significant cyber risks. For example, vibe coding by using an AI model to help develop software, giving away the entire codebase to an untrusted entity outside the organization can lead to vulnerability sweeping across multiple surfaces.

Vibe coding by using an AI model to help develop software, giving away the entire codebase to an untrusted entity outside the organization can lead to vulnerability sweeping across multiple surfaces.

This opens critical discussions towards how vibe coding could interfere with the positioning and implementation of trusted execution of the agentic queries. Consider an autonomous web of agents that relies on agents’ inputs to drive the operations. When the system is operating under low tolerance of failure and with non-tracking based agentic workflows, it could be computationally expensive to trust and verify each query in real-time that leads to the common trade-offs of memory vs execution.

Another risk to consider is the zero-day attack. When it happens, how will the system react? Would such an event be manageable without a total infrastructure breakdown? The scale of impact can be observed from over reliance on agentic ecosystems with only one trusted layer. This could mean that when failure occurs, the entire ecosystem could be exposed, just like there will be no autonomy if the backbone network is not available, which essentially means no layer to place trust.

An in-house experiment done at Queen’s University Belfast (QUB) provided an initial understanding of how the scale of agentic attacks could mean a lower window of vulnerability. The team focused on very popular de-authentication attacks and with agentic orchestration, the swift rate to do de-authentication attacks could go as low as 2 to 3 seconds. This gives little to no time to react and decide on patching the system.

There is another aspect of the large-scale agentic system, which establishes trust under asynchronous autonomy. Trust serves as a critical foundation for traceability. How would you ensure that all the agents operating towards a common goal are aligned and understand the delays associated with their goals?

Our team worked around this space, which at first involved demonstrating that the problem exists, and its impact and scale can be huge when you must prove trust under boundaries of asynchronous autonomy. Solutions towards such problems can be simplified by keeping things like AI-bill of material or leveraging distributed ledger technology that can provide underlying infrastructure of trust via traceability and immutability and keep the agentic activity and associated trust vectors agnostic to the platform.

Within trust, another factor that is not well explored but needs a thorough investigation is the concept of horizontal anomalies. It defines how agents interact differently with various sources under different settings. As agents behave correctly and align themselves with the architectural expectations for one specific task or application, that does not necessarily mean these can be trusted for their operations across all associated components. How to identify such anomalies and what methods can be employed without complying with such agents remain open questions and topics for further exploration.

The critical aspect is that utility of agents with semi to low trust governance offer short-term high benefits, but the cost of recovery when the system fails is yet to be explored, and this will not be a contained issue. We are looking into the system where agents are already sweeping into different entities and may not allow complete recovery. For example, a mere supply chain issue because an agent going rogue is now not a containable small task but needs sweeping across all the touch points of those affected agents. This essentially means despite the number of agents and their ability to trigger proxy-agents, which may not be directly linked to the wider ecosystem, there is a need to ensure that computationally expensive trackers are in place for all the agents.

Other relevant PhD works carried out in our research group are towards sovereignty of AI, exploring aspects of trust and accountability. Our hypothesis is that sovereignty and trust need to be governed together as onus of provenance is high on the host of agents. Thus, it needs understanding of laws governing trust-based executions of AI. The important challenge here is that there is a vital difference between missed information and missed instructions, and both have different impacts when it comes to trusted accountability.

The real-world issue with these systems lies in the failure to adopt approaches that historically have relied on state-based modeling when governing trust. In stateless systems where agentic autonomy is high, the convergence and reliability towards trust-provenance decreases significantly. Thus, it brings us back to the original question – does a true zero-trust even exist?

Can policies be trusted? If so, how should these be managed without falling into the trap of policy-based accessibility and control issues? Despite the argument that PEP can help manage access between the agents, placing a single entity and expecting it to scale towards all agentic interactions is underestimating the problem space.

Formal verification of trust is another part of a trust-based agentic ecosystem. When dealing with AI models, understanding the robustness helps to put trust in place for these models.

To build our case and settle around the challenges of trust embeddings in Agentic AI, within Cyber AI hub, we are exploring opportunities to help companies scale up as well as build their pipeline of agentic applications for commercial viability. However, the element that governs our regular work and decision making are scale of problem and number of agentic deployments, anomaly detection across the agentic workflows, continuous evaluation of the attack surfaces and vulnerability assessment, exploring differences in the pure agentic AI and task-driven multi-agent system.

We are working with industries where trust is a pre-requisite, and these organizations put trust as a guardrail managed via internal policies with a pure focus on securing the systems through policies rather than trusting the third-party agentic service providers. Additionally, trust in services is presented by ensuring constraints around their service models where agentic activities are tracked and managed via logs including management of their token revocation list to avoid replay attacks depending on the type of application. Formal verification of trust is another part of a trust-based agentic ecosystem. When dealing with AI models, understanding the robustness helps to put trust in place for these models. Things like balancing the adversarial accuracy along with certified adversarial robustness can help to determine how much the model can be trusted.

But the question is, can we settle for anything less than foolproof when it comes to deployment of agents in the real world? And if so, how much impact can be controlled, and who is responsible for the remaining component?

#3212. OpenAI lets businesses claim ChatGPT profiles and launch their own agents

Brands get a blue check, mention counts and a chat agent, which OpenAI also sells as an ad.

A mock-up from OpenAI of a verified business profile in ChatGPT, with a button to chat with the shop’s Business Agent.

OpenAI launched Businesses in ChatGPT in beta, letting businesses claim verified profiles, update their details and see aggregated data on how often ChatGPT mentions them. US ecommerce and online-service firms can also launch Business Agents, which OpenAI also sells as ads.

OpenAI is letting businesses claim their profiles in ChatGPT and launch AI agents that talk to customers on their behalf, the company said on Tuesday. The beta, called Businesses in ChatGPT, is aimed at the 1.2 billion people OpenAI says use ChatGPT each week.

Through a tool called Business Hub, verified companies get a blue check and can update their details, prices and stock. They can also see how often ChatGPT mentions them, how many people click through to their website and common topics in those conversations. OpenAI says it does not share users’ chats with businesses.

Eligible US ecommerce and online-service firms can also launch a Business Agent. When a business shows up in a ChatGPT answer, users can open its profile and chat with its agent, which answers using the company’s product details. The chat is labelled and kept apart from ChatGPT’s own answers.

The same agent can be sold as an ad. Businesses can sponsor it as the landing spot for ChatGPT Ads, building on Sponsored Agents, which OpenAI began testing in September. OpenAI says paying does not change how often ChatGPT recommends a business, Digiday reported.

Agents must say they are AI, keep prices accurate and avoid pressure tactics. Purchases and sharing personal data need the user’s explicit approval. For now, buyers are sent to the brand’s own website, though OpenAI is building agent payments with Visa.

The move deepens OpenAI’s push into advertising, which passed a $1B annual run rate in August and now has 100,000 advertisers. It could also squeeze startups such as Peec AI, which sell brands estimates of how visible they are in ChatGPT.

#3211. Skydance confirms HBO Max and Paramount+ ‘value’ bundle plan

HBO Max and Paramount+ customers will soon be able to pay for one subscription that unlocks both services. That’s according to Skydance, the company that came out of Paramount’s Warner Bros. Discovery acquisition.

Skydance announced plans for the HBO Max plus Paramount+ bundle today, promising to deliver the package deal early next year.

Skydance doesn’t say how much the bundle will cost or if it will have ad-supported options. Both HBO Max and Paramount+ currently offer cheaper subscriptions with ads as well as premium ad-free options.

HBO Max can also be bundled with Disney+ and Hulu today, though this is a package offering that we can probably expect to go away in the future.

Ultimately, it would make sense for Skydance to package a unified service that includes all of the content from both services. For now, at least, it sounds like the short-term plan is to sell the two services separately with an option to bundle and save.

If you've tried breathable bed sheets, oscillating fans and frozen pillows but you still wake up sweaty, I've found the solution. The Orion Sleep System, now with $600 off in Orion's Black Friday sale, is a smart cooling system that helps defeat night sweats by actively adjusting the temperature as you sleep.

One of the best smart beds you can buy online, this clever mattress cover is fitted with a series of (imperceptible) water tubes that cool or heat throughout the night. That means a sudden flush of cold if night sweats are coming on, or a gentle warming if things get too chilly.

This is just a cover, so you might need to buy a new bed to go with it — I recommend our best mattress guide for our top rated suggestions. But with $600 off in the Black Friday mattress sales, there has never been a better time to shop the Orion.

I've never seen a bigger price drop from Orion, as this massive $600 off sale takes a queen down to just $1,795 (was $2,395). That's an impressive price for a smart mattress cover with active temperature regulation, particularly as there are no hidden costs (a sleep tracking subscription is optional at $250/year). The extras are average for this type of sleep tech, with a 30-night trial and 2-year warranty.

When we review any mattress, temperature regulation is a key concern. It refers to how well a mattress can kick out excess heat so you don't wake up at 3 a.m. feeling uncomfortably sweaty.

Most of the best mattresses in a box achieve this through cooling materials. That is, copper-infused foams or phase change material (PCM).

The Orion takes a different approach. This smart mattress cover is fitted with a series of water tubes, which connect back to a control hub. During the night, the water flowing through those pipes either cools down or warms up, so you stay at just the right temperature.

And this sci-fi-esque sleep system is impressively effective. I purposely warmed myself up to see if the cooling kicked in (the only time you'll ever catch me doing nighttime jumping jacks) and was greeted by a flush of coolness. For hot flashes and night sweats, this is a dream.

Most of the time, however, the Orion delivers the kind of comfort you hardly notice. It's climbing into a bed that feels just right, sleeping through the night, and waking up feeling snug all the way down to your toes.

While the temperature regulation impressed me, I was less enthused by the Orion's sleep tracking. At $250 extra for a year's subscription, I think you can get better results for less with the Fitbit Air or Withings Sleep Analyzer. Or, for cooling and tracking, there's another solution...

I'm currently testing the Eight Sleep Pod 6, which uses water to cool and heat your mattress to just the right temperature. It's more expensive than the Orion — although you can save up to $200 in the pre-Black Friday sale and get a queen for $2,699 (was $2,899) — but the integrated sleep tracking is accurate and intuitive, delivering detailed insight into your rest. A subscription is required and starts from $17/month.

#3209. Today’s macOS updates fix security gap involving eMudhra certificates

Apple today released macOS updates that address a security gap involving compromised eMudhra certificates, after initially blocking them in Safari, Mail, and other apps in October. Here are the details.

A few weeks ago, Mozilla reported that private keys of eight intermediate certificate authorities operated by eMudhra, an Indian digital certification company, had been compromised.

In essence, these certificates are used to establish trust in digital certificates that verify website identities and enable secure connections.

With access to the compromised private keys, bad actors could potentially create fraudulent certificates that appear legitimate, allowing them to impersonate websites and intercept sensitive user information.

In response to the compromise, Apple began automatically blocking the affected certificates on October 19, followed by additional protections on October 23.

These changes were delivered through automatic certificate configuration updates, meaning users didn’t need to install a macOS update to be protected.

While these measures protected Safari, Mail, and apps that use Apple’s networking and security frameworks, they didn’t cover all of macOS, as certain command-line tools, including curl and git, could still accept the compromised certificates.

At the time, Apple published a support article with instructions for administrators to manually address this remaining security gap, while promising a fix in a future macOS update.

Today, Apple updated the document to confirm that the fix is now available.

As Apple explains, macOS 27.2.1, macOS 26.7.3, and macOS 15.8.3, released earlier today, prevent the affected command-line tools from accepting the compromised certificates, eliminating the need for administrators to manually address the issue.

The updates also remove five root CA certificates from /etc/ssl/cert.pem, including three additional eMudhra certificates that weren’t part of Apple’s original manual workaround.

Still, for users who are unable to install the latest macOS updates, Apple continues to provide instructions for manually addressing the issue in its support document, along with the names and SHA-256 fingerprints of the 12 affected certificates and five root CA certificates removed by the updates.

Apple also notes that “some apps and tools include their own list of root CA certificates and don’t use Apple’s block or /etc/ssl/cert.pem,” and advises users to contact the developer of those apps and tools.

#3208. Ohio State and Microsoft sign a five-year AI and cloud hospital deal

The deal expands AI note-taking for doctors and aims to shift up to 80% of the university's computing to Azure.

Ohio State and Microsoft signed a five-year AI and cloud partnership.

Ohio State University and Microsoft signed a five-year partnership to move up to 80% of the university’s storage and computing to Azure, expand AI note-drafting at its Wexner Medical Center and build “smart hospital” systems. No financial terms were disclosed.

Ohio State University and Microsoft have signed a five-year deal to bring more AI and cloud computing into the university’s Wexner Medical Center, Microsoft said on Tuesday. Neither side disclosed financial terms.

The biggest shift is in infrastructure. Ohio State aims to move 70% to 80% of its storage and computing to Microsoft’s Azure cloud, including pathology and medical imaging. It will also keep a backup of its electronic health records on Azure, so staff can still reach them if its own systems fail.

Doctors already use Microsoft’s Dragon Copilot to draft notes from patient visits, which they then check and sign off. Such AI scribes can still make serious errors, as NHS records showed this year.

Other parts are earlier. Two Ohio State buildings run a “smart hospital” system that links building and clinical equipment to save energy. A shared data platform for forecasting things like surgery demand and staffing is still at the design stage, and an AI tool for cancer case reviews is only being explored.

“Artificial intelligence represents one of the most significant opportunities to transform and improve how hospitals care for patients,” said John J. Warner, the medical centre’s chief executive.

Big tech firms are racing to sell AI to health systems. NHS England is rolling out Microsoft’s Copilot to 505,000 staff, and Google Cloud launched Gemini for healthcare on the same day as the Ohio State deal. Amazon’s AWS also unveiled a $100M health programme.

#3207. Apple Intelligence completes regulatory registration for iPad and Mac in China

Apple has completed an important regulatory step ahead of Apple Intelligence’s expected launch in China this December. Here are the details.

In late October, Apple published a press release on its Chinese Newsroom website confirming its intention to launch Apple Intelligence in China this December, as part of iOS 27.3.

Apple went on to release the first iOS 27.3 developer beta a few days later, allowing users in China to test Apple Intelligence ahead of its public launch.

In its press release, however, Apple also noted that the initial rollout would be limited to iPhones, as support for other platforms was still pending regulatory approval.

Now, as spotted by Reuters, Apple Intelligence “has been ‌registered for use on tablets and laptops in China, Shanghai’s cyberspace regulator said on Monday.”

For context, generative AI services must complete a regulatory registration process before they can launch publicly in China.

Apple Intelligence, which, in China, relies on Alibaba’s Qwen model to power certain AI features, had already received regulatory approval for iPhones in July, following months of delays and negotiations with Chinese authorities.

With today’s registration, Apple has cleared another regulatory hurdle ahead of Apple Intelligence’s launch in China. However, the company has yet to confirm whether iPad and Mac support will also arrive in December.

Electronic products now pack circuits, structures, thermal paths, and packaging into very small spaces. These physical domains interact with one another. A packaging choice can change how a shock load reaches a circuit board. Such interactions are hard to predict. Most are found during physical qualification, late in development. At that stage, the design is mostly fixed. A failure leads to redesign, rebuilds, and retesting. Physical tests give strong evidence of robustness, but they give limited insight into load paths and failure margins. Traditional simulation gives more detail, but it needs specialist skills and long manual setup. This white paper explains how guided virtual validation brings shock and drop assessment into the design phase. It reviews common test configurations, model inputs, and acceptance criteria. A packaged drop case study then shows how packaging can be optimized across all drop orientations and checked against physical test results.

#3204. Nvidia says it cut off Megaspeed in 2025, but Bloomberg found later imports

Bloomberg also found that Nvidia’s count of Megaspeed chips sold through partners ran 50,000 short. Nvidia’s lawyer had called a top Commerce official about Alice Huang’s detention in Singapore.

Nvidia says it banned all sales and shipments to Megaspeed in June 2025, and that the ban is still in place, a company spokesman told The Wall Street Journal. Since then, Commerce has allowed Nvidia to send it parts and replacement components, the spokesman said.

Malaysian trade records show that Megaspeed imported at least 17,544 of Nvidia’s GB300 chips, worth about $787m, in November 2025, Mackenzie Hawkins reported for Bloomberg. Nvidia gave US officials a count of chips sold to Megaspeed through hardware partners. It was 50,000 units short, Bloomberg found. Megaspeed is still an official Nvidia Cloud Partner. TNW has not independently verified the reports.

Megaspeed is the Singapore company at the centre of the Jensen Huang affair. Nvidia’s board opened an independent investigation after Huang admitted an affair with Alice Huang, a Megaspeed executive. US officials believe she is a Chinese intelligence asset. China has denied the espionage claims.

In mid-November 2025, Nvidia told Bloomberg that its inventory checks found everything where it should be. It also said it had asked the US government whether it needed to cut off Megaspeed, and was told no.

In December 2025, Nvidia told Bloomberg it had checked more warehouses that held the missing hardware. It did not say how many chips it found. Two of the eight data centre operators Nvidia told Washington it had visited said they had no Megaspeed hardware. Nvidia declined to comment on that to Bloomberg. Megaspeed’s largest landlord has since dropped it as a tenant.

About three months ago, Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter told a White House official that Alice Huang was “not as important” in Megaspeed as she made out, according to a person familiar with the call. He said that, because of the bad publicity around her, Nvidia had stopped doing business with Megaspeed.

In late summer 2025, Teter called Jeffrey Kessler, the Commerce under secretary in charge of chip export curbs. He asked whether Kessler’s Bureau of Industry and Security had a role in Singapore’s detention of Alice Huang. It did not, people familiar with the matter told Bloomberg. An Nvidia spokesperson said Teter did not know about the affair at the time.

It is unclear whether Teter made any specific requests of Kessler, according to Bloomberg. In the following weeks, bureau staff were told to route all requests of Nvidia through Kessler or get his approval. The people called that highly unusual, and unique to Nvidia. Staff were also told not to name Megaspeed or Speedmatrix, its Malaysian subsidiary, in external communications.

In late 2025, the Justice Department, which was working on the Megaspeed smuggling case with the bureau, asked it to pause. The bureau has made no progress since, despite having enough evidence to move forward, Bloomberg reported.

“BIS conducts all enforcement strictly by the book,” a bureau spokesman said.

“We work to resolve any allegations of ‘diversion’ promptly, to help government and our partners halt any would-be smugglers while serving the critical market of lawful customers that help America win worldwide,” an Nvidia spokesperson told Bloomberg.

In December 2023, Jensen Huang and a small group of colleagues met Alice Huang at an Italian restaurant in Singapore, according to The New York Times. She had just restructured Megaspeed. Four days after its ownership change, Nvidia named it a cloud partner, the Times reported on Tuesday.

Megaspeed went on to secure more than $4bn of Nvidia chips. In late 2024, the Commerce Department sent an official to inspect one of its data centres, where some Nvidia equipment was still packed in boxes. That year, Taiwan began monitoring Alice Huang’s trips to the island at the suggestion of the US government, a person familiar with the matter told the Times.

In 2025, Singapore barred her from leaving and questioned her in a probe into false import declarations. The investigations against her were closed for lack of evidence, the person said, but Singapore is still investigating Megaspeed. She later flew to Shanghai.

Megaspeed has categorically denied the chip diversion allegations. It told Bloomberg that Singapore’s probe ended this year with no adverse action against it. Its outreach to the US government went unanswered, it said. Nvidia and Megaspeed declined to comment to the Times. Alice Huang did not respond to the Times, and Bloomberg has been unable to reach her.

Senators Jim Banks, a Republican, and Elizabeth Warren, a Democrat, urged Commerce to suspend or reconsider Nvidia’s China export licences, Bloomberg reported. Their bill would temporarily bar Nvidia from selling Chinese customers any chip more advanced than the H200. Lawmakers are negotiating to add it to the annual defence bill, which typically passes in December.

“I think we’re going to work hard to make sure that those provisions make it into the final version of the National Defense Authorization Act,” House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said.

Senator Richard Blumenthal wants a Senate investigation, Semafor reported. In the House, three committee chairs have asked Huang to attend a closed briefing on 18 November.

#3203. Enbridge vs. Occidental Petroleum: Does a Midstream or Upstream Energy Focus Make for a Better Stock Buy for 2027?

Enbridge's revenue surged 22% while Occidental's fell, yet one trades at a fraction of the other's valuation multiple, a gap that may not last.

Investors choosing between infrastructure stability and production growth face a difficult decision in today's energy market. Choosing between Enbridge Inc. (ENB +0.76%) and Occidental Petroleum Corp. (OXY +2.04%) requires weighing steady dividends against commodity price exposure.

Enbridge operates as a midstream giant and utility provider, focusing on the safe movement of energy across North America. Occidental Petroleum specializes in the exploration and production of oil and gas, with a growing focus on carbon capture technologies. These two companies offer different ways to gain exposure to the energy sector based on your risk tolerance.

Enbridge is a leader in North American energy delivery, moving crude oil and natural gas through an extensive pipeline network. The company serves roughly 7.1 million gas customers and operates significant utility networks in both Canada and the United States. Its operations support critical infrastructure, including Gulf Coast export markets and partnerships with utilities like Duke Energy (DUK +0.66%).

In FY 2025, revenue reached $46.6 billion, representing a significant increase from the $38.2 billion reported in the previous year. Net income for the period was $5.4 billion, which improved from $3.9 billion in FY 2024. This growth shows the ability of the company to expand its earnings through its diversified energy delivery segments and growing asset base.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was 1.7x. This metric measures total debt relative to shareholder equity, indicating how much the company relies on borrowed funds for its capital structure. The current ratio was 0.5x, measuring short-term liquidity, and the company generated free cash flow of $2.2 billion for the year.

Occidental Petroleum operates as an international energy company with a focus on oil and natural gas exploration across the Permian Basin and the Middle East. It provides essential energy products to global refiners and utilizes midstream services through investments like Western Midstream Partners (WES +0.34%). The company is also expanding its presence among renewable energy stocks through its specialized carbon capture and storage initiatives.

In FY 2025, revenue reached $21.6 billion, a slight decrease from $22.0 billion in 2024. Net income for the fiscal year was $2.4 billion, down from $3.0 billion in the prior year. These results reflect the impact of changing market conditions on production earnings and a slight decline in overall revenue growth during the period.

Based on the December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was 0.7x. This figure helps investors see the balance between total debt and shareholder equity. The company maintained a current ratio of 0.9x, measuring its ability to cover short-term liabilities, and generated about $4.1 billion in free cash flow, providing significant liquidity for its operations.

Enbridge faces risks related to its extensive physical infrastructure. High exposure to catastrophic incidents, such as pipeline ruptures or leaks, remains a primary concern because of its aging assets and severe weather events. Additionally, the company must navigate intense regulatory scrutiny and evolving permitting hurdles for its large infrastructure projects.

Occidental Petroleum is highly sensitive to fluctuations in global commodity prices, which can lead to significant asset impairments if oil prices drop. The company also deals with operational hazards inherent in offshore drilling, including potential spills and seismic activity. Furthermore, high levels of debt may limit its financial flexibility and increase its vulnerability to changes in its credit rating.

Occidental Petroleum trades at a significantly lower multiple of its future earnings estimates than Enbridge does, though Enbridge trades at a lower multiple relative to its trailing sales.

Valuation metrics include those sourced from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from those of other data providers.

The Iran war has been good business for Occidental Petroleum. The American oil giant benefits far more greatly from the spike in world oil prices than the Gulf War harms it. That's because Oxy, as it is colloquially known, produces most (about 83%) of its oil in the United States, so it collects the higher price for oil that is set worldwide, with little of the higher costs or risks stemming from the Iran war.

Still, Wall Street sees Oxy as more problematic than other oil giants, because the business isn't growing its production volume as quickly as rivals, which means the business is more reliant on elevated energy prices to maintain its revenue and income levels. The business is also saddled with a good bit of debt, while Berkshire Hathaway (BRKA +2.60%)controls a lot of preferred equity, the support of which ties up some of Oxy's cash flow.

Wall Street sees revenues rising about 25% in 2026, to $27.8 billion--but that is slower than a lot of U.S. oil majors. Still, net income will more than triple to $7 billion, reflecting the higher prices and lack of higher costs for U.S. sourced oil due to the Iran war.

While midstream businesses are less volatile than other segments of the energy industry, there is a downside: Enbridge doesn't benefit directly from the spike in oil prices since the Trump administration launched its war on Iran in February. That's because, as a pipeline operator, nearly all of its capacity is sold in fixed-rate contracts. That is the downside to the "toll-road" model of a midstream energy business. That said, its expansion of capacity and recent acquisition of Tallgrass have the business set up for a fine 2026. Wall Street sees sales rising 25% to $81.5 billion this year, but with a slump in net income of about $1 billion to $6.1 billion. It is a stable dividend payer with a forward annual dividend rate of 5.8% at today's stock price.

So which energy giant is the stock to buy? Oxy looks cheap based on P/S and P/E ratios, but Enbridge's combination of less volatility in revenue and income and its juicy dividend yield makes it the choice for long-term investors.

#3202. Canadian court certifies class action against Apple over Google search deal

A British Columbia Supreme Court judge has certified a class action against Apple over allegations that its search agreement with Google stifled competition and inflated advertising prices. Here are the details.

In recent years, Apple’s deal with Alphabet to make Google the default search engine on Safari has drawn regulatory attention in the US, the UK, and Australia, while related search competition concerns have also come under scrutiny in the EU and Japan.

While the details of each investigation differ, they all raise concerns about the impact of Google’s dominance in search, as well as the extent to which its agreements with other companies might be limiting competition.

More recently, Apple’s agreement with Google received significant attention during the US Department of Justice’s antitrust case against the search giant, which included testimony from Apple executives Eddy Cue and John Giannandrea. The latter joined Apple from Google in 2018 and led its AI efforts until stepping down earlier this year.

As a result of the US case, a federal judge ruled in August 2024 that Google had illegally maintained its monopoly in online search through anticompetitive agreements, including its deal with Apple.

Now, evidence presented during that trial has become central to a class action against Apple in Canada, which a British Columbia Supreme Court judge recently certified.

The case was initially brought in 2021 by Spark Event Rentals Ltd., an event rental company based in British Columbia. The plaintiff alleged that Apple and Google conspired to limit competition in the search market, allowing Google to charge advertisers artificially inflated prices.

Apple, meanwhile, argued that its agreement with Google was a legitimate distribution arrangement rather than an unlawful conspiracy. The company also maintained that Google was the appropriate defendant, describing itself as an “innocent bystander.”

Interestingly, the lawsuit originally named both Apple and Google as defendants, but the plaintiff later dropped Google from the case following a dispute over an arbitration clause in its advertising contracts.

With Apple now the sole defendant, Justice Thomas has allowed the case to proceed as a class action, finding sufficient grounds to examine whether Google’s payments discouraged Apple from developing its own search engine.

The lawsuit seeks financial compensation for advertisers who allegedly overpaid for Google search ads, and the court has also allowed the question of punitive damages to proceed.

The class action covers Canadian residents who purchased search ads from Google since 2005, when Apple and Google first agreed to make Google the default search engine on Safari in exchange for a share of advertising revenue.

Importantly, the ruling does not establish that Apple engaged in anticompetitive conduct, but simply allows the allegations to proceed as a class action.

The central proposition raised by these pleadings is that Apple could have used its resources and distribution network to enter the search engine market, but chose not to because Google paid Apple billions of dollars in revenue-share payments to make Google the default search provider on Apple products. This arrangement gave Google market power, enabling it to charge supracompetitive advertising prices on search engines.

In my view, this pleads a common purpose to perform an act prohibited by s 45 of the Competition Act, such that it is not “clear and obvious” that the plaintiff has not pleaded an agreement between Google and Apple not to compete in the search engine market.

At one point in his decision, Justice Thomas cites Giannandrea’s testimony and directly quotes Cue’s from the US antitrust trial, before concluding that “this provides some basis in fact, supporting the inference that Apple did not compete with Google in the search engine market because of its Agreement with Google.”

Interestingly, the judge also acknowledges Apple’s objections to the evidence, agreeing that “the plaintiff has cherry-picked evidence to support his case,” but adding that, in his view, “it is appropriate to do so at this stage in the proceedings.”

With the class action greenlit, the case can now move forward toward trial, though no date has been announced yet.
