I live in one of the most densely populated states in the country, but even with New Jersey’s small size, there are still dead zones lurking around. Google Fi is tackling this persistent problem in 2026 with the rollout of its new "super network," which is designed to automatically switch between two 5G cellular networks in real time.

Google Fi’s "super network" switching is powered by Multiple Enabled Profiles (MEP) eSIM technology, which essentially allows a single physical eSIM to run two carrier profiles at the same time. Instead of treating the second connection as an inactive backup, the phone maintains active links to two separate cellular 5G networks. Therefore, if the signal degrades — whether due to congestion, tower interference, or physical obstacles — Google Fi's software automatically switches over to the secondary connection to prevent dropouts. It directly tackles the dead zones that cause reels to buffer or download speeds to crater.

While Google’s announcement doesn’t explicitly name which carriers it's partnering with to pull this off — choosing instead to label them simply as "two of America's fastest 5G networks" — there are plenty of clues. T-Mobile remains Google Fi’s primary host carrier, while the secondary partner providing the dual-coverage failover is described in as a "major carrier," defined as an "MNO or MVNO with more than 1 million customers in the U.S. as of March 2025."

Even the strongest cellular signal can struggle inside crowded spaces like airport terminals, shopping malls, and dense high-rises. That’s where Wi-Fi Auto-Connect+ steps in to supplement coverage by automatically identifying and linking your phone to high-quality public Wi-Fi networks. It does this without requiring manual logins, portal verifications, or toggling Wi-Fi menus, keeping the handoff completely seamless.

Google Fi is carrying the super network abroad as well, enabling real-time network switching and Wi-Fi Auto-Connect+ across international travel destinations. By pairing dual-carrier 5G failover on the road with automated Wi-Fi in crowded venues, Google Fi makes staying reliably connected practically effortless no matter where you travel.

#3200. Web Summit cancels Day 2 in Lisbon as Storm Charles hits Portugal

Portugal’s government advised Web Summit that Wednesday should not go ahead, citing flooding, transport disruption and high winds. The organisers aim to reopen on Thursday for the final day.

Web Summit’s main stage in Lisbon in November 2025

Web Summit has called off Wednesday’s programme in Lisbon because of Storm Charles. Portugal’s government advised the organisers that Day 2 should not take place. Web Summit told attendees by email on Tuesday evening that it aims to hold Day 3, on Thursday 12 November, as planned.

The government cited the risk of tidal flooding and severe disruption to public transport. It also pointed to the effect of high winds on outdoor structures, Web Summit said. The advice followed talks with the civil protection authority, ANEPC, and the Public Security Police (PSP).

“The safety and security of our attendees, staff and contractors is always our absolute priority,” the Web Summit team wrote.

Web Summit said it will keep working with the authorities and emergency services. It will contact those affected directly.

Earlier on Tuesday, Lisbon mayor Carlos Moedas said “everything indicates” the event could not run on Wednesday. Stephen Conneely reported his comments for The Irish Times. Moedas said more than 60,000 people were at the venue in Parque das Nações.

The government has declared a state of alert across mainland Portugal for Wednesday, The Portugal News reported. Schools and non-essential public services will close. Lisbon is shutting its tunnels, parks, gardens and cultural venues from midnight. The weather service IPMA forecast gusts of up to 120km/h.

Web Summit runs from 9 to 12 November. Last month, it released its tech industry survey. In it, 60% of people in tech said AI had increased their workload.

#3198. Instagram Effect Builder lets you create images with an AI prompt

Instagram launched an Edits app for iPhone back in 2025, with a Mac version introduced just a few days ago. Meta has now supplemented this with an AI-powered Instagram Effect Builder, letting users create imagery for Stories simply by describing what they want to see …

Instagram Edits is a free video editing app available for both iPhone and Mac. As you’d expect, the latter is the more powerful version, offering a larger workspace, more precise editing controls, and customizable keyboard shortcuts. Notably, the app supports multiple aspect ratios and allows exports as well as uploads, so can be used to produce video for any platform, not just Instagram.

Meta has now launched Instagram Effect Builder to create AI imagery for use in Instagram Stories. While it’s a standalone web-based tool, the company is describing it as an expansion of the Edits app.

One quirk is that any effect you create becomes available to any Instagram user. This usage will, however, link back to your profile.

Today, we’re expanding what you can create with Edits and introducing a new way to share your creativity on Instagram […] With Effect Builder, you don’t need design or coding skills, or prior experience making effects. Describe the look you want, preview it on your own photos, and publish. The effect shows up in Instagram Stories for anyone to use, and whenever someone uses your effect we’ll link back to your profile so that it’s easy for others to find your work.

The web app is currently limited to adult Instagram users in the US.

#3197. Ranger Energy (RNGR) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Ranger held firm on pricing while cost inflation and activity gaps squeezed margins.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Ranger Energy Services, Inc. (RNGR -9.78%) reported third-quarter results that reflected a transition toward higher-specification assets and technological differentiation despite navigating a period of customer budget exhaustion and competitive pricing pressures. Management stated that the company successfully eliminated all net debt associated with its prior acquisition of American Well Services while simultaneously funding the $27.5 million acquisition of STEP U.S. coiled tubing assets. This acquisition expands the company's operational footprint from a single-basin business into a multi-basin provider with specialized technology for long-lateral wells. While sequential revenue and margins were compressed by inflationary costs and activity gaps, the company maintained its pricing discipline and continued to build its hybrid electric fleet. Management confirmed that it remains focused on achieving a target of $100 million in annualized adjusted EBITDA supported by the integration of new assets and the continued delivery of contracted workover rigs through 2027.

Operator: Good morning, and welcome to the Ranger Energy Services' Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Conference Call. [Operator Instructions] Please note, this event is being recorded. I would now like to turn the conference over to Joe Mease, Vice President of Finance. Please go ahead.

Joe Mease: Good morning, and thank you for joining Ranger Energy Services' Third Quarter 2026 Results Conference Call. Before we begin, Ranger has issued a press release outlining our operational and financial performance for the quarter ended September 30, 2026. This press release, along with our most recent investor presentation, is available in the Investor Relations section of our website at www.rangerenergy.com. Today's discussion may contain forward-looking statements about future business and financial expectations. Actual results may differ significantly from those projected in today's forward-looking statements due to various risks and uncertainties, including the risks described in our periodic reports filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission. Except as required by law, we undertake no obligation to update our forward-looking statements.

Factors that could cause actual results to differ include, but are not limited to, changes in crude oil and natural gas prices, customer activity levels, operating risks, competitive pressures, weather conditions, integration risks related to acquisitions and other risks as described in our filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission. We will also reference certain non-GAAP financial measures during today's call, including adjusted EBITDA and free cash flow. Reconciliations of these measures to the most directly comparable GAAP financial measures are included in our earnings release. Joining me on the call today are Stuart Bodden, our Chief Executive Officer; and Melissa Cougle, our Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer.

Stuart will begin with an overview of the quarter and our strategic progress, including the completion of the STEP coiled tubing acquisition and the continued build-out of our ECHO rig fleet. Melissa will then walk through our third quarter financial results in more detail. Following their remarks, we'll open the call for questions. With that, I'll turn it over to Stuart.

Stuart Bodden: Thank you, Joe, and good morning, everyone. We appreciate you joining us today. Consistent execution and steady progress define Ranger. And this quarter, we continued to deliver against our strategic goals. Most notably, we completed the acquisition of the STEP U.S. coiled tubing assets, making Ranger the second largest coiled tubing provider in the Lower 48. In addition to this transaction, Chevron committed to 4 additional ECHO hybrid electric workover rigs, which will take our contracted ECHO rig fleet to 24 rigs by the end of 2027.

Finally, strong cash generation allowed us to fully repay the revolver borrowings from our American Well Services acquisition, allowing us to exit the quarter with 0 net debt less than a year after closing that transaction. This progress was a result of intentional and consistent effort from the organization that continues to strengthen Ranger as we approach 2027. I firmly believe Ranger has more ways to grow today than at any point in our history. First, a few words about the quarter itself. Ranger generated revenue of $162.8 million and adjusted EBITDA of $20.1 million in the third quarter, results that were softer than we expected.

Customers managed their budgets more closely, smaller competitors lowered price to win back work, and we absorbed cost inflation across several cost categories, the largest being an incremental $1.5 million in employee medical costs compared to the second quarter. Considerable time has been spent recently with our operating teams, evaluating ways to improve utilization and margins, and many of those efforts are already in flight. Melissa will walk through some additional color in the segment detail. Cash generation, however, remains strong. Ranger produced $20 million of free cash flow in the third quarter, which allowed us to fully repay our revolver borrowings while continuing to return capital to shareholders and giving us capacity to complete the STEP acquisition.

Now let me turn to the STEP asset acquisition, which we closed on October 8. I want to first welcome our new professionals to Ranger. The STEP team has earned a strong reputation for technical execution, service quality and solving customers' most challenging drill-out applications safely and reliably, and they are a tremendous addition to our organization. This transaction does 3 important things for Ranger. First, it gives our coiled tubing business scale. We have long been proud of our coiled tubing operation in the North, but it was a single-basin business. And in coiled tubing, scale drives utilization and returns.

STEP adds 13 coiled tubing units operating from the Bakken through South Texas with its largest presence in the Permian Basin, right alongside our high-spec rig fleet. We are now a multi-basin coiled tubing provider in the U.S. coiled tubing market estimated at $1.5 billion annually. Second, it gives us differentiated technology. The COIL+ Extended Reach Technology has helped operators successfully reach total depth on more than 60 long lateral wells with its deepest well exceeding 30,000 feet.

As laterals get longer, that capability lets us compete for the most demanding work in our basins, and it gives customers real flexibility in their drill-out programs because Ranger can now offer either a coiled tubing unit or a high-spec rig for the job. Third, it creates pull-through. The overlap between STEP's customers and our own is significant and a larger coiled tubing business lets us provide more services and equipment to those customers across more of their wells. We acquired these assets for approximately $27.5 million, and we expect STEP's coiled tubing assets to contribute more than $10 million of adjusted EBITDA in 2027 with significant further upside expected in 2028.

That is a compelling valuation for a business of this quality and exactly the kind of targeted M&A that continues to set Ranger apart. We are adding shareholder value at attractive prices in businesses we know well. Turning to ECHO. During the quarter, we were awarded contracts for 4 additional ECHO rigs. This represents additional expansion of our ECHO relationship with Chevron this year following the rigs committed to earlier in the year, and it will bring our total contracted fleet to 24 rigs by the end of 2027. Repeat orders from an operator of this caliber are the strongest validation of this technology we could possibly ask for. The ECHO Build program is also running slightly ahead of schedule.

5 ECHO rigs have been delivered through the third quarter with the balance of the fleet scheduled for delivery through the third quarter of 2027. Customer feedback has been positive, reinforcing both the efficiency of operations and the enhanced safety ECHO brings to location, and our current customer conversations point to additional rig commitments in the future. We are beginning to track safety and operational performance on these rigs and feel over time, their value proposition will become increasingly evident in the data, driving further demand. Importantly, ECHO represents growth where our customers are investing alongside Ranger. Our agreements include upfront customer payments or day rate premiums that support returns on the capital we invest.

And as ECHO's efficiency gains are solidified, we expect the fleet to help push down overall service costs for our customers. That is a powerful combination in a market where operators are looking to do more with less. We have also now passed the 1-year mark since closing AWS. We have realized approximately $5.2 million of annualized cost synergies ahead of the $5 million we targeted, and we have fully repaid the borrowings used to fund the transaction. The acquired high-specification rigs have largely tracked our expectations. While some of the ancillary service lines, particularly transportation, mixing plants and tubing inspection underperformed during the third quarter.

We have taken several operational steps to reorganize those operations to improve accountability, utilization and profitability. In high-specification rigs, customers managed their spending more closely in the third quarter, creating incremental white space across our fleet. At the same time, as Ranger has gained share through operator consolidation, smaller displaced competitors have offered price reductions to regain work and some budget-constrained customers took advantage of those savings. We have held our pricing discipline, which allows us to maintain our standards for safety and service quality, and we expect that decision to pay off as the market normalizes and budgets reset next year.

Elsewhere, our legacy rentals and plugging and abandonment service lines continue to perform well, with P&A supported by an expanding and steady base of work from the Texas Railroad Commission. Our Wireline segment performed as we expected with the breaks in customer well programs. The team managed the activity decline with timely cost reductions, demonstrating the progress made in creating a more responsive cost structure. New work programs began in October, and we believe that the fourth quarter will provide improvement from this quarter. Stepping back, crude prices moved sharply higher during the third quarter and U.S. production and land drilling activity continued to grow.

Although commodity prices have recently retreated somewhat, we believe Ranger's production-focused services, which deliver the fastest and lowest cost incremental barrels from existing wells are well positioned as our customers' budgets reset. As we head into 2027, we have a fast-growing ECHO fleet and expanded coiled tubing platform, reorganized ancillary service lines and a wireline segment that has shown its resilience. The moat is deeper now than it has ever been, and we remain focused on our goal of achieving $100 million of annualized adjusted EBITDA supported by these initiatives. With that, I'll turn the call over to Melissa.

Melissa Cougle: Thank you, Stuart, and good morning, everyone. I'll walk through our third quarter results in more detail with a particular focus on drivers and then cover cash flow, the balance sheet and capital allocation. Revenue for the third quarter was $162.8 million, a decrease of $13.7 million or 7.8% from $176.5 million in the second quarter and an increase of $33.9 million or 26.3% from $128.9 million in the third quarter of 2025. The sequential decrease reflects lower activity across our 3 segments, while the year-over-year increase reflects the contribution of the AWS business.

Net income was $2.5 million or $0.10 per diluted share compared to $6.9 million or $0.29 per diluted share in the second quarter and $1.2 million or $0.05 per diluted share in the third quarter of last year. Operating income in the quarter included a $3 million noncash benefit from a reduction in the contingent consideration related to the AWS acquisition. Adjusted EBITDA was $20.1 million, a 12.3% margin compared to $28.6 million and a 16.2% margin in the second quarter and a $16.8 million and a 13% margin in the third quarter of 2025.

Cost of services rose to 85% of revenue from approximately 81% of revenue in the second quarter, driven by 2 forces: lower activity, which created negative operating leverage against the cost base staffed for a busier quarter and higher costs, most significantly employee-related costs and fuel. The single largest contributor was employee medical costs across segments, which was $1.5 million higher than in the second quarter. General and administrative expense was $7.7 million, essentially flat with the second quarter, with both quarters including expenses related to the AWS integration and the STEP acquisition. Turning to High Specification Rigs.

Segment revenue was $110.5 million, a decrease of $2.9 million or 2.6% from $113.4 million in the second quarter and an increase of $29.6 million or 36.6% from $80.9 million a year ago. Rig hours were 143,500 hours, down 2% sequentially from 146,800 hours in the second quarter and up 29% year-over-year from 111,200 hours in the third quarter of 2025. Our average hourly rig rate was $770, essentially flat with $772 in the second quarter and up 6% from $727 a year ago, largely reflecting the pass-through of fuel surcharges and changes in asset and regional mix.

Segment adjusted EBITDA was $18.4 million compared to $20.6 million in the second quarter, and segment margins were 16.7%, down from 18.2% in the second quarter. With margins down roughly 150 basis points, I want to walk through a few drivers. The first was white space. Customers manage their spending more closely and operators laid down rigs for intermittent periods. A rig idle for a week still carries its crew and equipment costs, so even modest gaps in the schedule weighed disproportionately on margins. These were rig breaks that were not anticipated given the macro backdrop, but reflect budget exhaustion early in the year given the strong activity in the second quarter.

It is worth noting that our 24-hour rig activity increased about 6% sequentially as operators continued converting production work to around-the-clock operations, but that growth was more than offset by white space and rig releases, which brings me to our second driver. During the quarter, we contended with a couple of smaller new market entrants offering price reductions to win back lost share the past couple of years, particularly in the Permian Basin. A couple of key operators who are now budget constrained took advantage of those lower prices, which displaced a number of our daylight rigs. We made a deliberate decision not to follow pricing down.

That kept our rates stable, but it did cost us some activity in the quarter. The third was cost inflation. Labor and fuel costs both increased as a percent of revenue with employee expenses, including medical costs I mentioned and diesel prices running even higher this summer, deteriorating margins further. We are presently redeploying some of our displaced rigs with customers who have work available, restructuring some of our operations and working with key customers who see the value in Ranger differentiation on cost adjustments that reflect wage and fuel inflation. In Processing Solutions and Ancillary Services, segment revenue was $40 million, a decrease of $4.5 million or 10% from $44.5 million in the second quarter.

Segment adjusted EBITDA was $6.8 million compared to $10 million in the second quarter, and segment margins were 17% compared to 22.5% in the second quarter. Declines were attributable to a few service lines. Most notably, certain service lines we acquired through AWS, including transportation, mixing plants and tubing inspection saw significant declines in activity this quarter, which had a knock-on effect on margins. Torrent grew revenue on expanding contracts, but its results were affected by onetime charges, including legal fees, mobilization costs and unique rental charges, along with the loss of some higher-margin rentals. There were bright spots, though, with plug and abandonment as well as rental margins improving and reaching their highest level in the past several quarters.

In Wireline services, revenue was $12.3 million, an expected decrease of $6.3 million or 34% from $18.6 million in the second quarter. Our Wireline completion service line saw gaps in customer work schedules after the completion programs that drove our strong second quarter in closing. Segment adjusted EBITDA was $200,000 compared with $3.6 million in the second quarter. Turning to cash flow. Cash provided by operating activities was $30.5 million in the third quarter and $53.5 million year-to-date.

Free cash flow was $20 million for the quarter and year-to-date free cash flow was $18.3 million compared to $25.8 million over the same period in 2025, with the decrease primarily reflecting higher customer receivables resulting from a customer changing to 90-day payment terms, partially offset by internal efforts that have reduced our internal processing time. Capital expenditures were $10.5 million in the third quarter and $35.2 million year-to-date compared to $19.1 million over the same period in 2025, with approximately $16.8 million of this year's spend related to ECHO construction payments. Our ECHO contracts include upfront customer contributions, which we record as contract liabilities and recognize as revenue over the life of those contracts.

Short- and long-term contract liabilities totaled $19 million at the end of the quarter. As of September 30, we had no borrowings outstanding under our revolving credit facility and total liquidity was $76.2 million consisting of $70.2 million of revolver availability and $6 million of cash on hand, up from $61.3 million at the end of the second quarter. Paying down the outstanding borrowings this quarter means we fully repaid for the AWS acquisition within a year of closing. After quarter end, we funded the cash consideration for STEP with revolver borrowings, consistent with the plan we outlined when we announced the transaction.

Ranger expects to allocate the majority of its cash flows in the next several quarters to ECHO delivery payments and repayments on the borrowings used to fund the STEP acquisition. On the capital returns front, we repurchased 142,100 shares during the third quarter for $2.2 million at an average price of $15.74 per share. Since the inception of our repurchase program in 2023, we have repurchased approximately 4.8 million shares for $54.1 million at an average price of $11.31 per share. Year-to-date, we have returned $11.7 million to shareholders through repurchases and dividends or 64% of year-to-date free cash flow, well above our commitment to return at least 25%.

Our Board has also declared a quarterly cash dividend of $0.06 per share payable on December 4 to stockholders of record as of November 20. With that, I'll turn the call back over to Stuart for closing remarks.

Stuart Bodden: Thanks, Melissa. Before we open the line for questions, I want to leave you with a few thoughts. This quarter tested us, and our teams responded the way Ranger always does, by holding the line on safety, service quality and pricing discipline and by continuing to execute on the strategy that will drive our next phase of growth. That strategy is working. Within the span of a year, we have closed 2 acquisitions, AWS and now STEP at attractive prices, and we fully repaid the borrowings for the AWS transaction within a year of closing.

We are growing our contracted ECHO fleet to 24 rigs with conversations for additional rigs underway, and we have returned $11.7 million to our shareholders through share repurchases and dividends so far this year. I said earlier that Ranger has more ways to grow than at any point in our history. A fast-growing ECHO fleet, an expanded coiled tubing platform and a streamlined ancillary business with room to grow gives us more levers than we have ever had. I want to thank our professionals for their hard work and commitment this quarter and those who have recently joined the One Ranger family.

With a strong balance sheet and a consistent record of performance, we are confident in Ranger's ability to deliver durable long-term value. With that, operator, we can now open the line for questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] The first question is from Don Crist with Johnson Rice.

Donald Crist: I wanted to start with the STEP acquisition. I know you've only had it for a couple of weeks now and you're still integrating. But just the customer dynamic of having more flexibility to either use stick pipe or coil to drill out and do workovers with longer coil, et cetera. How are those conversations going? It seems like STEP was kind of underutilized for what they had in the U.S. And just how is that progressing as you've handled that last couple of weeks?

Stuart Bodden: Yes. Thanks for the question, Don. I think we're really encouraged by the conversations we've been having so far with customers. The Ranger coiled business was really a one-basin business. We were focused in the Rockies. And we had some of our biggest customers tell us they wish we were in multiple basins. And STEP obviously gives us that ability. And I'll just sort of say just the reputation that the STEP professionals have built around service quality, technology differentiation, et cetera. So we're pretty encouraged. It's kind of, as you said, early days.

I think we're a month and 2 days into it, but we feel like the customers have been really receptive to it and appreciate having the ability to either use stick pipe or coil kind of depending on the well profile.

Donald Crist: Okay. And I don't know if you really want to answer this question, but I'll ask it anyway. It seems like every couple of years, the market kind of ebbs and flows and tries to get cheaper services and then kind of goes back to more quality operators. And it sounds like that's kind of what happened in the third quarter. But how -- are you seeing customers kind of revert back to higher quality workover rig or coiled or wireline providers after going through a little bit of budget exhaustion in the third quarter and using some of the lower quality operators out there.

We've heard of a couple of accidents that have happened for low-quality operators and it seems like everything ebbs and flows over the past couple of years. But are you seeing people revert back now and kind of contract for next year?

Stuart Bodden: I think the honest answer, John, is that -- I mean, Don, is right now, I think it's too early to tell. As we said in the -- in my comments, we made a very conscious decision not to chase down that price. Our experience has been if you do that, it's almost impossible to get it back. And I think underpinning that is a belief that certainly the largest operators will stick with and go with the most reputable players. As far as the kind of shift back, right now, I think it's too early to say.

Donald Crist: Okay. Well, I fully believe that you'll gain more work going forward because it's better to be safe than to chase price. But that's just my opinion, and we'll leave it there.

Stuart Bodden: That assumption is correct.

Donald Crist: My last question -- yes, exactly. My last question is just on labor. Obviously, a lot of data centers and whatnot construction out there that seems to be a little bit more stable than oilfield work has drawn a lot of people away. Are you seeing any labor constraints or people leaving for other construction jobs out there?

Stuart Bodden: I think we feel like we are, Don. It doesn't feel like it's a full-blown labor crisis yet. But I think we do think that we are seeing the labor market tighten, and we expect it to continue into next year. So I think that's something we're pretty mindful of.

Operator: The next question is from Derek Podhaizer with Piper Sandler.

Derek Podhaizer: Just I guess maybe to kind of continue the conversation around losing some of the work to lower-priced competitors. And as Don mentioned, accidents, obviously, safety first and foremost. So what other challenges do you expect these customers to face going with lower price, lower quality work that would cause them to come back to Ranger next year when budgets reset? Just thinking through the operational challenges that E&Ps might face going to lower quality aside from safety and accidents, but what else should we think about that would bring back to these customers back to Ranger?

Stuart Bodden: I think what our experience has been, Derek, is I'd highlight a couple of things is, one is, out in the field, the company men get very attached to our tool pushers, our supervisors. And it is not uncommon for us to see the company men really start to raise a bit of a fuss and kind of ask for Ranger crews to come back. I think that's one thing. The second thing I would highlight, and it's related to safety, but is on inspections. So a lot of times, what we find is some of these smaller players aren't doing the proper inspections on their equipment.

And more than once, we've been in situations where we got a call and says, hey, you need to come out because we just did a spot inspection or a spot audit on a smaller player and the Derek, the blocks weren't properly inspected and we're not comfortable. So I would highlight that. It's -- we have certainly seen that historically as well. And then again, I think just the familiarity with our crews. We spent a lot of time and effort and money training our crews, and we feel like it really shows out in the field.

Derek Podhaizer: Got it. Okay. That's helpful color. And maybe just a bigger picture question, looking into 2027, just your initial views on it. Maybe you can kind of walk through the 3 different segments and what you expect to be some of the drivers as we go into next year and think about potential top line growth, margin expansion. You obviously have the couple of acquisitions getting up and running, but just more high level, big picture, just would love to get your initial views into next year.

Stuart Bodden: Yes. I think right now, we're -- we don't have kind of a firm view. There's obviously a lot of moving parts. But I think the things I would highlight were, obviously, we're encouraged, early days, but with the STEP acquisition, the asset acquisition, our ability to provide coil in multiple basins. I think that's something that we're pretty excited about. We've talked about ancillary some of the changes we're making to sort of drive more profitability and accountability. I think some of the things that we're kind of wrestling with right now, just as we think about next year, Derek, are we've talked about labor -- [Technical Difficulty] go up and ultimately from customers. I think that's one thing.

And just I'll kind of say the volatility in commodity pricing. We obviously seen a lot of volatility in the last week. So it's -- again, I think we're kind of cautiously optimistic, but I think it's kind of too early to just put firm numbers to anything.

Operator: The next question is from John Daniel with Daniel Energy Partners.

John Daniel: Stuart, hopefully you can hear me. I guess there's some background noise. But my question relates to the ECHO rig. I'm curious if you can characterize interest levels. Are they broadening yet? Or is it sort of the same 2 or 3 key customers coming back looking for more?

Stuart Bodden: Yes. It is starting to broaden. I think we're getting more people taking a look, hearing about it at conferences, et cetera. So again, we're not at the point where we have another customer that is contracted for one, but I would say it's fair to say that interest is growing for sure.

Operator: This concludes our question-and-answer session. I will now turn the conference back over to Stuart Bodden for any closing remarks.

Stuart Bodden: Thanks, operator, and thanks to everyone on the call. I appreciate your interest in Ranger and don't hesitate to reach out if you have any questions. Have a great week, everybody. Thank you.

#3196. Google DeepMind analysis proves Signal and WhatsApp encryption is secure

The Signal protocol has long been considered the gold standard for end-to-end encrypted messaging, with Edward Snowden a notable advocate. Now a Google DeepMind analysis has “formally verified” the security of the protocol.

In addition to its use in the Signal app, the same protocol is also used by WhatsApp and Google Messages, and the work has been described as “a landmark development” …

“Formal verification” is the term given to mathematically proving or disproving that a cryptographic algorithm or protocol satisfies its security claims under all conditions. It guarantees that there is no situation in which the protocol will fail. This is a far higher standard than traditional testing methods which seek to find vulnerabilities but cannot promise that others do not exist.

Using agentic AI to carry out formal verification is a huge breakthrough for cryptography and AI alike. It is, however, extremely computationally demanding, so Google told Wired it’s unclear as yet how practical it will be to use it more broadly.

DeepMind researchers emphasize that their findings are just one milestone in a larger process. “We are very excited by this result, but there is a long distance to go before we are able to scale this to all the software of the world, and we want to do that,” Swarat Chaudhuri, a DeepMind research scientist, tells WIRED.

It’s important to note that the validation is for the protocol itself rather than the Signal app as a whole. However, encouragement can be taken from the fact that when tested against older versions of Signal that contained known vulnerabilities, it identified those and flagged them as failing formal verification.

Also worth stating is that Google was able to build on some past formal verification work already completed without the use of AI. This analysis took four weeks, and the scale of resources required has not yet been disclosed, so we shouldn’t expect a whole array of other protocols to be validated overnight. All the same, this is a very big deal.

#3195. Mercedes’ US fast-charging network hits 100 sites in three years

Its 400 kW network hit 100 sites in North America, while its European hubs went to Electra.

Electric Mercedes-Benz cars at one of the carmaker’s high-power charging hubs in the US.

Mercedes-Benz’s US fast-charging network has reached 100 sites and nearly 1,000 ports in three years, with more than 550,000 sessions. The milestone comes a week after Mercedes sold its 47 European charging hubs to France’s Electra.

Mercedes-Benz’s fast-charging network in North America has reached 100 sites three years after opening its first station, InsideEVs reported. The milestone comes a week after the carmaker sold its European network.

The network now has nearly 1,000 charging points across 28 US states and British Columbia, all able to deliver up to 400 kW. Mercedes says they have handled more than 550,000 sessions for over 245,000 drivers since November 2023. Almost every site has both the older CCS plug and Tesla’s NACS plug, now standard on most new EVs.

Mercedes says its chargers are almost never down. It now focuses on how often a session starts at the first try, which rose from about 84% in 2023 to more than 90%.

Charging costs $0.35 to $0.60 per kWh, depending on the site, which are often near upmarket shopping centres. The largest, in Orlando, Florida, has 20 stalls.

Europe has gone the other way. Last week, Mercedes handed its 47 European charging hubs to French operator Electra, calling the business outside its core, Electrive reported. The US network stays “for the time being.”

Mercedes is also one of eight carmakers behind IONNA, a separate US charging network that has passed 180 sites. The US now has more than 80,000 fast-charging ports in total. US EV sales, meanwhile, remain about 40% below last year’s levels.

#3193. Apple Maps could soon factor in how long it takes you to park

On some journeys in busy cities, it feels like it can take you longer to park than it does to drive there in the first place. Code spotted in iOS 27.3 suggests that Apple Maps may soon factor in parking time when it provides journey ETAs.

Separately, Waze has partnered with Garmin to help improve the safety of cyclists by using real-time location tracking to alert nearby drivers …

Currently, the estimated time of arrival shown in Apple Maps only measures how long it will take you to drive to your destination. The door-to-door time can be significantly longer if it’s going to take time to park and then walk from the parking spot to the final destination.

Code sleuth pdfu has spotted a strong indication that Apple is working on the problem.

Apple may be working on parking-aware ETAs.iOS 27.3 adds a TimeToPark flag. When enabled, CoreRoutine uses background location and motion data to measure how long you spent near your destination before parking, and how long you walked afterwards. It saves both metrics per trip,… pic.twitter.com/gwgwtHvbgy

Drivers may not be expecting to find cyclists on some roads, and where there are high speed differentials or limited forward vision that can take drivers by surprise and leave cyclists at risk. Garmin and Waze have announced a partnership intended to mitigate the problem.

When a cyclist using a Garmin bike computer or smartwatch chooses to opt in to sharing their live track location, it will show up for drivers using Waze.

The feature is available on the Garmin Edge and any Garmin smartwatch when used with a compatible smartphone and the Garmin Connect app.

#3192. Ring’s wheeled and flying robots will patrol your home

Some people use a whole bunch of fixed cameras to monitor their homes, but Amazon has just announced a more flexible solution through wheeled and flying robots.

Both the $250 Drone Cam and $1,000 Rover Cam can respond to alarms or door and window sensor alerts in order to go check out what’s happening and send live video …

Amazon says they are the first two Ring Robotics products, with more likely to follow. Both are autonomous.

Ring Drone and Ring Rover are both powered by AI Pilot, a custom-built system that uses the devices’ cameras, specialized vision models, on-device sensors, and cloud processing to see, think, and navigate autonomously.

AI Pilot simplifies the customer experience, starting with setup. Simply carry Ring Drone through your space or let Ring Rover autonomously explore, and it turns what it sees into a floor plan. It intelligently identifies rooms and suggests patrol points: spots worth extra attention. This could be a side door, windows, a register, or a long corridor, helping eliminate guesswork while also allowing you to add additional points customized to your space and security preferences.

When a patrol or flight is initiated, AI Pilot plans the most efficient route to get to a preset point based on the map it’s created. From there, it reacts in real time—autonomously navigating around furniture, shelving, and any obstacle it encounters.

You can set either device to patrol on a fixed schedule, as well as activate them manually, but they will also automatically respond to sensor alerts and alarms.

When a Ring camera, sensor, or alarm is triggered, [either device] automatically [moves] to previously set patrol points to investigate […] Continuous person motion detection means Ring Rover can alert you and start recording the moment it detects motion in its view—even when docked.

The Ring Rover Cam will begin shipping on December 16 for $999.99, but you can preorder it today. The Drone Cam starts shipping in late January for $249.99, but there’s no preorder yet.

#3191. Howard Hughes: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Management's plan to lift return on equity hinges on moving capital out of commercial buildings and into insurance, a shift still being tested.

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 6, 2026, Howard Hughes (HHH -1.17%) announced plans to pivot toward an asset-light real estate model while scaling its insurance business. Shifting capital from physical buildings to higher-return opportunities alters how the company compounds value for shareholders over the next five years.

Management offers three takeaways on how this strategic transition works.

Capital locked up in commercial buildings earns lower returns than insurance operations. Partnering with third-party investors allows management to extract cash, generate fee revenue, and retain control of its master planned communities, which are large-scale, long-term property developments.

Management aims to elevate return on equity, a measure of how efficiently profits are generated from net assets, from lower double digits to high teens. Moving proceeds from commercial holdings into its Vantage insurance segment creates higher-compounding cash streams.

High mortgage rates create broader real estate friction, yet scarcity and full-service community design drive pricing gains. Rising land valuations replace the value of sold parcels, protecting the underlying balance sheet.

Operating performance across master planned communities remains resilient despite higher borrowing costs, and management takes pride in maintaining pricing power. Scarcity of land, long-term control over development, and recurring income from stabilized office properties support cash generation as leadership watches pricing discipline across property lines.

Unlocking equity from legacy physical assets creates flexibility to scale high-return operations without sacrificing community control.

#3190. Nvidia board hires ex-prosecutor Joon Kim to investigate Jensen Huang

The Nvidia board running the inquiry has no chair and no compliance chief, and its lead director once ran the company’s law firm. Three of Huang’s relatives work there.

NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang during his GTC 2026 keynote at the SAP Center in San Jose, 16 March 2026

Nvidia’s independent directors have hired the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to investigate chief executive Jensen Huang. The board retained Joon H. Kim, a former acting US Attorney in Manhattan, and his firm to run it. The board announced the choice on Tuesday, CNBC reported.

“The independent members of the NVIDIA Board have retained former acting U.S. Attorney of the Southern District of New York Joon H. Kim and his firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to conduct a thorough and independent investigation as was announced on Sunday,” the board said in a statement.

The board opened its own inquiry after Huang admitted an affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at the chip buyer Megaspeed. US intelligence agencies have concluded she was a spy for China, which has rejected the claims. Huang would not take part in choosing counsel and would keep leading the company, a spokesman had said, according to the Times.

The Nvidia board has a combined 161 years of service, Kalley Huang and Don Clark reported for The New York Times. Huang, Tench Coxe and Harvey Jones have sat on it since 1993, according to Nvidia’s proxy statement.

Sequoia Capital and Sutter Hill Ventures led a $2m round in Nvidia in 1993. Their investors, Mark Stevens and Coxe, then joined the board. Stevens left in 2006 and returned in 2008, the proxy shows. Brooke Seawell, a former Synopsys finance chief, joined in 1997. Jones and Seawell held Nvidia shares worth a combined $1.86bn as of June, the Times reported.

Before the hire, people familiar with the inquiry told the Financial Times it would probably be led by Stephen Neal, the lead independent director. Neal ran the law firm Cooley from 2001 to 2008 and is still its senior counsel. Cooley set up Nvidia in 1993 and has been its main outside counsel since, CNBC reported, citing the firm. Neal did not respond to CNBC.

Average director tenure is almost 15 years, nearly twice the S&P 500 norm, Semafor reported. No director is a current or former S&P 500 chief executive, and none has national security experience. None of the directors responded to the Times.

Nvidia has a lead independent director instead of a board chair. The proxy says this gives each member “an equal voice”. Huang told Bloomberg’s Emily Chang that he skipped the chairman role so the chief executive could be held accountable, Bloomberg reported.

“Unlike many CEOs, I’m completely fireable,” Huang said.

Nvidia’s code of conduct tells staff and directors to avoid any activity that conflicts with the company’s interests, the proxy says. That includes anything that looks like a conflict. The company does not have a chief compliance officer, the filing confirms. Nvidia has said a committee of its finance, operations and human resources heads checks that staff follow its policies, Fortune reported.

Nvidia’s annual report does not name Huang as a key person. It says the company depends heavily on its longstanding executive team.

“Failure to ensure effective succession planning, transfer of knowledge, and smooth transitions involving executives and key employees could hinder our strategic planning, execution, and long-term success,” the filing says.

Huang is Nvidia’s co-founder, chief executive and president. He has 33 direct reports this week, according to internal records reviewed by CNBC. He told CNBC in September 2025 that he had as many as 60. The proxy says the senior managers who work directly with him give the board a pool of candidates for promotion.

Huang owned 3.58% of Nvidia in March, the proxy shows, and he has no special voting rights, the Financial Times reported. He told Bloomberg he hoped the next chief executive already worked at Nvidia. In January, he said a chief executive who does not do the job “is let go”, the Times reported. He added a second thought.

“There will never be one like me, and the reason for that is because I was raised by the company,” Huang said.

Three relatives work at Nvidia. His son Spencer is a director of product management in robotics, and his daughter Madison is a senior director of product marketing, according to the Times. His son-in-law, Nico Caprez, works on business development, the Times reported. Fortune gives his title as vice president of global AI infrastructure growth.

Nvidia paid Madison about $1.23m and Spencer about $1.32m in its 2026 financial year, the proxy shows. Neither is an executive officer, shares a household with Huang or reports directly to him. Their pay was set under the company’s normal practices without Huang’s involvement, the filing says.

Nvidia reports its third-quarter results on 17 November. A day later, House committee chairs expect Huang at a closed-door briefing on Megaspeed.

#3189. Adobe unveils new AI tools for Photoshop, Premiere, and more, with MCP support coming in 2027

Adobe today announced a sweeping set of updates at its annual Adobe MAX conference, focused on giving users more ways to automate complex workflows, edit content, and work across its creative apps. Here are the details.

At the Adobe MAX event today, the company unveiled a series of features, many of them AI-powered or AI-assisted, that will begin rolling out across its suite of creative platforms as early as today.

In Photoshop, the new Relight tool offers a way to non-destructively and dynamically add, reposition, and resize light sources in the composition, while Generative Restylelets users** prompt the platform to generate variations of an image’s style and fine-tune the results using adjustable sliders.

Photoshop is also adding a Quick Compare slider to make it easier to track before-and-after results, and is getting several features in the beta app, including, per Adobe:

Following its acquisition of Topaz Labs, Adobe is also introducing two new AI image enhancement models: Wonder 4, which combines upscaling, denoising, deblurring, and sharpening into a single operation, and Image HDR, which converts standard images into HDR with improved brightness and detail.

Adobe Premiere is also getting generative tools that make it easier to prepare raw files for a project, including Enhance Audio, Separate Crosstalk, and Separate Sound Source. Adobe is also adding a Generative Remove tool to Premiere in beta, “bringing you the power to remove unwanted objects, like boom mics and logos or background distractions, directly on your timeline,” says the company.

Premiere is also getting Color Mode, a new color-grading tool starting today, which “supports everything from quick corrections to more advanced grades while keeping your video as the focus.”

Another interesting tool making its way into Premiere is Generative Media Tool. Here’s Adobe:

The Generative Media Tool brings Generate Video, Generate Sound Effects, Generate Soundscape and Generate Music directly into your timeline in Premiere. You can generate missing b-roll, background music or sound for a scene using context from your edit, then keep refining the result in your timeline. You can also choose from Adobe Firefly and models from partners including Google, Kling, Runway and Luma based on the creative needs of your project.

As for iPhone users who rely on Premiere Mobile, Adobe announced that its newly established partnerships with UMG and WMG will bring hundreds of thousands of licensed music tracks to the app (for non-commercial use) starting today, with users able to explore trending songs, discover featured artists, and create videos using artist-inspired templates.

Premiere mobile is also getting agentic tools soon, including Quick Cuts, which generates a first cut based on the user’s prompt and the materials they add, and an AI Assistant, which helps users find the right editing tools and execute tasks based on natural language instructions.

In Lightroom, the company is adding multiple new tools that make it easier to edit or more quickly fix small imperfections. That includes Glow, which “adds soft, cinematic light to your photos,” Blemish Removal for quick skin fine-tuning, Open Eyes in beta, and an improved and expanded Camera Tethering on Desktop and the iPad, with support for more cameras and advanced shooting controls, plus the ability to connect cameras directly to an iPad for live previews and photo editing.

Adobe is adding new brushes, gradients, patterns, and graphic styles to Illustrator, alongside new Blend controls, which “make it easier to develop and refine designs with a persistent control panel and live preview,” per the company.

As for InDesign, a new Co-editing feature, available in beta, streamlines collaborative work, while the new Flex Layout tool dynamically adjusts content based on the canvas size and artwork. InDesign is also getting Check Document and Rewrite that more quickly “help identify common editorial and accessibility issues while you’re still working.”

While it will not launch until 2027, this feature will enable users to connect Photoshop, Illustrator, Premiere, and After Effects to the AI tools and agents they already use.

In practice, this will mean connecting Photoshop to ChatGPT and having them work in tandem to adapt an entire campaign based on new artwork you develop and attach to your prompt.

This integration will also account for other connected tools, so the user can ask ChatGPT to make edits, add new files to a Google Drive folder, update the team on Slack, and so on.

Here’s Adobe on the upcoming MCP integration:

Because it runs locally on your computer, your agent works directly in your native project files, and your layers, vectors, bins and sequences stay editable.

The company notes that MCP integrations will enter private beta in early 2027, and users can sign up here to learn more.

According to Adobe, Firefly is getting even better at helping users organize and edit their raw material for tasks such as turning travel clips into a vlog, creating social media campaigns, or assembling videos from storyboards.

The new Firefly Video lets users organize scenes, assemble clips, add captions, and generate transitions and B-roll, while Firefly Design brings illustration, image editing, animation, and 3D tools into a single canvas.

Adobe is also adding Quick Actions for common editing tasks, Firefly Graph for creating reusable workflows, and Firefly Builder (in private beta) for prototyping websites and apps using natural language.

Firefly’s AI Assistant is also getting new capabilities, including Plan Mode, which lets users review and approve an agent’s proposed actions, and Model Selector, which lets them choose which AI model to use.

Adobe is also previewing Always-on agents, which can handle recurring tasks such as organizing assets, checking quality, and preparing content for different platforms in the background, even when users step away.

Adobe is also expanding its Creative Agent across Creative Cloud, with AI Assistants now available in beta in Illustrator, Premiere, InDesign, After Effects, and Frame.io, as well as the Photoshop beta app.

These assistants allow users to execute complex, multi-step tasks using natural language prompts. In Premiere, for example, users can ask the assistant to apply effects to an entire sequence, track subjects across frames, or adjust color and exposure across multiple clips.

To learn more about these and other features announced at Adobe MAX today, stay tuned to the company’s blog.

Including which is best at banishing hot flashes so night sweats don't wake you up at 3 a.m.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Type: Smart mattress coverSizes: 6 (twin–Cal king)Sleep trial: 30 nightsWarranty: 2 yearsSubscription: Yes (from $17/month)Price (on sale): From $1,899 at Eight Sleep

Type: Smart mattress coverSizes: 3 (queen–Cal king)Sleep trial: 30 nightsWarranty: 2 yearsSubscription: Optional ($250/year)Price (on sale): From $1,795 at Orion

Type: Hybrid mattressSizes: 7 (twin–Split king)Sleep trial: 365 nightsWarranty: Limited lifetimeSubscription: NoPrice (on sale): From $1,298 at Bear

Just yesterday I was sweating through a scorching summer night and now when I climb into bed, it’s like stepping into an igloo. Either way is bad news for my sleep and can result in 3 a.m. wake-ups. No wonder all the best mattresses we’ve tried have passed rigorous temperature regulation tests.

The best cooling mattresses use heat dissipating materials to kick out night sweats and counteract heatwaves so you’re able to snooze soundly. And when it comes to cooling beds, the Bear Elite Hybrid is the best we’ve ever tested.

But recently I’ve been hands-on with the Eight Sleep Pod 6 and Orion Sleep System, two of the best smart mattresses that use active cooling to create even temperatures. These high-tech systems deliver impressive hands-on cooling but at a high price. So in the Black Friday mattress and sleep sales, which should you buy? I'm here to advise you based on our extensive testing and my own experience with all three cooling beds.

The Eight Sleep Pod 6 is the most expensive of the three, with a queen coming in at $2,899 MSRP. The Orion is cheaper with an MSRP of $2,395. The Bear Elite Hybrid has an MSRP of $2,284 for a queen, but regular Bear mattress sales can knock it as low as $1,370.40.

Keep in mind, both the Eight Sleep Pod 6 and the Orion are covers only. The Elite Hybrid is the only option that's actually a mattress.

As well as being the priciest upfront, the Eight Sleep Pod 6 is the only one with a mandatory subscription. Starting at $17/month, it includes sleep tracking and is essential for operating the Pod. Orion also has a sleep tracking subscription but it's optional (although more expensive at $250/year). Bear, of course, is subscription-free.

Bear blows both smart covers out of the water when it comes to benefits, offering a 365-night sleep trial and a limited lifetime warranty. Orion and Eight Sleep both offer just a 30-night trial and 2-year warranty.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

With the launch of the Pod 6, Eight Sleep expanded into twin sizes, offering more options for solo sleepers. A twin is now only $1,899 (was $1,999) while there's $200 off larger sizes. Eight Sleep sales are never blockbusters so this is a noteworthy price drop, although we're hopeful more discounts will appear before Black Friday.

A queen-size smart mattress cover for under $2,000 is a rare bargain and in the Orion Black Friday sale there's up to $600 off this climate control system. Sizes are limited (just queen, king, and Cal king as of writing) but the price is fantastic. A bigger discount is unlikely, so now's the time to shop.

The Bear Elite Hybrid sells at a competitive price for a cooling hybrid mattress, particularly one with a luxury pillow-top. There's usually 30% off at Bear but keep an eye out for the 35% off deal that reliably appears over the holidays. Right now, though, you can get 40% off plus free accessories when you use our TOMS40 code at the checkout, bringing the price of a queen down to $1,370.40.

The Pod 6 and Orion Sleep System both come in two parts: the cover and a control tower. The cover is fitted with water pipes, attach to the tower via tube.

In terms of design, the tower is the primary difference between the two. The Orion tower is bigger and bulkier but also has a more design-forward finish. The Eight Sleep Pod 6 is quieter, however.

The Bear Elite Hybrid is an entirely different beast. One of the best hybrid mattresses, it's made from layers of mattress springs and foams. The cover is woven with Celliant fibers to draw away heat, while a copper-infused foam layer further aids temperature control.

The Eight Sleep Pod 6 and Orion covers are designed to make minimal difference to the support and cushioning of your mattress. I tested both on the Leesa Original mattress and, overall, I think this is accurate. That means your comfort is dependent on the mattress beneath.

As one of the best mattresses in a box you can buy, we were impressed with the support and cushioning of the Bear Elite Hybrid. It comes in three firmness levels (I tried the Medium and it's one of my favorite mattresses for side sleepers) so there's an option for nearly all sleep styles.

Dive into our Bear Elite Hybrid mattress review to learn more about the pressure relief, edge support and motion isolation of this top-rated mattress.

The Eight Sleep and Orion take a hands-on approach to temperature regulation. Both are active climate control systems, pumping water through tiny pipes in the mattress cover so the surface retains the perfect feel.

From my experience, both are highly effective. I slept on the Orion Sleep System during the change from summer to fall, meaning some days I had all the windows open, and other days I was flirting with turning the heating up. Right now, I'm using my Eight Sleep Pod 6 on some frosty nights.

Both covers keep the temperature at 'snug', staying far away from 'shivering' or 'sauna'. I haven't had a sweaty 3 a.m. wake-up in months.

Under our thermal cam, the Orion Sleep showed its prowess. It kept a steady feel the entire time, with no temperature swings even when tester Frances Daniels climbed on. And while normally a thermal outline remains long after our tester has left the mattress, on the Orion, all signs of Frances were gone in minutes.

The Bear Elite Hybrid has a more traditional approach to cooling. (Although with its Celliant fibers and copper-infused foams, it's hardly simple.)

Despite its lack of active cooling technology, our hands-on testing showed heat didn't linger in the Bear Elite. And our thermal cam backed us up. While the Bear Elite Hybrid warmed quickly, it kicked out excess heat at an incredible pace. After just four minutes of our tester leaving the mattress, it had nearly returned to the original temperature.

While the Bear Elite Hybrid is impressive, it's not as versatile as the Eight Sleep or the Orion Sleep System. And nothing touches the Eight Sleep when it comes to quick changes — buttons on the side of the cover allow you to adjust the temperature without unlocking your phone.

Orion and Eight Sleep both offer sleep tracking alongside their advanced cooling features. For Eight Sleep, the sleep tracking is part of the mandatory subscription. For Orion, it's an optional add-on.

I've tested both alongside my Oura Ring 5, our top rated sleep tracker this year. Overall, I've been impressed with the quality and accuracy of the information. Both capture sleep stages and duration that line up with both the data from my Oura Ring and my recollection of the night.

However when it comes to the details, the Eight Sleep Pod 6 is the winner. It captures a massive amount of data and displays it in easy-to-read graphics. For the Orion, sleep tracking feels like an add-on. With Eight Sleep, it's integral.

Eight Sleep also has a smart alarm built into the the cover, which vibrates when it senses a light sleep stage. Orion preps you to wake up with gentle warmth but the Eight Sleep Pod 6 does a better job at rousing you.

✅ You experience hot flashes: The Eight Sleep's hot flash mode works to quickly counteract sudden temperature fluctuations. It should kick in while you're sleeping but you can also turn it on in the app if you feel a hot flash coming on.

✅ You want detailed sleep tracking: Eight Sleep's Autopilot delivers accurate and detailed sleep data. Plus, it puts it all into handy graphics to give you an instant picture of sleep trends and changes.

✅ You want control at the touch of a button: Simply press the button on the side of the cover to turn the heat up or down in the night. The Eight Sleep isn't a mind reader, so this allows you to tweak it to fit your needs.

✅ You want smart cooling without the expense: The Orion can match the Eight Sleep (and the Bear Elite Hybrid) when it comes to temperature control, offering active cooling at a lower price.

✅ You and your partner can never agree on the thermostat: Both the Orion and Eight Sleep allow you to set a different temperature on each side of the mattress. With the Orion, you can do so for less.

✅ You need a new bed: If you go for the Orion or Eight Sleep, you'll need to buy a new mattress as well (or stick with the one you have). The Bear Elite Hybrid doesn't just offer cooling — it's a great bed all round.

✅ You don't experience major temperature swings: If you often wake up stuffy but hot sleeping isn't ruining your night, you might not require high-tech active cooling. The Bear will keep you comfortable without the expense.

#3187. Another report backs OLED iPad Air early next year

Following the recent update to the iPad mini, we’re expecting the iPad Air to be next in line to be upgraded to an OLED screen.

Previous reports have gradually narrowed down the launch to early 2027, and a new supply chain report echoes this …

OLED screens were initially exclusive to the iPad Pro. That finally changed last month when Apple gave the iPad mini its biggest update in years. The new model is thinner and lighter and powered by an A20 Pro chip, while the headline news is the new OLED screen.

The iPad Air got a chip update earlier this year, but nothing else. An upgrade to OLED is expected next year, with recent reports suggesting that it will be in the first half of 2027. That’s now backed by a new supply chain report by DigiTimes.

Given past timings, the smart money would be on the OLED iPad Air being announced in March. With the precedent set by the latest iPad mini, we can likely expect the new iPad Air to have similar specs, which means sticking with Touch ID and a 60Hz display.

#3186. Speech Processing Pioneer Bishnu Saroop Atal Dies at 93

IEEE also bids farewell to innovators in space, power, and telecom

Bishnu Saroop Atal received the 2013 IEEE Jack S. Kilby Signal Processing Medal for “fundamental and pioneering contributions to speech coding.”

Bishnu Saroop AtalAcoustics and signal processing pioneerLife Fellow, 93; died 19 August

Atal was an acoustics and signal processing researcher at Bell Labs in Murray Hill, N.J., and later at AT&T’s Shannon Laboratory, in Florham Park, N.J. His pioneering work on voice-coding techniques became the foundation for efficient, high-quality voice transmission over cellular networks. He received the 2013 IEEE Jack S. Kilby Signal Processing Medal for “fundamental and pioneering contributions to speech coding.”

He joined Bell Labs in 1961 as a communications researcher, and his early work there focused on speaker identification technology. During the 1960s he helped develop linear predictive coding, a powerful method for analyzing and compressing speech. LPC is now the most widely used method for encoding speech at a low bit rate.

Atal developed increasingly sophisticated low-bit-rate speech-coding techniques. They included multipulse LPC, which improved the quality of compressed speech.

He also worked with his colleague Manfred R. Schroeder to develop code-excited linear prediction, a method for producing high-quality speech at very low bit rates. CELP became a foundational technique in modern speech coding, letting digital communications systems carry voice using less bandwidth. The extra efficiency expanded cellular capacity, allowing wireless networks to handle more simultaneous calls.

Later in his career, he led the acoustics and speech research departments at Bell.

The company named him a Fellow in 1994. When AT&T Bell Laboratories split into separate research organizations in 1996, Atal continued his career at the AT&T Florham Park headquarters, and he was named a Fellow the following year.

He retired in 2002 and became an affiliate professor of electrical engineering at the University of Washington, in Seattle. There he continued his research in speech processing, speech recognition, and high-dimensional computing.

Atal was elected to the National Academy of Engineering in 1987 and the National Academy of Sciences in 1993. He received numerous awards including the 2018 International Speech Communication Association Medal for Scientific Achievement and a 2003 medal from the Franklin Institute.

He received a bachelor’s degree in physics in 1952 from the University of Lucknow, in India, and a master’s degree in 1955 in electrical engineering from the Indian Institute of Science, in Bengaluru. While working full time at Bell he earned a Ph.D. in EE in 1968 from the Polytechnic Institute of Brooklyn (now New York University’s Tandon engineering school), in New York City.

Darryl Palmer Jr.Chair of the IEEE Central Illinois SectionSenior member, 55; died 30 August

Palmer was a dedicated IEEE volunteer, serving as chair of the Central Illinois Section and as the government relations chair of Region 4. He was a member of the IEEE Industrial Electronics Society and its industrial activity committee. He also served as associate editor of the IEEE Transactions on Industrial Informatics.

In 1986, at age 16, Palmer completed a summer internship at NASA’s Glenn Research Center, in Cleveland. He helped develop FoilSim, an interactive educational software program that introduces aerodynamic engineering to preuniversity students.

While studying computer science at Cleveland State University in 1996, he joined the university’s Allen-Bradley PLC lab as a research assistant. He designed hardware and software systems for the Glenn Research Center to collect and process thermal wave imaging data. He also designed software for General Motors’ North American robotic and welding division.

In 1999 he completed a second internship at the research center and helped develop EngineSim, an educational software program that models jet engine design and testing.

For his work, NASA recognized him with a Space Act Award.

In 2000 he earned his bachelor’s degree in computer science and became a software engineer at the Danfoss Drives manufacturing facility in Loves Park, Ill. He worked on embedded control systems for variable-frequency drives and high-power equipment. He also developed sensorless control technology for beam pumps used in the oil and gas industry.

In 2014 Palmer and his wife, Alexandra “Sasha” Goodwin, founded Janus Choice, a health technology platform that matches hospital patients with post-acute care facilities. He served as its CEO until the company closed in 2020.

From 2018 to 2023, he was a lead software engineer at Adept Coalescence, a startup in Rockford, Ill., focused on developing front-end software for control systems. He then worked in Peoria, Ill., as a control systems team lead at Caterpillar, a manufacturer of construction and mining equipment.

Henry Leopold RichterTelecommunications engineerLife senior member, 99; died 12 August

Richter was a spacecraft engineer at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory, in Pasadena, Calif., before starting his own public safety communications consultancy.

He earned a bachelor’s degree and a Ph.D. at Caltech in 1952 and 1956, respectively. In 1955 he joined JPL as an engineer and supervisor of its new circuit elements group. Later, he was assigned to NASA’s Explorer program as project manager for satellite design, serving as a liaison between the organization’s satellite instrumentation group and its operations and data groups. Since 1958 the program has launched more than 90 missions for physics, geophysics, and astrophysics research.

As NASA prepared to launch Explorer 1 in January 1958, Richter worked with the San Gabriel Valley Radio Club in Los Angeles to set up stations across the United States to track the satellite.

He eventually was named JPL section chief and was responsible for scientific instruments on the lunar Ranger, Surveyor, and Mariner programs. He also helped develop NASA’s Deep Space Network, an international tracking and communications system.

Richter left NASA to become vice president and technical director of Xerox Electro-Optical Systems, in Pasadena, Calif.

In the mid-1970s, he joined the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department as a communications engineer, overseeing the department’s microwave and mobile radio networks.

He later ran a telecommunications consulting practice for more than 20 years. His clients included federal, state, and local government agencies, school districts, universities, and organizations. His work covered strategic technology planning and the design and implementation of public safety radio, microwave, CCTV, and paging systems.

He wrote several books including America’s Leap Into Space: My Time at JPL and the First Explorer Satellites (2015), a personal account of his experience working on the Explorer 1 and America’s space program.

In 2019 the Radio Club of America presented him with its Lifetime Achievement Award for “significant achievements and a major body of work that has advanced the art and science of wireless technology.”

Raymond L. GiordanoFormer RCA engineerLife member, 91; died 19 July

Giordano was an electrical engineer who designed integrated circuits and defense electronics at companies including Harris, Intersil, and RCA.

After earning his bachelor’s degree in electrical engineering in 1956 from the Newark College of Engineering (now the New Jersey Institute of Technology), Giordano joined RCA in Moorestown, N.J., as an engineer. He helped develop a video formatter for the company’s missile and surface radar division, and he taught in-house engineering courses, eventually attaining the rank of senior technical staff member.

Later he developed technologies for General Electric (which acquired RCA in 1986), Intersil, and Harris. He designed the circuitry for Kodak’s Cameo cameras and one of its laser printers.

Giordano was awarded several patents for his designs including a smoke detector chip for Siemens, a speed control chip for Ford, an engine control system for Delco Remy, and a control component for Chrysler.

He earned a master’s degree in EE in 1964 from the University of Pennsylvania, in Philadelphia.

Delano D. WilsonPresident of Power TechnologiesLife Fellow, 92; died 26 May

Wilson was president and CEO of Power Technologies, a consulting firm in Schenectady, N.Y., that specialized in electric power systems.

He was a director of R&D at General Electric in Schenectady until he joined Power Technologies in 1974 as a principal engineer. He developed utility systems and software for the company.

Wilson authored six books and 65 technical papers, and he held two patents.

Outside of his engineering work, he served on the boards of several hospitals, YMCAs, Rotary clubs, and chambers of commerce.

After returning to his hometown of Great Falls, Mont., in 1995, he volunteered as a court-appointed advocate, a trained community volunteer appointed by a judge to represent the interests of children in foster care.

Daniel I. Amey Jr.Electronic packaging engineerLife Fellow, 84; died 12 March

Amey was an electronic packaging engineer, working at several companies including General Dynamics, Sperry Univac, and E.I. du Pont de Nemours (now DuPont). His research interests included connectors, chip packages, and high-frequency materials.

He began his career in 1963 as an engineer in the General Dynamics electronics division, where he designed military electronic hardware including analog and digital support equipment for aerospace applications.

In 1967 he joined Sperry Univac in Blue Bell, Pa. From 1972 to 1981 he was engineering manager of packaging techniques, responsible for interconnection hardware for small and medium computer systems. His work focused on large-scale integration packages, hybrid circuits, connectors, and printed wiring board processes.

He left the company to serve as director of electronics technology at Thomas & Betts of Raritan, N.J. He led research and development of packaging and interconnection products there.

In 1986 he became a director of Elco, an electrical component manufacturer in Huntingdon, Pa., where he was responsible for the design and development of connector and packaging hardware.

In 1988 he joined E.I. du Pont de Nemours as director of its electronics and communications technology group in Research Triangle Park, N.C. He worked on packaging technology development, high-frequency materials characterization, and applications engineering. He retired from there as a research fellow.

Amey wrote or cowrote more than 70 technical papers and held more than 14 patents. He developed courses on electronic packaging and printed wiring technology for education companies McGraw-Hill and Cobblestone (formerly the Center for Professional Advancement).

He received the International Microelectronics Assembly and Packaging Society’s 2004 Wagnon Technical Achievement Award and the Electronic Industries Association’s 1984 Distinguished Engineering Contribution Award.

After receiving a bachelor’s degree in electrical engineering and a master’s degree in engineering science from Pennsylvania State University, he earned an MBA from Lehigh University, in Bethlehem, Pa.

Amanda Davis is a freelance writer based in San Diego.
