#3185. AI firms sign Macron’s Paris Call, but safety group says it lacks teeth

OpenAI, Anthropic and Microsoft promise shutdown switches and outside testing, but there are no shared risk limits.

The Paris Call meeting at the Élysée Palace on 9 November, with leaders and AI executives joining by video

OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft and Mistral are among ten AI companies that have signed a new declaration on the safety of advanced AI models. The Paris Call for AI Safety and Security was agreed on Monday at a meeting hosted by French President Emmanuel Macron.

L’intelligence artificielle avance très vite. On l’a déjà vu : cela implique des risques réels pour notre sécurité collective.

Notre travail pour developper nos technologies doit aussi être celui de l’anticipation et de la maîtrise de ses risques.

J’ai réuni à Paris et en visio une cinquantaine d’acteurs : chefs d’État et de gouvernement, dirigeants des plus grands laboratoires d’IA, chercheurs et experts.

Le constat est partagé. Il faut agir ensemble. Nous avons obtenu des engagements de tous autour de trois priorités : mieux évaluer de façon indépendante et publique les risques des modèles les plus avancés, mieux partager les alertes en cas d’incident grave et responsabiliser les acteurs qui développent des modèles.

Notre ambition est claire : faire de l’IA un progrès pour tous, avec une sécurité garantie par l’engagement de chacun.

— Emmanuel Macron (@EmmanuelMacron) November 9, 2026

The announcement came on the opening day of the Paris Peace Forum, where AI was one of the main topics of discussion.

Six countries signed the declaration: France, Canada, Finland, Norway, the Netherlands and Bahrain. The other participating companies are Hugging Face, Cohere, Black Forest Labs, Domyn, Sakana AI and Synthesia. Yoshua Bengio’s AI safety organisation LawZero is among the research groups supporting it.

Around 50 people joined the discussions by video, including OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman, Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei and Microsoft president Brad Smith.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent also took part, although the US is not among the signatories. Google, Meta and China have not signed the declaration either.

Macron said AI was advancing rapidly and posed “real risks to our collective security”, calling for governments and companies to work together to address them.

The signatories have committed to developing fail-safe mechanisms that can shut down their AI models, including during training and internal use. They will also provide clearer information about what their systems can and cannot do, and allow qualified independent experts to test them where appropriate.

The declaration also calls for a shared approach to assessing and managing the risks of frontier AI. This would cover malicious uses, including cyberattacks and weapons development, as well as the possibility of AI systems acting independently or moving beyond human control. Non-sensitive test results would be published in a common format.

Governments and companies will also share early warnings about serious incidents, while whistleblowers will have access to secure channels for reporting concerns.

The commitments have drawn criticism from French AI safety organisation CeSIA, which signed the declaration but argues that it leaves important gaps.

It sets no common risk thresholds for deciding whether a model should be developed or released, and does not guarantee that independent testers or governments will have access to the systems they need to assess.

CeSIA also wants governments to have the authority to suspend a model when its risks become too high. It argues that developers need clearer obligations and a timetable for meeting them.

“These decisions must rest with public authorities,” said Charbel-Raphaël Ségerie, CeSIA’s executive director.

The Paris Call follows an initiative launched by Norway and Finland in September to bring frontier AI under greater oversight, which France later joined. It also builds on earlier global safety commitments made by AI companies in Seoul and discussions at the G7 summit hosted by France in Evian.

The declaration remains open to other signatories, but it sets no deadlines. The shared testing framework it proposes has yet to be developed.

On Tuesday, the forum turned to another concern for Macron: the effects of AI on children. Speaking at a summit on children in the AI era, the French president called for AI tools to undergo checks before being made available to young users.

“We will push for pre-certification of all artificial intelligence solutions,” he said.

Macron compared the idea to the safety checks required for children’s toys, arguing that parents would not give a child an untested toy and that AI tools should be held to the same standard.

He also warned that the effects of AI on young people’s mental health were already becoming apparent, as more children and teenagers turn to chatbots that can influence their emotions and how they see the world. A charter on safer AI for children was due to be signed later on Tuesday.

President Emmanuel Macron also received a report, titled “Protect without preventing”, from a government-appointed panel of experts examining generative AI and human vulnerability.

#3183. Ready Capital: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Management has stopped selling distressed commercial real estate loans at steep discounts and is now working to stabilize nonperforming loans and foreclosed properties first.

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 6, 2026, Ready Capital (RC -2.88%) announced that it substantially completed its balance sheet repositioning and liquidity plan. The real estate finance company absorbed significant book value declines to eliminate debt and protect capital.

Generating $2.3 billion in liquidity required hard trade-offs, including dividend cuts and book value write-downs. With corporate debt paid down, the company is shifting from defensive cash conservation to earnings recovery.

The Small Business Administration 7(a) program, or SBA 7(a), provides government-guaranteed small business loans that generate gain-on-sale income while requiring minimal capital. Expanding origination volume offers immediate quarterly revenue gains to offset commercial real estate drags.

Management stopped selling distressed commercial real estate (CRE) loans at steep discounts to raise quick cash. The company is now actively managing nonperforming loans and real estate owned, or REO properties acquired through foreclosure, to stabilize net operating income before seeking exits.

Expense reductions take center stage as Ready Capital matches operational spending to a smaller balance sheet. The company leverages its high-yielding loan platforms and patient property management to rebuild cash flow while watching noncore business sales.

Recycling legacy assets and expanding high-return channels remain critical to bringing distributable earnings back to breakeven.

#3181. Zendesk moves to pay-per-result AI pricing with its new Outcome AI Platform

Customers will pay when AI resolves an issue, and a new directory helps AI assistants find official support.

Zendesk is changing how businesses pay for its AI, charging them for problems solved rather than for the number of people using the software. The customer service company announced the change on Tuesday at its AI Summit in San Francisco, as part of a new Outcome AI Platform.

Under the new plans, customers set an ‘Outcome Budget’ and pay for each eligible issue the AI resolves or task it completes. Zendesk checks each result for quality and completeness, so customers can see what counts towards their budget. As a result, businesses can start small and spend more as the AI takes on more work.

Zendesk has backed this model before. Earlier this year, it argued alongside Sierra that AI agents should be paid per result, not per seat, and OpenAI has started trying a similar approach with some customers.

Tapan Patel, a research director at IDC, said the change reflects how business buyers now want to pay for AI. Linking cost to verified results, he added, makes it clearer what customers get for their money.

The platform is also built for a world where people send their own AI assistants to deal with companies. To help with that, Zendesk is launching the Open Service Directory, a public list where brands can register their official support channels. AI assistants can then use it to find verified help, even for brands that do not use Zendesk.

Brands control what they share and when a human must step in. The directory does not access private customer data or take any action itself. Early members include Betterment, ElevenLabs and Telekom Payment.

Meanwhile, a tool called Zendesk Bridge lets businesses connect AI agents and apps of their choice, such as ChatGPT, to Zendesk’s systems. Setting up a connection starts with a name, which is kept for audit logs, and a plain description of what the outside agent should and should not do.

Administrators then choose exactly what each agent may do, such as reading, creating, answering, updating or merging tickets. An assistant called Admin Copilot suggests which tools to switch on, based on the description.

Every action then passes through Bridge, which checks permissions and company rules and asks for human approval where needed. An observability page shows how many requests came from AI agents and how many from people, which ones were blocked and why. It also includes a kill switch. Bridge is in early access, and the directory is launching soon.

“People don’t think about which channels, systems, or departments they need to navigate to interact with a business,” said Zendesk chief executive Tom Eggemeier.

Other new tools, now generally available, help teams build and improve their AI agents. AI Agent Launchpad studies past customer conversations and suggests where AI could take over. In Zendesk’s demo for a scooter rental firm, it proposes a step-by-step process for rides that will not end, using a connected billing system such as Stripe.

Similarly, Agentic Analytics lets managers ask questions about their data in plain language, such as how many tickets are still open. They can then see whether changes are cutting repeat contacts.

The launch reflects changing habits, according to a Zendesk survey. It found that 52% of consumers are comfortable relying on personal AI assistants for everyday tasks. Even so, 84% said human help should always be available.

The announcement follows Zendesk’s purchase of Forethought, its biggest deal in two decades, as it builds out its AI agents.

#3179. I tested the Google Pixel Tag and it’s the most findable tracker for Android phones — plus it does something Apple AirTag can't

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Unlock and manage exclusive Tom’s Guide member rewards.

Join the Tom's Guide Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Pixel Tag delivers an outstanding tracking experience for Android users, matching the AirTag’s $29 price point while beating it out with superior Precision Finding range and persistent alerts when the batter level gets low.

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

Over the past few years, I’ve tested my fair share of Bluetooth trackers — ranging from wallet-thin cards like the Statik SmartCard Incognito to the Pebblebee Halo, which can potentially help elderly individuals in emergency situations. Google has expanded its Find Hub network, finally giving Android users plenty of options, but many of these trackers share one glaring limitation: pinpoint proximity tracking.

While iPhone users have long enjoyed the superb performance of Precision Finding — leaning on Ultra Wideband (UWB) for pinpoint accuracy — most Android trackers don’t have that luxury. Instead, they rely on basic Bluetooth proximity that only shows broad geographic circles on a map.

Google’s Pixel Tag is one of the few Android trackers that packages Ultra Wideband (UWB) and Bluetooth Channel Sounding directly into Google’s native ecosystem. As a result, the Pixel Tag delivers true visual Precision Finding to Android devices. After putting it to the test, I found it holds one distinct advantage over the AirTag and one of the best Bluetooth trackers you can get.

Ultra-Wideband (UWB) + Bluetooth Channel Sounding

Easily the best feature of the Pixel Tag is its ability to lock down an exact position with outstanding Precision Finding range, which actually managed to outperform even Apple's AirTag 2 in my testing. Using the Find My Device app on an Android phone, you get intuitive on-screen visual guidance, complete with compass-like directional arrows and real-time distance readouts that point you right where you need to go.

While the AirTag 2 tapped out around 74 feet in my testing before dropping its Ultra Wideband connection, the Pixel Tag held on slightly farther, reaching roughly 82 feet. That extra reach eliminates the guesswork of tracking down misplaced gear, like my keys when I've completely forgotten where I left them. Plus, you can still trigger a loud audio chime if the tag slips deep between couch cushions and you can't spot it right away.

The AirTag has an unmistakable look, but Google has delivered an equally compelling design — especially when it comes to size. At just 5.4mm thick, the Pixel Tag is significantly sleeker than the AirTag, making it far less conspicuous when slipped into a standard wallet. With its minimalist, matte-finished polycarbonate body, I really dig the pebble-like aesthetic, which does a far better job of masking smudges and fingerprints than the AirTag's scratch-prone stainless steel back.

Even with that slimmed-down profile, Google didn’t cut corners on durability, outfitting it with a rugged IP67 dust- and water-resistance rating. Plus, swapping out the CR2032 coin-cell battery is painless — all it takes is a quick twist of the back cover.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Beyond tracking down my keys, wallet, backpack, or other gear, the Pixel Tag offers another standout feature you won’t find on the AirTag: the ability to ring your phone. With a simple double-press of the physical button on the front, you can instantly trigger your phone to ring at full volume — even if it's set to silent or vibrate. This reverse-finding capability is a lifesaver in a crunch when you're rushing out the door and can't find your phone anywhere.

One of the biggest annoyances I have with the AirTag is discovering weeks or even months later that it's dead. Sure, my iPhone might have sent a low-battery notification, but those alerts are easy to forget. That’s why I’m stoked about the Pixel Tag’s persistent automated reminders, which offer huge peace of mind if I overlook that initial heads-up.

Google rates the user-replaceable CR2032 coin-cell battery for up to a full year of typical use. While I haven’t had the Pixel Tag long enough to drain it down and trigger an alert firsthand, knowing Find Hub will send a notification “every 2 weeks until it’s replaced” ensures it won't quietly drop off my radar. Usually, I’m not a fan of that level of notification nagging, but in this case, it's a welcome safety net.

Despite having some key advantages over the AirTag, there’s one area where the Pixel Tag falls behind its rival: accessory availability. You can find an AirTag mount, leather loop, rugged clip, or pet collar attachment with a quick search online. The Pixel Tag, however, launches with very few options.

In fact, Google doesn't even offer any official accessories right out of the gate. The only ones I’ve been able to track down so far are basic silicone cases from Walmart. Because the Pixel Tag’s design doesn't include a built-in lanyard hole or keyring cutout, you'll need a dedicated case or adhesive mount just to attach it to your keys or backpack. For early adopters, finding the exact style or mount you want right now will require some patience while third-party makers ramp up production.

Considering how long the Pixel line has been around, you’d think Google would’ve come out with its own AirTag rival sooner. Even so, the Pixel Tag is a long-overdue addition — and it’s easily one of the most capable and well-rounded Bluetooth trackers on the market.

Between its class-leading Precision Finding range, compact design, and reverse-phone-ringing feature, it addresses the pinpoint tracking compromises that have long plagued the Android ecosystem. The only other real alternatives with Ultra Wideband support are Motorola’s Moto Tag and Samsung’s SmartTag3. You still get all the essential safeguards expected from a flagship tracker, too, including left-behind alerts and a dedicated Lost Mode that allows anyone who finds your gear to scan it and get in touch.

At $29 for a single one (or $99 for a four-pack), Google matches Apple dollar for dollar — but delivers greater range and features the AirTag simply can’t match.

Apple today launched a neat new accessibility feature for the Apple TV streaming service. Users will now have the option to watch with a sign language interpretation for some of Apple’s original movies.

The feature is launching this Friday with the debut of the new film Being Heumann, as well as F1: The Movie. Support for more titles will follow later.

#3177. iPadOS 27.3 adds new iPad setting I instantly turned on

iPadOS 27.3 is currently available in beta, and it introduces a new iPad setting for app windowing that I instantly turned on. Here are the details.

I use the iPad Pro as my primary computer, and for the most part have found Apple’s software changes in iPadOS 26 and 27 to be great upgrades.

But with the powerful new windowing capabilities, there have definitely been some quirks that need refining. One of them involves resizing windows with the traffic light controls in the top-left corner.

For example, in iPadOS 27 the controls move locations and even disappear depending on the size of the window. It can be pretty frustrating.

I need to just get better about learning keyboard shortcuts for window controls. But in the meantime, iPadOS 27.3 adds a new optional setting that I instantly turned on and have been loving.

If you use your iPad mostly with touch input, or simply haven’t used keyboard shortcuts enough to remember them, this new setting is a great way to quickly resize windows.

When the setting is enabled, two taps (or a double-click with the trackpad) will zoom the window to take up the full screen. Then you can double-tap again to revert it to its previous size.

I generally keep my app windows in specific size setups, but regularly find myself wanting to go fullscreen temporarily. The new setting provides a convenient way to do that quickly without needing the traffic light controls or my keyboard, and is a welcome refinement to iPadOS windowing.

#3176. Claude’s new Personal Finance tool aims to help analyze your spending – read-only, of course

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Anthropic has released what appears to be its answer to ChatGPT Finances.

You can now share your financial information with Claude and ask the chatbot for insights on your spending.

Also: Researchers asked people to use AI chatbots for election info

Personal Finance in Claude, which Anthropic announced Thursday, reviews your connected accounts through read-only access via Plaid. That security measure follows OpenAI’s equivalent feature, ChatGPT Finances, which launched in May. Here’s what to know.

Functionally, this feature appears similar to ChatGPT Finances: It lets you link as many bank and credit card accounts as you’d like to Claude via Plaid with read-only access. You can then ask Claude where you spent your money this month or whether you can afford to take a vacation in six months, for example.

(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, ZDNET’s parent company, filed an April 2025 lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)

Also: Stop sharing your passwords with AI agents

According to Anthropic, the feature is a response to existing use patterns: the company’s April usage report found that financial advice was one of the main topics users ask Claude for help with.

“For the accounts you choose to connect (and only those), Claude sees the bank’s name, each account’s name, type, and last four digits, balances and credit limits, and up to two years of transactions. When you chat with Claude in the Personal Finance hub, those conversations aren’t used to train our models.”

The idea behind the feature is that you can ask follow-up questions and request more insights about spending habits, trends over time, and future goals based on what Claude finds, similar to any other Claude conversation. The tool will also generate tables and charts to visualize your financial information.

“You can ask for a weekly spending chart, a calendar of what’s due, or a dashboard of the numbers you choose, and Claude builds it as an artifact you can keep adjusting and coming back to,” an Anthropic representative told ZDNET via email.

Also: I connected ChatGPT to my bank, and it’s my go-to finance app now

You can also expect an ad-free experience in the feature.

“Like the rest of Claude, Personal Finance has no ads or sponsored recommendations, and it doesn’t offer credit cards, loans, or savings accounts of its own, so your money questions get a straight answer,” the company said in the announcement.

The company added that because Claude is using actual transaction data and not memory, the feature shouldn’t hallucinate.

“It can list the exact transactions behind any number so you can check its math,” Anthropic said via email. “Like any AI, it can make mistakes, so for anything important, we recommend confirming with your bank.”

Still, the difference — and for many, the appeal — here is the natural language interface. Other finance apps don’t necessarily have an easy, accessible chat function where users can shoot off quick questions like they would to a human financial planner. These assistants also present historical budget analysis in plain English, rather than requiring users to interpret dashboards themselves, which users may see as a perk.

Also: 5 ways to use AI when your budget is tight

On Reddit, many users find ChatGPT Finances to be accurate and reliable. One Reddit user said ChatGPT Finance seemed to have Mint or Monarch potential, but noted it was still “weaker” than those apps in some areas, such as historical syncing, high-quality dashboards, and generating full statement PDFs.

“ChatGPT has genuinely helped me make better financial decisions,” she wrote.

Anthropic noted that users shouldn’t look to Personal Finance for Claude as a total authority. “Personal Finance is a first step. For life’s bigger money decisions, we think people are best served by Claude working alongside the licensed professionals and regulated firms they trust,” the company said in the announcement.

“We’re exploring how to make that possible in Claude, and we’d like to hear from banks, wealth managers, and financial services companies who want to help shape it” — indicating a more integrated financial planning system within Claude may be on the way.

#3175. Crescent Capital BDC (CCAP) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Buyback and new joint venture unveiled as watch list ticks higher.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Management reported that Crescent Capital BDC, Inc. (CCAP +12.34%) achieved stable net asset value while introducing multiple capital allocation initiatives focused on deleveraging and addressing its stock price discount. The company announced a $50 million share repurchase program and a separate $25 million purchase commitment from parent company Sun Life. To facilitate these actions and return to target leverage ranges, the company is forming a new $150 million joint venture to be seeded with performing first lien assets. Management indicated that despite subdued buyout volume in the broader market, the company maintained improved interest coverage across its diversified portfolio of 190 companies.

Operator: Good morning, and welcome to Crescent Capital BDC, Inc.'s Third Quarter ended September 30, 2026, Earnings Conference Call. Please note that Crescent Capital BDC, Inc. may be referred to as CCAP, Crescent BDC or the company throughout the call. I'll start with some important reminders. Comments made over the course of this conference call and webcast may contain forward-looking statements and are subject to risks and uncertainties. The company's actual results could differ materially from those expressed in such forward-looking statements for any reason, including those listed in its SEC filings. The company assumes no obligation to update any such forward-looking statements. Please also note that past performance or market information is not a guarantee of future results.

I'll now turn the call over to Dan McMahon.

Daniel McMahon: Thank you. Yesterday after the market closed, the company issued its earnings press release for the third quarter ended September 30, 2026, and posted a presentation to the Investor Relations section of its website at www.crescentbdc.com. The presentation should be reviewed in conjunction with the company's Form 10-Q filed yesterday with the SEC. As a reminder, this call is being recorded for replay purposes. Speaking on today's call will be CCAP's Chief Executive Officer, Jason Breaux; Chief Financial Officer, Gerhard Lombard; and President, Henry Chung. With that, I'd now like to turn it over to Jason.

Jason Breaux: Thank you, Dan, and good morning, everyone. I'll begin by reviewing our third quarter results, touch on the current market environment and then outline our key priorities and some of the actions we're announcing today. For the third quarter, we reported net investment income of $0.37 per share, an increase from $0.36 per share in the prior quarter. Our earnings exceeded our $0.34 base dividend, and we also paid the second of our 3 previously announced special dividends of $0.03 per share during the quarter. Our net asset value remained largely stable at $17.72 per share as of September 30 compared with $17.82 at the end of the prior quarter. No new investments were placed on nonaccrual during the quarter.

Turning to the market. Sponsor-backed M&A remained subdued during the third quarter. Direct lending volumes supporting leveraged buyouts was down roughly 21% from the prior quarter and 60% from the third quarter of last year. While limited new buyout activity has moderated new platform financing opportunities and delayed some realizations, demand continues through add-on acquisitions, refinancings and other needs within existing sponsored portfolios. Add-on financings remain an important source of activity for Crescent. Our private credit platform includes more than 250 lower middle market portfolio companies, providing a foundation for originations beyond new LBO transactions. Over the last 12 months, add-on financings accounted for approximately 50% of Crescent's total deal count and 25% of total dollars committed.

Competition for attractive credit remains even as portions of the nontraded BDC market continue to face redemption pressure. In this environment, our long-standing sponsor relationships and familiarity with existing borrowers allow us to remain selective on credit quality, structure and pricing. Despite subdued new activity, the Crescent private credit platform remained active, committing approximately $1.5 billion of capital during the third quarter. As we emphasized last quarter, CCAP remains an important part of Crescent's private credit platform. The permanent fee reductions implemented earlier this year demonstrate Crescent's economic commitment to those objectives. And today, we're building on that commitment with several actions designed to drive NAV accretion by capturing the current discount in our stock.

First, our Board has authorized a $50 million share repurchase program for the purpose of repurchasing shares of our common stock in the open market at certain thresholds below our net asset value per share in accordance with applicable law. We believe our current share price materially undervalues CCAP, making repurchases at substantial discounts to NAV a compelling use of available capital. In addition to the CCAP repurchase program, Crescent's parent entity, Sun Life, will purchase up to an additional $25 million of shares in the open market at certain thresholds below our net asset value per share in accordance with applicable law.

This commitment underscores Sun Life's confidence in CCAP's long-term value and further strengthens the alignment of Sun Life, Crescent and the leadership team with CCAP's shareholders. The timing, manner, price and amount of any share repurchases under the CCAP repurchase program and the Sun Life purchase program will be determined by the company and Sun Life, respectively, in their respective discretion, based upon the evaluation of economic and market conditions, stock price, applicable legal and regulatory requirements and other factors. In order to accelerate share repurchase activity, we expect to announce the formation of an unconsolidated joint venture. The joint venture is expected to be seeded with approximately $150 million of performing first lien assets from CCAP.

CCAP expects to commit $30 million of equity to the joint venture, along with a $30 million expected equity contribution from the joint venture equity partner. In addition to the equity contributions, the joint venture is expected to be capitalized with an ABL facility. We are targeting a low to mid-teens ROE at the joint venture, which we expect to be accretive to our gross yield. The joint venture is expected to be completed during the fourth quarter of 2026. CCAP expects to use the proceeds from the JV to reduce leverage to our target range and fund share repurchases. Together, we believe these actions support our deleveraging objectives and create opportunities for per share accretion.

Finally, I'd like to highlight a recent announcement regarding Crescent's broader platform. On October 26, Sun Life announced GreenOak, a unified global brand, bringing together Crescent, BGO, InfraRed Capital Partners, SLC Fixed Income and Advisors Asset Management. The platform represents approximately $326 billion in assets under management across credit, real estate and infrastructure, supported by a global distribution network. The brand transition will take place over the next 12 months. On the fixed income side, GreenOak brings together Crescent's alternative credit expertise and SLC Fixed Income's investment-grade public and private credit capabilities, providing a broader range of investment solutions and opportunities for collaboration. For CCAP, our investment processes, investment committees and investment personnel remain unchanged.

We will continue to manage the portfolio with the same disciplined underwriting approach and focus on income generation and capital preservation, supported by the resources and reach of the broader GreenOak platform. With that, I'll turn the call over to Gerhard to review our third quarter financial results in more detail. Gerhard?

Gerhard Lombard: Thanks, Jason, and hello, everyone. Net investment income was $0.37 per share for the third quarter, up from $0.36 in the second quarter and covered our $0.34 per share regular dividend. Compared to the second quarter, total investment income increased by approximately $0.6 million to $36.9 million. Interest income increased by approximately $0.9 million to $35.6 million. This was offset by lower dividend income, which declined to approximately $0.9 million from $1.2 million, primarily reflecting lower distributions from the legacy Logan JV as the vehicle continues to run off and deleverage, as discussed in prior quarters.

Total expenses and excise taxes remained stable at $23.2 million with modestly higher financing costs, offset by lower income and excise taxes and professional fees. Turning to the balance sheet. Our investment portfolio totaled approximately $1.6 billion at fair value as of September 30. Total net assets were $653 million or $17.72 per share. On Slide 9, we provide a graphical analysis of the quarter-over-quarter change in NAV. We recorded $0.06 per share of net realized losses, largely offset by reversals of previously recognized unrealized losses on those investments. Net unrealized depreciation, including these reversals, totaled $0.04 per share. Valuation movements reflected slight spread widening, while company-specific credit movements were broadly neutral.

Overall, portfolio valuations were generally stable with NAV per share changing from $17.82 to $17.72. Let's shift to our capitalization and liquidity. I'm on Slide 18. Our debt-to-equity ratio remained 1.42x or 1.36x net of balance sheet cash compared with 1.37x net in the prior quarter. Gross debt outstanding declined to approximately $924 million from $935 million. And cash, cash equivalents and restricted cash totaled approximately $36 million at quarter end. While leverage ended the quarter above our long-term target range, we continue to maintain sufficient liquidity with approximately $247 million of cash and available borrowing capacity as of quarter end.

We expect that pending portfolio realizations and the previously discussed joint venture will bring net leverage to within our target range by year-end. Our Board declared a fourth quarter dividend of $0.34 per share. We will also pay the third and final previously announced special dividend of $0.03 per share on December 15. Our supplemental dividend framework remains in effect, although no supplemental dividend is payable for the quarter under that framework. And with that, I'll turn it over to Henry to discuss the portfolio.

Henry Chung: Thanks, Gerhard. We ended the quarter with approximately $1.6 billion of investments at fair value across 190 portfolio companies. The portfolio remained highly diversified with an average investment size of approximately 0.5% and 91% invested in senior first lien loans. The broader portfolio continues to perform generally in line with our underwriting expectations, with the majority of portfolio companies demonstrating resilient operating performance and year-over-year EBITDA growth. Approximately 84% of investments remained rated 1 or 2, indicating performance at or above expectations. Our weighted average portfolio risk rating remained at 2.1 and weighted average interest coverage improved to 2.3x. Turning to Slide 16.

Our watch list increased modestly from 15% to 16% of the portfolio at fair value, driven by 3-rated investments increasing from 12% to 13%. Investments rated 4 and 5 declined from approximately 3% to 2.4%. We had no new nonaccruals during the quarter. Nonaccruals declined from 4.8% to 4.7% of debt investments at cost, reflecting the sale of a small legacy First Eagle investment previously on nonaccrual. Measured against the total investment portfolio at cost, nonaccruals were 4.4%. Moving to investment activity, with leverage currently above our target range, our new investment activity was limited during the third quarter in order to prioritize deleveraging.

Gross deployment totaled $24 million, the majority of which consisted of follow-on investments in existing portfolio companies. Aggregate exits, sales and repayments totaled approximately $39 million, resulting in net realizations of approximately $15 million for the quarter. With that, I'll turn it back to Jason for closing remarks.

Jason Breaux: Thank you, Henry. Before we open the call for questions, I'd like to leave you with a few closing thoughts. Our primary focus remains the rotation of our watch list. The work remains ongoing and active portfolio management remains a critical component of driving strong recovery outcomes over the long term. Crescent's alignment with our shareholders has been a critical component of how we manage CCAP. Today's $50 million share repurchase authorization and separate $25 million investment by Sun Life build on the permanent fee reductions implemented earlier this year. These initiatives demonstrate the continued commitment of Crescent and Sun Life to CCAP. Finally, we look forward to the opportunities for greater collaboration across the GreenOak platform.

A unified market approach, combined with the continuity of Crescent's investment teams and disciplined investment processes, positions us to build on more than 3 decades of private credit experience for the benefit of CCAP's shareholders. On behalf of the entire Crescent team, I'd like to thank our shareholders for their continued support and confidence. Operator, we'd now be happy to take your questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Your first question comes from the line of Christopher Nolan with Ladenburg Thalmann.

Christopher Nolan: For the JV announcement, are you guys looking to this to be the first of multiple JVs down the line?

Henry Chung: Chris, this is Henry speaking. As far as the JV goes, we've done a JV in the past. We had one in place in 2019, which we fully realized and wound down in the '22 time frame. This particular JV is in line with our stated objectives here of deleveraging as well as funding share repurchases. And as we sit here today, we are not contemplating any further JVs in the near term.

Christopher Nolan: Okay. And then the comments were that the JV is expected to generate low to mid-teen returns. I presume that's return to the JV equity holders. So we should be looking for mid-teen potentially returns from this investment or from the scheduled investments?

Henry Chung: That's correct. And as noted in prepared remarks, the JV will be capitalized both with equity capital from CCAP and the JV partner as well as asset-based leverage facility at the JV level. The combination of the leverage as well as the underlying assets here will deliver that mid-teens ROE that we referenced.

Christopher Nolan: And if I may, just one last one. Your average debt portfolio yields are 9.6%, which tends to be on the low end of the spectrum for BDCs. Is the JV part of a strategy to raise that average portfolio yield?

Jason Breaux: The strategy around the JV is really focused on our core near-term strategic initiatives around deleveraging the balance sheet at CCAP to within our target leverage range as well as creating excess capacity for share repurchases. So I would say that while it is accretive to the gross yield of the portfolio as a whole, the rationale for the JV and the formation of the JV is really focused on those 2 former strategic goals of ours.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Finian O'Shea with Wells Fargo.

Finian O'Shea: I'll stick with the JV. Can you give some color on the sort of quantum and nature of assets that you'll drop down in the beginning and the sort of mix of old and new origination that are planned to ramp it?

Henry Chung: Fin, this is Henry. I could take that. To start, the JV will be capitalized with approximately $150 million to establish the seed portfolio. It's going to be a diversified seed portfolio, all first lien that takes into account the composition of both the JV and the remaining CCAP portfolio. The -- in terms of the future capitalization of the JV, we expect the sizing to be around $150 million to $200 million in total size going forward here. So we don't expect the size to meaningfully grow as far as the asset profile of the JV goes. It's going to be consistent with the broader CCAP portfolio focusing on first lien investments.

Finian O'Shea: So should we expect the buyback to be rather swiftly executed?

Jason Breaux: Fin, it's Jason. I think that's -- part of the objective here is to accelerate the ability to generate liquidity and deleveraging for CCAP so that we can both get leverage into our target range as well as start to capture some of the discount on the stock price through buybacks.

Henry Chung: Just to add to that, the buybacks are going to be executed through a broker under our Rule 10b5-1 plan. So the pace of the buyback is going to be subject to the plan's trading parameters as well as the applicable regulatory requirements.

Finian O'Shea: Okay. That's helpful. And one more. Jason, you gave some color on the GreenOak reorg rebranding and flagged that as a line of support to the BDC. Can you talk about what changes, what improves for the CCAP BDC under GreenOak?

Jason Breaux: Yes, Fin, thanks for the question. The GreenOak announcement is really bringing together a variety of capabilities that sit within Sun Life across credit, real estate, infrastructure and on the credit side, both investment grade as well as below investment grade. I think it's going to be able -- it's going to enable us to really represent ourselves as more of a unified brand and go-to-market with more solutions for our clients and sponsors. But as far as CCAP goes specifically, I don't anticipate any change to the investment strategy at CCAP. CCAP is a direct lending focused strategy, servicing the lower and core middle market for sponsor-backed companies and expect that to continue to be the case.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Paul Johnson with KBW.

Paul Johnson: Fin asked the question, but I'll just ask you one more time, maybe a slightly different way. But is there any component, I guess, of the buyback that's governed by the pace of repayments and sales to the JV as that capital becomes available?

Henry Chung: Yes. The pace of the buybacks for the JV, the primary governor there is going to be the parameters of the 10b5-1 plan. As noted, the rationale for the JV itself is to create excess capital and liquidity to be able to fund those purchases without -- I should say, while maintaining leverage within our leverage target range. So if you think about the parameters and the governors around pacing, the primary governor, I would think of as the 10b5-1 plan trading parameters itself as well as the other related regulatory requirements.

Paul Johnson: Okay. Got it. And in terms of new originations, you have some near-term dynamic with offloading some investments into the new JV. But I guess like how long would you expect to sort of gate originations in CCAP in order to, I guess, continue to create capacity for the buyback? I mean do you expect to be kind of continued for the duration of buyback as long as, I guess, it's active? Or do you see any point, I guess, within next year where you kind of return to sort of a more normalized origination cadence?

Henry Chung: It's going to depend on the pace of realizations within the portfolio itself. A few quarters ago, we stated that our goal here when we had net leverage above our target net leverage range was to get that back within our range by year-end. As we noted in prepared remarks, rotation activity has just been slow given that we've been in a bit of a quieter LBO environment, particularly in the second half of the year to date. And as a result, the rationale for pursuing the JV part of that was to accelerate that path to deleveraging by year-end.

And then the other component of that was to create that excess capacity relative to our leverage range to be able to buy back shares, just given where the stock is trading today. Based on where we are -- there are -- we are expecting further, I would say, organic portfolio realizations by year-end. And depending on the pace of further rotation within the portfolio, we would look to replace that with new originations just that are generated across the Crescent platform here. But I would think of the primary governor there as, first, the pace of just the organic rotation of the portfolio.

And secondly, where we are relative to our target leverage range, factoring in realizations as well as buyback activity.

Paul Johnson: Okay. Got it. And in terms of the consolidation of the asset manager, I guess, I'd ask what -- how much or what percentage does private credit AUM? And maybe if I can go one step further sort of this core middle market overlapping AUM with CCAP's portfolio, does that sort of represent within the broader AUM of the consolidated asset manager?

Jason Breaux: Paul, let me take a stab at that. And if I didn't answer your question, give me another try. But -- so if you think about GreenOak broadly as over $300 billion of AUM, credit is inclusive of below investment grade and investment grade would be over $200 billion of that $300 billion of AUM. And then when you drill down a bit further, if you think about Crescent AUM today, which is all below IG credit, that's about $54 billion, $55 billion of AUM today, of which 3/4 of that is below investment grade private credit, so call it $40-plus billion or so is below IG private.

Operator: Your last question comes from the line of Mickey Schleien with Clear Street.

Mickey Schleien: Just wanted to touch on the pipeline with earnings season amongst the BDC sort of coming to a close. I've pretty consistently heard optimism about the M&A pipeline going into year-end and potentially into next year, given some reduction in macroeconomic uncertainty. I'm not sure I agree, but I'm very interested in understanding how you're thinking about the scope of the pipeline relative to everything that's going on, whether it's uncertainty about what the Fed is going to do or the Iran war or changes in Washington, et cetera?

Henry Chung: This is Henry. I can start off there. I think what we've observed here, just really in the second half of the year, and part of that is attributed to several of those macro factors that you referenced are that the LBO environment, particularly within where we focus in the lower and core middle market, just has been quite a bit quieter relative to the first half of the year. And even if you were to look at the same time period on a year-over-year basis.

I will say that there's certainly a lot of early looks and early reads out there, which may indicate that the pipeline going into the end of the year, beginning of next year will be quite a bit more robust in terms of deal activity. But where we sit here today in terms of just broader activity within our core market segments has quite candidly just been a bit quieter relative to what we've seen at the beginning of the year.

Mickey Schleien: And it sounds like your expectations for next year are for things to more or less remain as is. Is that correct?

Jason Breaux: Mickey, Jason Breaux here. Look, I think that right now, as Henry said that the pipeline is pretty light. What doesn't change is the continued pressure from investors for liquidity and monetizations. And with each passing day, those pressures continue to build. So there is a fair amount of, what I would call, macro uncertainty out there that is restricting some activity at this point in time. But I think we still do believe that there will be a pickup in activity going into 2027, simply driven by really more of the concern around investors needing to see liquidity from their sponsors.

Henry Chung: I think to add to that as well -- I was going to just add, what we've observed historically is that the pipeline can turn back on relatively quickly here as well. As I indicated, there's quite a bit of early preemptive deal work going on, I would say, within the market segments that we focus on, both on the sell side, where there's early looks or reads and valuations for companies that are looking to trade. So based on that, when we think about just the backlog that is resident within the core lower middle market, there certainly is the addressable market.

I think what we're just looking for here is the volumes to actually convert in the near term.

Operator: Your final question comes from the line of Robert Dodd with Raymond James.

Robert Dodd: A lot going on. I hate to go back to the JV. But if I can, on that, is that intended to be a permanent vehicle? I mean it sounds from the way you're describing it that you're selling assets down into it primarily to release liquidity for buybacks and deleveraging. And that could obviously be done if it was kind of a static pool vehicle with a static pool CLO kind of structure. And then it would attrite away over some period of time. So I mean is this meant to be a permanent JV vehicle? Or is this a tool that may have a finite life for you?

Henry Chung: Robert, this is Henry. It's -- I would think of it as a -- this is not a static pool where we're establishing a seed portfolio and having that runoff on this JV will be reinvesting. And our expectation in the near term, we'll continue to manage it as a permanent part of the CCAP portfolio, albeit it will be -- we're expecting roughly 2% of the portfolio going forward. Longer term, we'll continue to evaluate that relative to broader origination that we're seeing across the space. But for the near term, I would not consider this a one-off static pool, and we are expecting to replenish assets into the JV as the initial seed portfolio rotates.

Robert Dodd: Got it. Got it. And on the credit, obviously, I mean, nonaccruals improved a little bit. There was a legacy asset gone there. It takes a while to turn these. Your 3s ticked up a little bit. So I mean, it sounds rather like credit is kind of stable, but not where you'd want it to be, but stable. I mean can you give us any update? And I realize, again, it doesn't change very quickly quarter-to-quarter, but on like how the restructuring or turnaround progress is going within the troubled asset pool that you have?

Henry Chung: This is Henry. I could take that. I would say that with respect to the watch list, I would agree with your observations that we are seeing stability where we sit today relative to underwriting expectations and additions to the watch list that we have seen this quarter are really due to company-specific challenges that we're seeing in certain portfolio companies as opposed to broader credit degradation as a whole across the portfolio.

With that being said, and I think this is something that we've continually been clear about here is, especially in an environment like we're in today, where portfolio turnover velocity has just been muted, given the LBO environment that we're in, I would expect that the rotation of assets, particularly those on the watch list, are just going to be longer-term exercises in terms of maximizing recovery. We're not looking to fire sale any assets just to get them off the watch list.

And as a result, we're prepared and looking to maximize long-term recoveries by taking a long-term approach to each of these assets, whether it's truly just a one-off short-term watch list inclusion or a longer-term change of control. So hopefully, that gives you some color in terms of just what we're observing to date, but our expectation here is that we'll continue to look towards maximizing longer-term recoveries with respect to the watch list.

Operator: We have one more question from Christopher Nolan with Ladenburg Thalmann.

Christopher Nolan: Given the slow LBO market and so forth, is that forcing you guys to extend the maturity of maturing investments?

Henry Chung: Thanks for the question, Chris. We've seen that become more prevalent within investments where sponsors are electing to extend duration for investments as opposed to looking to sell them today at current valuations. And what we're seeing here is that this is not necessarily indicative of companies that are in stress, but more so a determination from the sponsor's perspective that there's further value creation that can happen at the underlying portfolio companies, whether it be organically or inorganically. And as a result, they're looking for -- from support from the lenders to be able to continue to execute on their equity thesis.

Typically, how we approach these discussions is it's an opportunity for us to reprice the respective loans when those asks come across. So what you'll typically see in conjunction with an extension ask is fees or an increase in spread or both. So we take that as an opportunity to reunderwrite as well as reprice the loan to the extent that we would like to stay in the loan. And to the extent that we would not like to stay in the loan, then we elect to get taken out. So that's our approach, but we're absolutely in an environment where extension asks are certainly more commonplace than they have been several years ago.

Operator: There are no further questions at this time. I will now turn the call back to Jason Breaux for closing remarks.

Jason Breaux: Okay. Thank you, operator. And I just wanted to say thank you to our shareholders and analysts for their interest in CCAP and all the questions, and we look forward to speaking with everyone again soon.

Operator: This concludes today's call. Thank you for attending. You may now disconnect.

New this year is Camera Looks, a setting that changes how images will be processed before you take them. To change this, head to Settings > Display > Screen Resolution. Bump the setting from “High resolution,” which is 1080 x 2404, to “Max resolution,” which is 1344 x 2992.

We’ve all accidentally swiped away an important notification or missed a notification in a sea of updates. The Pixel 11 offers two notification features to help you stay on top of things.

Notification History is a feature that logs every alert from the last 24 hours, including those you swipe away. This is off by default, meaning when you dismiss a notification, it’s gone forever. With this on, you get a searchable, chronological backup.

AI Notification Summaries, as the name implies, takes long multi-notification threads and stacked notifications and turns them into bullet points. This feature is powered by on-device Gemini Intelligence, and you can choose which apps to summarize.

You can find both of these under Settings > Notifications > Notification history & Notification Summaries.

Most HR professionals say they believe employees can be reskilled for AI jobs, yet companies still often seek outside hires. Here's why.

HR leaders are confident that current employees can be trained for jobs created by artificial intelligence. Organizations are hiring externally instead.

That’s the finding in new research from Careerminds, a global provider of workforce solutions. The study, published in Careerminds’ white paper, The AI Redeployment Gap: What Companies Lose by Hiring over Reskilling, reveals that 92% of HR professionals and 88% of people managers believe employees within their organizations could be reskilled for AI-related roles.

Also: Nearly 70% of workers use AI regularly now – but many get no time to upskill

Yet 51% of HR professionals and 47% of people managers report that their organizations are hiring externally for new AI-related positions, compared with just 42% in each group who report redeploying existing employees.

The research was conducted in partnership with Censuswide and surveyed 595 US HR professionals and 547 US people managers, ages 25–65, working at organizations with 500-10,000 or more employees. The research was conducted May 15–26, 2026.

Also: Businesses finally seeing AI ROI, but 62% can’t handle the storage demands

“Companies are investing in AI while potentially overlooking one of their most valuable resources: the people they already employ,” said Mark Saddic, senior partner at Careerminds, in a press release.

“Our research shows that organizations largely believe their employees can adapt to AI-driven change, but that confidence isn’t consistently translating into opportunities. Before looking outside the organization, leaders need to understand the skills they already have, identify where employees can grow, and establish a clear process for making those transitions possible.”

Reskilling, especially for AI, isn’t easy to track. Limited visibility into individual skill sets and which employees should be reskilled was cited as a potential barrier by 43% of HR professionals and 34% of managers.

Also: Pearson’s Workera deal targets a big workplace problem: No time to AI upskill

It’s not the first time that the management of skills development has come up regarding AI. In September, educational giant Pearson agreed to acquire Workera, the AI-native skills platform used by organizations such as ServiceNow, Accenture, and the US Space Force.

Careermind’s data revealed that 87% of HR pros and 84% of managers believe their organizations are adequately considering reskilling employees for future roles. However, the findings suggest that these organizations may believe they are prioritizing internal talent development, even though their hiring practices reveal otherwise.

Response to AI-related workforce needs isn’t equal across the board. The findings reveal significant differences in how industries are responding to these needs.

Also: Your AI-polished resumes are recruiters’ new top stressor

For example, in the technology and telecom industries, external hiring outpaces redeployment by 15%. At the same time, media and entertainment is the only sector surveyed in which both groups report redeployment at least as frequently as external hiring. Among HR professionals in that industry, 56% report redeploying employees, compared with just 25% who hire externally.

Separate research from The Josh Bersin Company, cited in the Careerminds white paper, reveals that external hiring can cost three to five times more than filling comparable roles internally — and on average takes up to 20 days longer.

#3170. NASA’s Voyager 1 to Cross Historic One Light-Day Milestone on Nov. 18

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Traveling one light-day took the space probe 49 years. it would take a human 612,015 years to walk that distance.

NASA’s Voyager 1 spacecraft is on track to set another historic record as its mission approaches the half-century mark. On Nov. 18 at 5:16 a.m. ET, the probe will reach a distance of one light-day from Earth, a journey of nearly five decades that places it farther from our planet than any human-made object in history.

It’s quite an accomplishment for a spacecraft built in the mid-1970s One light-day is the distance that light travels in a single day at the speed of light, which is approximately 186,282 miles per second. That translates to 25.9 billion kilometers or about 16.1 billion miles in a single day. At an average human walking speed of 3 mph, it would take a human 612,015 years to walk that distance.

Fortunately, Voyager 1 has been traveling a bit faster than that. It currently zips along the cosmos at a steady 37,763 mph, a speed it achieved in 1980 after a gravity-assisted Saturn flyby. It has been flying at that speed ever since.

The milestone comes 14 years after its previous one, when Voyager 1 crossed the heliopause, the point where the sun’s heliosphere ends, and entered interstellar space. It’s also 28 years after passing Pioneer 10 to become the human-made object that has traveled the farthest into space.

The historic milestone isn’t without its drama. Voyager 1 has been in space for nearly half a century, and in that time, NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory has done everything it can to extend the life of Voyager 1. That includes troubleshooting issues, performing maintenance and shutting down various systems to save power and extend the spacecraft’s life-span.

Several of those efforts took place in 2026. The team running Voyager 1 spent weeks shutting down three devices and powering on three low-power alternatives to reduce overall power usage. This initiative, which was internally called The Big Bang, was also performed on Voyager 2. The transition was completed in early September, giving Voyager 1 more time with its dwindling power supply while also keeping it warm enough to continue operating in the frigid conditions of interstellar space.

It was a tricky maneuver that required the team to simultaneously turn multiple instruments on and off. The difficulty of the maneuver was amplified by the fact that it took almost a full day for any signal to reach Voyager and another full day for Voyager to send a signal back, with hours of downtime while the spacecraft performed the operations.

All of this took place several months after Voyager 1 experienced a sudden drop in power, which necessitated shutting off one of its three remaining instruments still in operation. Voyager 1 now has only two instruments still in operation.

Making it a whole light-day away from Earth is likely going to be Voyager 1’s final milestone while it still has enough power to communicate with Earth. Voyager 1 is powered by three radioisotope thermoelectric generators. They are essentially nuclear-powered batteries that generate energy by converting the steady heat from decaying plutonium-238.

When Voyager 1 first launched, its radioisotope thermoelectric generators produced about 470 watts of power. But plutonium-238 doesn’t last forever, and after 50 years in space, the RTGs now produce about 215 watts of power, with an average loss of about 4 watts per year. Most of that power is used to keep Voyager 1 up and running, which is why NASA has shut down eight of the 10 instruments that Voyager had when it launched.

At its current rate of usage and decay, Voyager 1 is expected to shut down its final science instrument in the 2030s and will eventually lose communication with Earth in 2036 due to insufficient power to send back a radio signal.

The same fate is expected for Voyager 2, Voyager 1’s twin, which has also spent half a century in space. While it is labeled the sequel, Voyager 2 actually launched 16 days before Voyager 1, and the two have spent nearly identical amounts of time traversing the cosmos. Thanks to its slower speed and trajectory, it likely won’t reach the one light-day distance until after its instruments shut down.

Thanks to the vastness of space, Voyager 1 will lose all of its power before it hits its next milestone, which is the beginning of the Oort Cloud, a vast, icy shell of comets at the edge of our solar system. It’ll take about 300 years for Voyager 1 to make it there.

Thanks to the near-perfect vacuum of outer space, Voyager 1 will continue to fly at its current speed even after it shuts down entirely. So it’ll still hit that milestone; it just won’t be able to phone home to tell us about it.

#3169. Apple will monitor your public iCloud links now, starting with iOS 27.3

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Under Apple's new policy, the company will scan publicly shared iCloud links for harmful content - and possibly ban violators.

Be careful what you share in your iCloud. Apple announced it will start monitoring public iCloud links for harmful content — and potentially disable accounts that violate company policy.

Also: How to free up your iPhone storage almost immediately

The change comes with the impending release of Apple’s 27.3 build across its operating systems. If an iCloud user selects “Anyone with the link” when sharing something in a group chat or Discord server, it’s considered a public link; Apple is within its rights to scan for anything that violates company policy or is potentially illegal.

If you try to upload harmful content, Apple says it reserves the right to “move, refuse, modify, remove, or delete” your content at any time. Furthermore, Apple outlines possible actions it may take, including:

Apple’s announcement did not explain what “harmful content” would mean in practice. While there are obvious violations like drug sales and child sex abuse material, the new policy’s vagueness is concerning.

Once an iCloud link is shared under the “Anyone with a link” designation, end-to-end encryption is removed, even if either party has enabled Advanced Data Protection, which allows Apple to view the link’s content.

If you select “People you choose,” which limits access to users who have been invited or approved, the encryption remains in place, and Apple won’t be able to see what you’re sharing.

The new policy does not lay out an appeals process if you think your account or content has been falsely flagged as harmful. However, Apple does have a web page that provides information on how to appeal for other reasons. So there is a framework in place to push back if you think you’ve been caught in the dragnet by accident.

Grail, Agility Robotics, and Sandisk could deliver multibagger gains in the future.

It might not seem like the best time to invest in high-growth stocks. Elevated Treasury yields are still weighing down stocks, and the market is digesting the impact of the midterm elections -- in which the Democrats took over the House, Senate, and several governorships.

But if you can look past those near-term challenges, you'll find plenty of promising growth stocks that could deliver massive gains for investors who can stomach a little volatility. Let's see why three of those growth stocks -- Grail (GRAL -2.61%), Agility Robotics (AGLT +4.56%), and Sandisk (SNDK -2.99%) -- could be a great place to lock up a fresh $10,000 investment.

Grail develops Galleri, a blood test designed to detect dozens of cancers before any symptoms appear. The FDA hasn't approved Galleri yet, but Grail sells it on a cash-only basis to affluent customers, certain businesses, and hospital pilot programs for about $949 per test.

Through those cash sales, Grail's revenue rose from $93 million in 2023 to $147 million in 2025. But by 2028, analysts expect its revenue to reach $275 million as an FDA approval expands its market to include private insurance and Medicare plans. In late September, the FDA endorsed a premarket approval for Galleri based on its safety, efficacy, and potential benefits. Those endorsements are non-binding, but they suggest it could be fully approved in the near future.

With a market cap of $5.8 billion, Grail isn't cheap at 34 times this year's sales. But if the FDA fully approves its blood test, it could grow much larger as it's adopted by more hospitals. That's why its stock still has more upside potential -- even after its 44% year-to-date gain.

Agility Robotics, a developer of humanoid robots for warehouses, logistics hubs, and manufacturing plants, went public through a merger with a special purpose acquisition company (SPAC) on Nov. 4. Its stock opened at $11.38 per share on Nov. 5, but it's pulled back to about $9 as of this writing. However, it could have plenty of room to grow.

Agility's flagship robot, Digit, can move heavy items and navigate aisles, stairs, and ramps on its own. Its top investors include Nvidia and Amazon. Its growing list of enterprise customers includes Toyota, GXO Logistics, MercadoLibre, and Schaffer.

Agility only generated $1.8 million in revenue in 2025, and it hasn't deployed its first Digit v5 robots yet. However, it has a backlog of over $300 million. Agility believes it can deploy its first Digit v5 robots by the end of 2026, and accelerate its annual deployments to 800 units in 2027, 7,000 units in 2030, and up to 25,000 units in 2035. To keep those robots running, its customers will need to pay recurring "robot as a service" (RaaS) subscription fees.

With a market cap of $489 million, Agility might seem expensive relative to its near-term revenue growth. But at its estimated $8,500 monthly RaaS rate, it could generate $2.55 billion in annual revenue from 25,000 deployed robots. That's why Agility's stock could deliver multibagger gains over the next few years as economies of scale kick in.

Sandisk, which was spun off from Western Digital in early 2025, is one of the world's largest producers of NAND (flash) memory chips. Its stock has declined 64% after hitting a record high of $2,335 on June 25, but that pullback could be a golden buying opportunity.

Sandisk is usually considered a cyclical stock that follows the memory market's boom-and-bust cycles. But as the AI market expanded over the past few years, Sandisk launched ultra-dense enterprise solid-state drives (SSDs) that consolidated dozens of hardware server racks onto single drives. These SSDs are also smaller, faster, more power-efficient, and less prone to physical damage than platter-based hard disk drives (HDDs).

In fiscal 2026 (which ended this July), Sandisk's revenue surged 176% as it turned profitable. From fiscal 2026 to fiscal 2029, analysts expect its revenue and EPS to grow at CAGRs of 44% and 62%, respectively. It looks ridiculously cheap at 4 times this year's earnings -- because it's still valued as a cyclical stock -- but it could command a much higher valuation if the AI market's acceleration continues to boost its enterprise SSD sales.

The new Claude models show greatly improved metrics in areas like coding (don’t they all?), reasoning, vision, cybersecurity and biology. The latter of which have strong safeguards against misuse in the Fable model, which give Anthropic enough confidence to release it to the public.

Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 generate output up to 30% faster than their predecessors and are available at lower prices — a trend we’ve continued to see lately with most new AI model releases.

Anthropic dropped a series of benchmarks showing off how much better the new models are compared with the previous ones. And generally, they’re impressive. Fable 5.2 outperforms Fable 5.1 in one agentic coding benchmark at 49.1% versus 32.4% at “Xhigh effort,” bringing a meaningful distance in performance. As far as cybersecurity benchmarks are concerned, Mythos 5.2 scores a jump from 61.7% to 76.3% — a rather impressive jump — if you’re using the model to its fullest potential.

Anthropic says Claude Mythos 5.2 is its most capable model for cybersecurity engineering. The new model is capable of catching more vulnerabilities and is better at reproducing and fixing them. That said, Mythos 5.2’s cybersecurity features are locked to a specific group right now: Anthropic’s Cyber Verification Program.

The company boasted about enhanced capabilities in the latest model improvements in mathematics, science and engineering. It also says that testers of Fable 5.2 found the new model more capable of more ambiguous tasks that require abstract reasoning when it came to research and analysis.

Anthropic makes a big deal about the alignment of Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2. Alignment tracks whether and how the intention of the (human) user is executed by the model. And as agentic AI becomes more prevalent, there are more stories of AI deciding to go out of its way to complete a task, even with devastating consequences. Fable 5.2 includes guardrails that block risky cybersecurity activities — like penetration testing and exploit generation — and advanced biology capabilities.

If you open an app and ask Siri what it can do in the app, the digital assistant should give you some examples of its capabilities.

#3159. Alpine Linux and OpenSSH patch flaw that’s as bad as it can get

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

This dangerous Linux security hole must be patched as soon as possible.

The perfect nightmare scenario for a Linux server is when all an attacker needs to do is reach the server’s Secure Shell (SSH) port, waltz right in, and take it over. That’s what happened to Alpine Linux, the popular, lightweight Linux server. Adding insult to injury, this happened only days after Alpine Linux dodged a security hole-sized bullet to its GitLab implementation.

Also: Linux Mint 27 arrives next month, and I like it already: What to expect

How bad is it? As bad as it can get. Alpine Linux explained in its security advisory that if an attacker can reach a vulnerable server’s SSH port, they can get in “with one connection,” and the attack “works every time, and needs no retries.”

As security engineer Gregory Bryant explained in his LinkedIn post:

Most authentication bypasses come from complex logic chains, but yesterday’s Alpine Linux OpenSSH vulnerability (CVE-2026-123158) comes down to a single character: *.”

If you run Alpine Linux (or another musl-based distro) with the default openssh-server package (no Pluggable Authentication Modules (PAM)) and PasswordAuthentication enabled, an attacker can log into password-disabled, or key-only accounts simply by sending a password between 257 and 1024 bytes long.

Alpine Linux isn’t the only operating system that uses musl, a lightweight version of the standard C library (libc). Other operating systems that use musl and are potentially vulnerable include Adélie Linux; Void Linux; Sabotage Linux; OpenWrt, an Android variant,  and the Yocto Project, which is used to build embedded Linux distributions.

Also: This clever banking scam keeps phishing by faking its own demise

Wind River, which produces the commercial embedded Linux distro, Wind River Linux, is also looking into the issue. A company representative told me, “Wind River takes security seriously. We are actively reviewing the reported vulnerability and assessing its potential impact. We will take appropriate action as needed.”

Behind the scenes, when OpenSSH is built without PAM, it verifies passwords by hashing the password attempt using the C library’s crypt() function. It then compares the result to the account’s stored password field. So far, so good.

But when a key is longer than 256 bytes, musl’s crypt() function returns the string * as an error indicator. That is also what the password field holds for any account with no password, such as a key-only account. Thus, the “hash” matches and the login succeeds, and the attacker walks in.

Also: The new Cutefish Linux distro might be the best MacOS clone around

To exploit it, an attacker only needs the name of such an account. The attacker also needs at least one other account on the machine with a 5 or 6 password hash, and then to send a password of 257 to 1,024 bytes. According to Alpine, one user with a password is enough to make every passwordless account accessible.

In Linux systems that use glibc’s crypt(), which is almost all of them, the same attempt would return NULL on error, which sshd already rejects, so Debian, Ubuntu, Fedora, etc., aren’t affected.

According to *sshole, the group that uncovered the problem, this is a side effect that has been hiding since 2016.

Alpine said every release it checked is affected: 3.21 through 3.24, edge, and the older 3.16 to 3.20 branches. Exposure requires the following:

Root is not directly exposed in most cases. It has shipped as root:* in the base image since about Alpine 3.16, but OpenSSH’s default PermitRootLogin prohibit-password blocks it. Another account that can become root, for example through doas, still gives an attacker a route to root.

Alpine singled out its official tiny-cloud images, versions 3.18.11 through 3.24.3, as especially vulnerable. These ship with an alpine user with a * password field and passwordless doas. They are safe on first boot but become exploitable once any 6 hash exists on the machine. That can happen when an administrator sets a console password or when user data adds a user with a hashed password, which means, essentially, all of them.

Alpine released 3.21.10, 3.22.8, 3.23.8 and 3.24.4 on Thursday, with the OpenSSH fix among the security changes. It also published fixed packages for each release back to 3.16. Alpine 3.21 reached end of support on Nov. 1.

The just-released OpenSSH 10.6p2 avoids the problem in sshd. Alpine’s stable branches carry a patch for the same problem. You should run apk upgrade -U -a and then restart the daemon with rc-service sshd restart. Alpine stressed that upgrading the package does not replace the running daemon. Anyone who cannot update should set PasswordAuthentication no and restart sshd, after confirming that key login works.

Also: Maze Linux is the best security-focused distro I’ve ever tested

To check for an attack, Alpine told administrators to search /var/log/messages for “Accepted password for” lines that name an account with no password. It also advised reviewing dedicated OpenBSD application subexecutor (doas) use and recently created users, files, and authorized keys. “If you cannot rule out a login, treat the machine as compromised.” Just what you wanted for your weekend, I know, but here we are.
