#3158. AI-Driven Tech Layoffs Could Trigger a 1.6 Million Job Recession

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

With more than 200,000 job cuts in the tech industry in 2026, the bigger question is if layoffs will spread to retail and finance.

When Meta began laying off 8,000 people in May, it felt like an omen. Meta, the parent company of Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp, had seen several high-profile failures, from the death of the metaverse to its multibillion-dollar court setbacks. The Magnificent Seven — the tech giants that drive US stock market gains — seemed to hit a plateau over the last year, as more investors expressed concern about a potential AI bubble.

A wave of recent tech layoffs and buyouts reveals a growing volatility in the tech industry, as major companies restructure to cut costs and redirect spending toward AI. In just the last few weeks, Google extended its voluntary buyout program to select employees in five countries, and the graphic design platform Canva reduced its staff by 22%, laying off or relocating 1,271 employees.

Companies that have laid off or offered buyouts to 1,000 or more employees this year include Microsoft (60,000), Oracle (21,000), Amazon (17,000 in addition to 14,000 in 2025), Uber (3,300) and Netflix (1,000). According to the TrueUp tech layoffs tracker, layoffs are accelerating faster than last year, with over 200,000 workers reduced so far in 2026. The cuts aren’t limited to struggling companies, but are affecting profitable organizations with strong revenues.

The dominant factor behind layoffs has been AI. Companies have spent billions of dollars on the technology, plus a terrifying $3.2 trillion (with a “T”) that, Goldman Sachs says, doesn’t show up on balance sheets. With current returns failing to justify the massive scale of capital expenditure, companies are slashing labor costs and relying on AI to offset the resulting productivity losses.

While the US isn’t officially in a recession (yet), there are growing fears that mass layoffs could spread to other sectors, such as retailers and financial companies, creating a large wave of workforce reductions in the country. Analysts warn that if job losses extend beyond the tech industry, it could result in another 1.6 million people being laid off, bringing the formal unemployment rate closer to recession-level.

With several economic pressures at play — inflation, higher interest rates and rising energy and computing costs — buyouts and layoffs allow company executives to reduce operating expenses while investing heavily in AI infrastructure, automation and specialized technical talent. That hasn’t worked out in all cases. A handful of companies, including Salesforce and Ford, ended up rehiring or hiring new people after AI-driven layoffs.

Even companies currently reducing their workforce, such as Canva, appear to be offering friendly terms, potentially to avoid burning bridges. As part of its severance package, Canva gave outgoing employees $10,000 grants, MacBooks, six months of salary and a year of healthcare. For many workers without a union contract, that will be the best-case scenario if the economy goes south.

Canva’s terms for departing employees are both exceedingly generous and a window into modern tech:* Six months salary* A year healthcare* A year of LinkedIn premium* A $10k grant to start a business* Keep your MacBook https://t.co/Hqdegdb8Ek pic.twitter.com/pKuj8lJDvB

Job instability, stagnant wages and rising prices have been the norm for several years, arguably since the last major US recession in 2020, at the start of the pandemic. Given that recessions historically occur about every six years (regardless of which party is in the White House), a larger downturn could be on the horizon, especially if an AI market correction triggers further stock declines and widespread layoffs. If high-cost data centers lose clients and major IPOs falter, enterprises will likely slash spending and jobs as the promise of AI-driven efficiency fades.

So far, layoffs don’t appear to be spreading to other industries, and overall job cuts are the lowest since 2022. But the job market has become increasingly precarious, especially for younger workers, according to Lisa Countryman-Quiroz, CEO of JVS Bay Area, a workforce nonprofit.

For example, entry-level hires are down by a third in the most AI-exposed occupations since 2021, which could affect sectors like retail and finance —typical entry-level gateways for many young people. Household wages aren’t keeping up with expenses, and many job seekers have found themselves unemployed for more than six months. “While we may or may not see broadening layoffs, I’m concerned about the erosion of stable career pathways,” Countryman-Quiroz said. The one bright spot seems to be in healthcare, with 42,000 jobs added last month.

The 2026 midterm elections could also indirectly affect tech layoffs, mainly due to changes in the political and regulatory environment around AI and data centers. In the lead-up to the midterms, the backlash against data centers and tech billionaires became a pressing issue for candidates. Campaigns around data center moratoriums helped some Democratic candidates, including Gina Hinojosa, the surprise gubernatorial winner in Texas, where Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk has his home and business headquarters.

Pausing new data center construction will be a shot in the arm for communities protesting the drain of AI infrastructure on local resources. But any slowdown in the buildout could also reduce demand for construction, chip suppliers or technical roles tied to AI expansion.

The midterm elections also affected financial markets, with technology and AI-linked stocks falling as investors worried that Democrats might impose new guardrails on AI. A weaker market can often make companies more cautious about hiring, capital spending and staffing, which could exacerbate cost-cutting pressures and lead to more layoffs and buyouts.

Countryman-Quiroz suggested that Congress could address AI’s disruption by investing in more job training, especially in growing areas like healthcare. “Current federal funding is only sufficient to train about 200,000 workers per year, a fraction of what’s needed,” she said. “Workforce development has historically enjoyed bipartisan support, so there is an opportunity for both parties to work together on solutions.”

#3157. Why AST SpaceMobile Plunged Today

Strong revenue growth wasn't enough to offset competitive and interest rate concerns.

Shares of AST SpaceMobile (ASTS -8.67%) were down as much as 13.4% on Tuesday, before recovering to an 8.7% decline following the release of the company's third-quarter earnings report.

The results likely didn't matter as much in the wake of today's hotter-than-expected inflation report. AST currently has very little revenue, so a potential rise in interest rates disproportionately reduces the present value of AST's future profits.

AST's stock price has already fallen by a whopping 100 points from its late May high of $133 per share, and today's price action adds insult to injury. The primary reason for the stock's precipitous fall over the summer was likely competitive concerns regarding Elon Musk's Space Exploration Technologies (SPCX +0.72%). SpaceX announced, in conjunction with its June IPO, that it will pursue a direct-to-cell mobile service, AST's turf, whereas SpaceX had only previously tackled broadband.

Last night, AST reported third-quarter results, with revenue growth of 187.3%. Still, that growth figure was off a tiny base and slightly missed expectations. Overall revenue came in at just $42.3 million, while adjusted (non-GAAP) operating expenses came in at $133.6 million, up in the mid-teens.

The sharp increase in revenue against slower expense growth was welcome, but it may take more to get investors back on the AST SpaceMobile bandwagon amid pressure from SpaceX. In fact, AST still uses SpaceX for some of its satellite launches, essentially paying what is now its biggest competitor to run its business. That being said, AST management recently announced its own 20-ton reusable rocket called Blacklift, which management said should be ready for launch in late 2028.

Nevertheless, today's hotter-than-forecast inflation report means the Federal Reserve could raise interest rates, which would disproportionately hurt capital-intensive, loss-making businesses such as AST.

Therefore, today's move may have less to do with yesterday's results and more to do with attaching higher discount rates and risks to AST's future revenue and profits, which should ramp up in the years ahead as it puts more satellites into orbit.

#3154. iOS 27.2 adds new features in six iPhone apps, details here

iOS 27.2 recently launched with new features for iPhone users, including improvements across six Apple apps. Here’s what’s new.

One of my favorite additions to Messages this year, Suggested Actions, debuts in iOS 27.2.

Suggested Actions appear underneath messages in a conversation when relevant. They can suggest creating a calendar event or reminder, adding to a note, and more based on the context of the message.

The feature was originally part of the iOS 27 beta this summer, but didn’t make the public build. Now it’s back in iOS 27.2, new and improved. There’s also an option to fine-tune which types of suggestions you’ll see.

Read more: iOS 27.2 adds new Messages feature that’s already a favorite

Every major streaming service has its own profiles feature, letting users on the same account keep their viewing history and recommendations separate. Apple TV has long offered such a feature in tvOS, but now with iOS 27.2 and iPadOS 27.2 it’s coming to iPhone and iPad too.

When you launch the TV app in iOS 27.2, you’ll be greeted by a new profile selection screen. You can easily disable it if you don’t want to see if again. But if you ever share your iPhone with kids, the new profiles feature should come in handy.

Read more: iOS 27.2 gives Apple TV a new profiles feature on iPhone

Dual Capture is one of FaceTime’s best new features in years. Added in iOS 27, on compatible iPhones it lets you keep your front and rear cameras both active at the same time while on a FaceTime call.

iOS 27.2 brings a key upgrade to Dual Capture: it’s now available for Group FaceTime calls.

To use the feature, just hit the flip camera button like usual, and by default on iPhone 17 and newer you’ll stream both camera feeds simultaneously.

Read more: iOS 27.2 makes FaceTime’s best new feature even better

Timed with its new Home products push, Apple adds a pair of new Home app features in iOS 27.2 for compatible smart locks.

‘Lock After Closing’ is a new automation setting that lets you choose how long after a door is closed that it should lock automatically. Previously you could only set a duration based on the time since a door was unlocked, not closed.

‘Door Left Open’ tackles a related, but distinct problem: a door being left open too long. With compatible locks, you can configure the Home app to automatically notify you if a door has been left open for a certain period of time.

Read more: iOS 27.2 has three new changes just added this week

Apple Podcasts keeps getting better, with AI-powered automatic chapters and transcripts some of my favorite features. And in iOS 27.2, Apple has a welcome change to the Up Next queue on the Home tab.

Up Next is now split into two separate queues: New Episodes and Continue Playing.

New Episodes contains only the latest episodes from shows you follow, while Continue Playing is a hub for all the episodes you’ve previously started but haven’t yet finished.

Apple’s Games app introduces some small updates in iOS 27.2 as well.

The Home tab now shows you recently downloaded games that you haven’t yet played. Previously, you would only see games with some play activity. And Apple says achievement progress and leaderboard scores have been updated in the Home tab to be easier to track. Finally, the Friends tab “provides context on friend suggestions and shows recent games played on friends’ player pages” per Apple.

Which new iOS 27.2 features are you most excited about? Let us know in the comments.

#3153. Ford Just Proved Its EV Battery Health Barely Degrades After 5 Years

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

2021 Mustang Mach-E electric SUVs have kept most of their battery and range after thousands of miles on the road.

Real-world battery life for phones, laptops and other electronic devices can diminish over years of use, but does the same happen to electric cars after thousands of miles and hundreds of recharges? According to data published by Ford this week: Yes, but not as badly as you might fear.

The automaker published a report analyzing the battery state of health of more than 36,000 Mustang Mach-E electric SUVs sold to customers across the US and Canada during the initial 2021 model year. After more than five years on the road — and an estimated 2 billion cumulative miles driven — the fleet averaged 92% battery health.

I call that impressive, but not totally surprising. That battery durability data is largely in line with what I’ve seen reported across the industry by other automakers and independent analysts.

One of the biggest concerns of early EV adopters a decade ago (also shared by fence-sitters today) is long-term reliability. The battery is by far the most expensive component of an electric car, and owners want to know their shiny new EV will last as long as the combustion car it replaces.

Battery longevity is particularly important as more used EVs enter the market. Many experts (myself included) have touted pre-owned and off-lease EV deals as a way to bypass the electric-car price premium, but shoppers may be hesitant to roll the dice on higher-mileage vehicles. Many fear a used EV won’t meet their range needs or, worse, could blindside them with an expensive battery replacement.

Ford’s study is another data point that could help allay those worries.

Ford examined more than 36,000 individual vehicles delivered to customers across all 50 US states and Canada during the EV’s first year of sales. A little more than five years later, the automaker says that around 95% of vehicles surveyed retained between 87% and 97% of their battery health (an average of 92%) across the entire 2021 fleet after an estimated 2 billion cumulative miles driven.

Better battery health means an EV keeps delivering more of its advertised range as the odometer climbs. The 2021 Mustang Mach-E rolled off the assembly line with an EPA-estimated range between 211 and 305 miles, depending on the spec, which means that owners lost around 16 to 24 miles of range over time, according to my back-of-the-napkin math.

That said, there’s no beating the chemistry. Around 2,000 vehicles in the group crossed the 100,000-mile mark, retaining around 91% health. A smaller subset of about 30 drivers reached 200,000 miles in their Mach-Es, with an average battery health of 88%. More miles, it seems, means more wear.

At the extreme anecdotal end of the spectrum, one owner put more than 400,000 miles on his original battery — though Ford didn’t state the specific health of that 2022 Mach-E.

An independent study published by Aviloo earlier this year adds credence to Ford’s reported numbers. An Austrian EV battery diagnostics firm analyzed over 500,000 EVs from 20 global brands to measure battery degradation — at 50,000, 100,000 and 150,000 kilometers — finding that many popular models maintained over 90% battery health at high mileage.

Tesla’s Model Y, which competes directly with the Mach-E, was found to hold around 90.3% battery health at 150,000 kilometers (93,205 miles). Aviloo reported that the Volkswagen ID4 and Hyundai Ioniq 5 showed 90.6% and 92.8% retention, respectively, over the same surveyed mileage. The first-generation Nissan Leaf — a much older EV with a smaller battery — showed more degradation at 86.3%, an unfortunate double whammy given its shorter initial range.

According to Ford’s engineers and battery chemists, the Mach-E’s battery was designed to last at least 10 years, adding that the 2021 models in the study use an older nickel-cobalt-manganese, or NCM, chemistry.

Ford’s new Universal Electric Vehicle platform, which will underpin the upcoming Fathom small electric pickup, will use a newer lithium iron phosphate chemistry. That will come with unique charging needs and different battery management calibration than its Class of 2021. The UEV architecture is also built around robust bidirectional charging, so we’ll have to check back in five or so years to see how using your car to power your home affects long-term battery health.

#3152. Samsung’s new SmartTag 3 debuts with next-gen Bluetooth – and one big problem

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

The Galaxy SmartTag 3 supports emerging Bluetooth tracking tech, but it's not a match for Samsung's OS exclusivity.

Samsung’s Galaxy SmartTag 3 is now available for purchase in the US, promising a smaller, lighter design than previous generations, compatibility with iOS devices, 550 days of battery life, an NFC-powered Lost Mode, Left Behind Alerts, and an IP67 dust- and water-resistant rating.

Though the Galaxy SmartTag 3 is compatible with iOS devices, the features available to Apple fans are limited, with Ring Phone, Left Behind Alerts, and Compass View reserved for Galaxy users. Compass View is enabled by Bluetooth Channel Sounding, an upgraded Bluetooth distance-finding technology. Despite Samsung embracing a low-cost boost to device tracking, Channel Sounding is locked inside the Galaxy ecosystem, a blow to the technology’s intended purpose.

Also: 3 ways Bluetooth 7 upgrades your devices beyond lossless audio

Channel Sounding is also Google’s Pixel Tag and Motorola’s Moto Tag 2, but these manufacturers open the technology to all compatible Android phones. However, Samsung’s SmartTag 3 doesn’t rely on Android’s vast but fragmented Find My Device network; instead, Samsung’s take on Channel Sounding will rely exclusively on the Galaxy Find Network. If a semi-closed ecosystem can help make evolving Bluetooth tech more reliable, does it matter that its implementation is counterproductive?

Samsung is the Goldilocks of device ecosystems. It’s not considered a walled garden like Apple, but it’s not as open to full third-party interoperability as Google. Many of Samsung’s most useful features are reserved for use within its Galaxy ecosystem. However, Samsung’s OS is built on top of Android, allowing for more flexibility than iOS, but still offering OS-exclusive features and, more importantly, feature reliability.

Full access to Samsung’s Galaxy Find Network is exclusive to Galaxy devices, similar to how full access to Apple’s Find My tracking features is reserved for Apple devices. On the other hand, Google’s Find Hub can accommodate Android phones from several manufacturers, including Samsung.

Also: Android is getting my favorite iOS tracking feature – what to expect

According to a press release, nearly 900 million Galaxy devices exist on the Galaxy Find Network. Each one’s constant Bluetooth signals contribute to an expansive network of crowdsourced data, extending the Galaxy FindTag 3’s reach and surfacing location data faster.

Google’s Find Hub’s greatest benefit is its scale: it can work with headphones, earbuds, Bluetooth trackers, smartphones, and smartwatches from multiple manufacturers.

However, different ecosystems limit tracking features to basic functionality, showing only where a device was last seen before it was powered off, or emitting a chime if you lose it. Live location data and accurate direction and distance finding from your smartphone aren’t possible.

Also: Apple has a Bluetooth problem, and Android is taking advantage

Implementing Bluetooth Channel Sounding aims to break down ecosystem-specific barriers, especially in a device-tracking context. If your smartphone, headphones, and smartwatch all support Channel Sounding, you could access fine-ranging tracking on all of them, regardless of device manufacturer.

Despite Samsung’s ecosystem providing it a device-tracking advantage, it defeats the purpose of Bluetooth: democratization. Basic Bluetooth connectivity allows any Bluetooth-compatible device to connect to another; that’s why you can wirelessly pair a pair of AirPods with a Lenovo laptop.

Also: Google’s Pixel Tag tracker has a big advantage over AirTags

Channel Sounding’s goal is no different in that it aims to bring more accurate distance awareness to Bluetooth-enabled devices, allowing you to finely track a pair of Sony headphones with an iPhone — that’s the goal, but not yet reality.

Samsung instead adopted Channel Sounding for its first consumer-ready endpoint within the boundaries of its ecosystem. Only Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, Galaxy Z Fold 8, Galaxy S26 Ultra, and Galaxy S26 Plus users can unlock the Galaxy SmartTag 3’s Channel Sounding capabilities when engaging its Compass View feature.

Also: Beware of Bluetooth sniffers: How your favorite gadgets could be exposing your data

All of these phones support Bluetooth 6.0 and Channel Sounding, but the Galaxy SmartTag 3’s Channel Sounding abilities will only be available to them and future Galaxy phones with Channel Sounding.

Conversely, Google’s Pixel Tag offers Channel Sounding to all Android phones that support it, including Galaxy phones. The result is that the Galaxy SmartTag 3 will operate just like any other Bluetooth tracker when paired with a base-model flagship phone, an older Galaxy phone, or an iPhone.

During this year’s WWDC, Apple announced Channel Sounding support for iPhones with its N1 networking chip and third-party Bluetooth 6.3 devices. Bluetooth 6.3 devices aren’t on the market yet and won’t be for a few years.

I assume Apple’s announcement of faraway future support is to give itself time to decide how Channel Sounding will fit into its walled garden, similar to Samsung’s implementation in the Galaxy SmartTag 3.

Also: How to tell if a hidden AirTag is tracking you – and disable it ASAP

Sure, Google’s Find Hub still needs some maturing; just last year, Google boosted the opt-in opportunities to add more devices for crowdsourced data, Find People is coming to Wear OS, and Find Hub is getting “Notify when left behind” alerts soon.

Apple’s and Samsung’s device location networks may be more feature-rich thanks to their closed ecosystems, but Google is working toward a truly open, easy-to-use network of devices powered by Channel Sounding. Which one is more important to you is for you to decide when it’s time to make a purchase.

#3150. NASA Just Made a Bunch of Moon Base Announcements: Here’s What They Are

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

The agency just unveiled new lunar missions, a nuclear-powered rover and $10 billion in contracts to build a moon base for astronauts.

NASA just wrapped up its Max Power event, the agency’s first-ever aerospace technology expo that took place Wednesday through Sunday at the Kennedy Space Center in Florida. Featuring discussions, panels, announcements and technology demonstrations, the biggest part of the event was NASA’s update on the Ignition initiative, which promises to put a base on the moon by 2032.

The Moon Base Program is an expensive endeavor that requires the help of various space companies to complete on time. Max Power discussed the various technologies and projects to make a base work, including the new CLPS 2 contract, a nuclear-powered moon rover and other lunar architecture.

NASA will rely heavily on commercial aerospace companies for many of these components: Blue Origin, Firefly Aerospace, Intuitive Machines, Lockheed Martin, Northrop Grumman, SpaceX, Voyager Technologies and ispace-US. Most of those companies have also been supplying tech for the Artemis program, which is slated to launch its third mission in 2027 and send people back to the moon in 2028. While the Artemis missions are important in their own right, NASA is also using them as a precursor to the Moon Base. That’s one of many reasons why it was a huge deal when Blue Origin’s New Glenn rocket exploded in May.

“We are building the moon base mission by mission,” NASA administrator Jared Isaacman said during Max Power. “When our astronauts return to the moon, they will arrive with the first elements of the moon base already waiting for them on the surface.”

The CLPS 2 contract is part of NASA’s Commercial Lunar Payload Services initiative, which plays a pivotal role in the moon base’s construction. The goal is to send materials and equipment to the moon ahead of time, so humans can immediately start building the base when they arrive.

The CLPS 2 contract builds on the CLPS 1.0 contract to develop the infrastructure and vehicles, including cargo landers, necessary to continuously ferry supplies and crew between Earth and the lunar surface. To fund these efforts, NASA paired the $10 billion CLPS 2 budget with an expanded CLPS 1.0 budget, which increased from $2.6 billion to $4.2 billion.

The cargo landers get cargo from space to the moon’s surface, but they also have to be transported there. NASA announced $1.3 billion in funding to Blue Origin, Arrow Science and Technology and Impulse Space to perform this step. They’ll make Orbital Transfer Vehicles, or OTVs, that act like “long-distance freight trucks” to carry the cargo landers and eventually deploy them safely to the moon’s surface.

In addition to building the vehicles that do this, NASA says three missions are slated for completion. First, research must assess how to reduce human risk and determine the best ways to deploy the CLPS landers. Second, NASA’s MoonFall drones will assess the moon and find the most optimal spot for a base. The third mission is to test the infrastructure to ensure it works as designed.

NASA took some time to talk about Promise, also known as Polar Rover for Observation, Mapping and In-Situ Exploration, an important vehicle for early moon exploration. The agency awarded Blue Origin a $94 million development contract, plus a performance-based $140 million for lunar delivery. Once deployed, the nuclear-powered rover will be managed by NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory at Caltech, which oversees NASA’s other rovers, NASA’s Deep Space Network and the Voyager probes.

Unlike solar-powered rovers, Promise’s nuclear core allows it to operate continuously through two-week lunar nights and in permanently shadowed regions where the sun never reaches. Its goal is to analyze regolith, hunt for ice and conduct general exploration.

While most of NASA’s recent announcements focused on getting hardware to the moon, the final segment laid the groundwork for surface infrastructure, specifically, long-term habitability so astronauts can actually be there.

To power this presence, NASA awarded contracts for energy storage and transmission to Honeybee Robotics (a Blue Origin company) and Yank Technologies. Their solar arrays, batteries and wireless power hardware will culminate in the Mini-Communications and Solar Tower (miniCast), assembled at NASA’s Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama, before being deployed to the moon.

NASA is also trying to tackle the myriad problems that must be solved for a moon base to succeed. One of the initiatives announced at Max Power is the Moon Base Student Challenge, which asks students to help build humanity’s future on the moon, with $1 million in prizes for winners with the best ideas.

“We are inviting students from across the country to help solve some of the problems that stand between humanity and a permanent presence on another world,” Isaacman said during his speech, which was packed with students and kids, according to Space.com.

While the initiative isn’t aimed at anything specific, it challenges students to tackle whatever they can regarding lunar base problems. NASA has tapped students before to help solve problems such as dealing with lunar dust clouds and human-capable landers.

#3149. Hesai: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Pricing in Hesai's core lidar market is settling into rational competition, a shift that matters for whether margins hold as newer businesses scale.

On its third quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 10, 2026, Hesai (HSAI +0.63%) reported that non-automotive robotics businesses reached over 50% of total revenue. This expansion transforms the company from an automotive component supplier into a broader physical artificial intelligence infrastructure platform. Three key takeaways from management explain where the business is heading next.

Fast-growing robotics applications and software tools are diversifying revenue away from legacy vehicle lines. Hesai's strategic growth initiatives, or SGI, generated 135 million Chinese yuan in nine months, exceeding its original full-year target.

Humanoid robots require dozens of specialized motion modules, creating a high-volume hardware market beyond optical sensors. Hesai designs core components in-house to capture market share as customer deployments expand.

Price competition in main light detection and ranging, or lidar, sensors is stabilizing following severe industry discounting. Multi-sensor configurations per vehicle help protect overall margin structures.

Robotics demand is expanding faster than legacy automotive supply chains, supporting near-term gross margins close to 40%. Hesai retains an edge through in-house component integration, proprietary chips, and global manufacturing standards while tracking pricing discipline across emerging segments.

Long-term execution relies on shifting customer vehicle architectures toward multi-lidar arrays and establishing hardware standards across humanoid platforms.

#3146. Ring’s Flying Home Security Drone Is Finally Here, and It’s Surprisingly Affordable

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Ring's $250 flying indoor security camera is set to arrive in January. We got a first look at the Drone Cam in action.

Ring Home Security has taken flight, and the brand’s tiny new home security drone is less expensive than we thought. The Ring Drone Cam, a $250 mini indoor drone camera, was announced on Tuesday as part of the brand’s new arm, Ring Robotics. It uses a learned map of your home to zoom around autonomously for up to 8 minutes at a time with custom routes to record places a couple of fixed cameras can’t.

The small drone weighs just 5.8 ounces and houses a pair of 2K-resolution cameras mounted on the front and bottom, respectively. The cameras use bright LED lights to enable day or night monitoring, sending a live feed or recorded video to your device. The LEDs are also meant to ward off potential intruders peering in from the outside.

You can program the flying cam to make regular flights or send it on specific missions to check on the dog or see if the stove was left on. The Drone Cam also syncs with other Ring cameras and sensors to respond automatically when windows and doors open at certain hours.

If you’re thinking, “Wait, didn’t Ring already launch a drone camera?” you’d be right — sort of. The brand “launched” the Ring Always Home Cam in 2020. The $250 indoor drone had a limited, invitation-only release but was never available for public sale. We’ve been assured this latest iteration is ready for prime time, though it’s still not available for preorder on Amazon.

Ring founder and CEO Jamie Siminoff demoed the drone, which has been in development for more than five years, in an event space set up to replicate a home. During the demo, the small drone lifted gently from the dock and rose to about eye level, where it hovered as if to say “hello” to the group of journalists gathered around.

Once airborne, the drone turned toward the adjacent room and whirred off to investigate. After a few seconds of scanning, the drone returned to the first room, docked and resumed charging.

While in flight, the Ring Drone Cam made a notably loud buzz reminiscent of a golf cart in reverse. Siminoff quickly noted that the sound was intentional, meant to deter potential intruders and alert home dwellers to the drone’s presence.

The 1-minute flight was enough to cover two medium-sized rooms, though the drone can fly up to eight minutes on a full charge before needing about an hour to recharge. Ring reps told me it can monitor a home up to 3,500 square feet – more than enough for most – but Siminoff says it plans to improve the range over time.

If you’re worried about the drone knocking over vases and flying into ceiling fans like I was, Siminoff assured us the preprogrammed coverage zone is tight.

#3144. Ready for a Siri AI agent? Apple under pressure to upgrade its assistant faster

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Home & Office > Smart Home > Smart Assistants

Apple's public-facing satisfaction with the Siri AI launch obscures internal pressures and tensions.

Apple’s recently appointed CEO, John Ternus, is allegedly pushing the company internally to ramp up its AI strategy — including making Siri an AI agent.

Also: My 5 favorite Siri AI ‘onscreen awareness’ tricks

According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, the CEO is publicly pleased with the Siri AI launch, but privately encouraging Craig Federighi, Apple’s SVP of software engineering, to move faster.

“Desiring more and frustrated by what he sees as a reluctance to embrace AI with the same urgency as competitors, Ternus pushed his software chief to accelerate the company’s road map and move quickly beyond merely making necessary improvements to Siri,” Gurman wrote. He added that the tension stems from Federighi’s reputation as an AI skeptic.

The revamped Siri AI is now a much better voice assistant with some helpful features. Gurman noted he thinks Siri AI’s ability to automatically fix your weak passwords is already somewhat agentic behavior, though AI-generated passwords have their own issues.

But Siri AI isn’t yet on par with increasingly autonomous agents from AI-first companies that aim to proactively organize your tasks, use your computer, and write advanced code. Still, those rival agents deliver a patchwork of capabilities: while some, like OpenClaw and Anthropic’s Claude Code, are highly functional, others, like Google’s Gemini Spark, aren’t quite there yet.

Also: I tried replacing Claude Code with a free local AI stack

Regardless, the issue here is time. Despite developing powerful hardware perfectly suited for running local AI models, Apple has remained slower than competitors on the AI software front. Competitors have demonstrated they can make promised agent features a reality, some quicker than others.

On the other hand, the fact that Apple hyped Siri AI for two years only to release an improved voice assistant (rather than a groundbreaking AI product) may mean users are ready for more advanced features.

In addition, AI companies are working on their own hardware. “If they can combine that software with AI-native devices designed from the ground up around assistants that see, remember and act, Apple’s longstanding advantages could begin to matter less,” Gurman wrote.

An agentic Siri would most likely build on what users already like about the new version.

The on-screen awareness feature, for example, is currently limited to what’s visible on your screen in that moment, meaning only the part of a long email that you’ve actively scrolled to. An agentic Siri could ideally scroll all the way through an email on its own and surface the insights you’re looking for.

Also: The iPhone made Apple a giant – but the Mac could help it win the AI era

But in the short term, Ternus’ push will likely just deliver on existing promises. Gurman also pointed out that Siri AI still lacks advanced in-app actions, which Apple initially announced in 2024 and would let third-party apps create plug-ins for and pathways through Siri.

“This functionality would let Siri tap into both in-house and third-party applications with more precision,” Gurman wrote. “This past week, as part of the first beta version of iOS 27.3, Apple finally began talking about the feature again.”

(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, ZDNET’s parent company, filed an April 2025 lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)

Plus, if we’re talking about agents specifically, newcomers like OpenAI’s Dot and Anthropic’s Duet aren’t competitive themselves yet: ZDNET’s AI vetter-in-residence David Gewirtz found both to be “a little odd” and not “quite ready for prime time”.

Also: I tested OpenAI Dot and Anthropic Duet for weeks – and all I got was one helpful notification

For users who appreciate the subtlety of Siri AI, though, anything similar to ChatGPT or Claude on their devices might not land, unless each feature is opt-in.

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

AMD has admitted a bug within its External Events Utility is wearing out SSDs, and promises a fix.

Under normal circumstances, an SSD might go all day without needing to access or write files. But for some AMD Radeon users, anything but normal circumstances are causing drives to continuously write and re-write data. The External Events Utility (EEU) that AMD installs alongside its CPU and GPU drivers is reportedly the culprit.

Also: Nvidia RTX 50 GPUs hit with more price hikes

Fortunately, there are a few workarounds available to avert disaster while AMD works on a more permanent solution.

Reports of the issue first surfaced in July on AMD’s official PC user forum, with one user stating that the External Events Client Module and EEU were constantly writing information to their SSD after installing a Radeon 9060XT graphics card. Subsequent comments on the thread this month confirm that the issue has persisted despite several bug fixes and patch updates, with two users reporting hard numbers for data usage ranging from 0.3 MB/s to as much as 1.5 MB/s.

Also: The best laptops: Expert tested and reviewed

This week, Reddit user darklinkpower posted that the AMD Adrenaline Edition desktop application also had the EEU driver bug, using up to 1% of their drive health per month for around 16 months. That might not sound like much, but it can cause catastrophic problems if left unchecked.

AMD seems to be aware of the issue; a company official who goes by AMD_Vik on Reddit commented that it will “hopefully [be] fixed in the next [update].” While there’s little indication of how quickly a permanent, official patch will be pushed to users, there are a few ways you can protect yourself from the bug and prevent your storage drive from collapsing.

This seems to be the most consistent fix for most AMD users reporting issues, but disabling the EEU can cause its own problems, such as disabling AMD FreeSync support or introducing display glitches if you hot-swap screens while your PC is powered on.

The AMD Adrenalin Edition desktop app lets you control how your PC components communicate with one another, and it might be another facet of a complex problem. By allowing your CPU to access your graphics card’s memory, you can temporarily boost performance, but the EEU bug seems to let it and your GPU run rampant, eating up every bit of memory they can find. Changing a few settings within the app may help:

Also: I tried local AI on HP’s Omnibook Ultra

This is a more niche solution that carries its own risk of introducing communication issues between your CPU and GPU, so I only recommend trying this route if disabling the EEU itself doesn’t resolve the issue. AMD’s official fix may be in the works, but without a firm timeline for release, users are left twisting in the wind trying to stop their PCs from hemorrhaging storage capacity.

#3139. Crescent Capital: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Add-on financings now make up half of Crescent's deal count, a shift that shapes how the firm is working through a slow buyout market.

On its third quarter of 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 10, 2026, Crescent Capital (CCAP +12.34%) announced a $50 million share repurchase program and a new joint venture to reduce balance sheet leverage. Capital allocation shifts and deleveraging, or reducing debt relative to equity, directly influence net asset value accretion for shareholders during slow deal markets. Three takeaways from the call stand out for long-term investors.

Management authorized a $50 million share buyback, and parent company Sun Life committed up to $25 million for additional open-market purchases. The business plans to repurchase shares when the stock trades below its net asset value (NAV), which represents total investment assets minus outstanding liabilities per share.

The company is seeding a $150 million joint venture (JV) with performing senior loans to lower its leverage ratio back into its target range. The arrangement utilizes asset-based borrowing and $30 million of equity from Crescent Capital to enhance return on equity (ROE), a measure of net earnings generated per dollar of equity.

Direct lending for new leveraged buyouts (LBOs)--company acquisitions funded primarily through borrowed debt--dropped 60% year over year in the third quarter. Management navigated the market slowdown by providing growth financing to existing portfolio companies.

Subdued market activity slows portfolio turnover, but leadership works through underperforming loans methodically rather than rushing exits. Broad diversification across 190 portfolio companies provides cash flow stability while leadership maintains strict underwriting standards.

The firm's ongoing integration into the GreenOak global distribution platform expands institutional investor reach while keeping investment decisions with the existing team.

#3138. Apple to investigate accident that killed three workers at iPhone parts factory in India

Reuters reports that three contract workers died after inhaling gas during an inspection at a Tata Electronics factory that produces iPhone components in India. Here are the details.

As frequent 9to5Mac readers probably know, Apple’s supply chain in India relies heavily on Tata, which manufactures iPhone components and accounts for a significant share of the country’s iPhone assembly operations.

Since Apple began diversifying its manufacturing operations away from China, India has emerged as a major production hub, with roughly a quarter of the world’s iPhones now manufactured in the country.

Earlier this year, Apple found itself linked to an environmental controversy in India, after the Tamil Nadu Pollution Control Board investigated allegations that wastewater from a Tata facility had contaminated nearby farmland water.

A few weeks later, however, Tata said the regulator had dropped further action against the facility after the company addressed the concerns raised.

At the time, Tata said it had ordered separate testing related to the facility and that the results supported its position that the plant was operating within the rules.

However, the matter was apparently not fully resolved, as just three days later, Reuters reported that local health officials were still investigating complaints from nearby farmers.

And while there had been no major developments reported about the wastewater investigation since then, Reuters reported today that three contract workers died in an accident at the same Tata facility.

The three contract workers died during maintenance work on an effluent treatment ​plant operated by Nalco Water at the Tata facility, which is located in Hosur in Tamil Nadu, ​district official Dinesh Kumar said, adding that the deaths occurred when the workers inhaled gas while inspecting an external nano-filtration tank.

Reuters added that “Apple’s team is visiting ​the plant to assist in ​the ongoing investigation,” though the company did not respond when reached for comment.

The report added that Tata and Tamil Nadu authorities are also investigating the fatal accident, and noted that “production was not affected as the facility was closed for the Hindu festival of Deepavali this week.”

#3137. Adobe Is Giving Its AI Agents Even More to Do

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Across Firefly and Creative Cloud, apps are getting even deeper into creative work.

Would you use an always-on AI agent such as Claude Duet or OpenAI’s Dot to edit your photos? At Adobe Max on Tuesday, the company announced it’s expanding its local MCP integrations with more third-party companies to enable more autonomous creative work.

MCP, or Model Context Protocol, is an open-source protocol for connecting AI systems to external apps and databases. AI agents and MCPs act as a two-way street. Agents, or fancy bots, can complete tasks independently.

For example, if you wanted your OpenAI agents (or Dots, whatever you call them) to edit a project in Photoshop, the MCP pathway would allow ChatGPT to run agents to edit the design in the Photoshop beta desktop app — no need to search through the toolbar if you’re not familiar with it.

The new MCP integrations are in preview now. The idea is to give people more choice by letting them use their preferred AI app to help them work in select Creative Cloud apps.

Over the past year, Adobe has been working with AI companies to bring its creative knowledge and tech to ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Copilot as Adobe plugins. It’s also brought external models from AI companies into Firefly, Adobe’s AI hub. Now, Adobe is deepening its relationships with third-party AI vendors to adapt to the agentic AI era.

Bringing your own agents offers a degree of user control, according to Shilpa Anand, vice president of global strategic partnerships. “These new models allow me to actually do things faster, experience the full power of the application and really make it more accessible to a broader set of users who are not experts in our workflow,” Anand told me.

Agentic AI has been a huge focus for tech companies this year. It’s the next step for companies that want to move beyond mere chat and information-gathering AI capabilities.

Adobe has been driving toward this vision for a while. It released AI assistants in Photoshop and Adobe Express that set the foundation for June’s official launch of Adobe creative agents.

But AI agents from frontier labs such as OpenAI and Anthropic caused trouble this summer when they escaped testing environments and hacked real websites. Anand told me that safety and security are “table stakes” for Adobe and that there haven’t been any issues aligning with other AI companies on safety precautions.

When considering partnerships, the company also considers which AI models will be most useful for Adobe’s creative customers, which is why Firefly includes models from big players including Google, as well as more specialized AI companies, such as ElevenLabs for AI audio tech. (Adobe acquired Topaz Labs, which makes AI photo editing software, earlier this year.)

Those creative AI agents are getting new capabilities across Creative Cloud apps, too. In Firefly, the company’s AI hub, its AI assistant should now be better at multistep or more complex tasks, and it has a new “plan mode” in preview that lets you review the agent’s plan before it starts running.

New “always-on” Firefly AI agents do exactly what the name implies: They’re always working and can handle predefined tasks, such as assessing image quality in new asset uploads. They’re in preview now, too. And across Illustrator, InDesign, Premiere, After Effects and Frame.io, those AI assistants are getting upgraded capabilities as well.

Adobe is also expanding its partnerships. Microsoft Photos will have a built-in Adobe Express integration, and Microsoft’s Arm-based Windows PCs are getting “optimized” Adobe apps. Disney is also deepening its relationship with Adobe, bringing Adobe’s Firefly AI tech to its creative teams.

Partnerships with AI companies and the integration of agentic capabilities will continue to be a focus for Adobe next year, Anand told me. “Agentic software is really going to enable us to reach more users and empower everyone to create, which is our mission.”

#3133. Can you still trust Proton?

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

The company’s reputation took a major hit two weeks ago, when 404 Media published a detailed report, based on leaked Slack messages and interviews with anonymous insiders. The story detailed a push by Proton CEO Andy Yen to — in his own words — “ruthlessly smash everything that stands in the way of AI velocity.”

Also: Is your browser’s free VPN enough? I tested 4 against Proton VPN

After one employee proposed spending at least a few days on penetration testing before shipping new code, Yen reportedly said, “That’s bullshit and loser thinking. Of course it’s possible to be fast and secure. Stop thinking always of how to be slower, and focus more on how to be faster.” According to 404 Media’s account, Yen’s message for Proton engineers was to “stop lovingly handcrafting all our code and use AI more.”

After the original story broke, 404 Media posted a follow-up story reporting that the company had canceled its “re-interviews” that were intended to assess how developers were adopting AI. A 404 Media podcast was titled “Proton’s CEO Is Putting AI Before Security.”

Reddit has an especially active Proton community with 345,000 weekly visitors. It quickly filled up with so many comments — the majority of them negative — that moderators created a single megathread to help keep track of the different threads, including pages for general criticism, support of the AI usage, and “leaving your goodbyes.”

Also: Best VPN services 2026: Expert tested and recommended

Given the level of interest, it’s not surprising that Yen chose that forum to post a public message to the community. In it, he apologized for “hurtful” remarks, adding that he’s “determined to do better.”

He also addressed the topic of AI-based security reviews:

But most importantly, I need to categorically state that our use of AI will never be at the expense of security. In the past year, contrary to what has been alleged, actually additional layers of security review have been added to meet the threat posed by hostile AIs scanning Proton’s open source code for vulnerabilities. Fast and secure need not be mutually exclusive. We also leverage AI to find vulnerabilities in our own code before attackers do. Our code is open source, and its security remains open for all to verify. [emphasis in original]

Nothing in the 404 Media reporting demonstrates that Proton weakened its encryption or shipped insecure code because of AI. The damage is different: Yen’s remarks undermined confidence that management will consistently respect the security processes its customers rely on.

In a blog post that Proton shared with ZDNET ahead of its publication today, the company followed up on Yen’s promise to “lift the hood on how we use AI internally at Proton.” The post, titled “How Proton keeps your data secure in the age of AI,” was signed by the Proton Team and emphasizes Proton’s secure architecture, with end-to-end, zero-access encryption:

We do not hold the keys to your emails, files, or passwords, so we cannot read them, and no AI tool can, either. Our documented security governance policies have not changed since June 2024, before AI was even a major factor in our work here, and they all still apply.

On Reddit, Yen said, “AI is here, and it will unquestionably change how software is developed forever, and Proton must also change.” Today’s post clarified that code receives the same checks whether it is written by a human, by an AI agent, or by a combination of both. Every change receives automated security scans but also requires human approval; sensitive changes, such as core cryptography work, require review by specialist teams. Major feature designs are also reviewed for security, dependencies, testing, and deployment plans.

Also: I can access my home PCs remotely for free – no VPN needed

Those policies address the most serious technical concerns raised by the current controversy, although outsiders have no way to know from the policy alone how consistently those safeguards are followed in day-to-day development.

Should a modern software company use AI for security? Proton argues that it can’t afford not to.

Because of AI, attacks that once might have required a nation-state can now be executed by almost anyone. A defender relying on manual processes and hand-crafted tools is bringing a knife to a gunfight. An attacker only needs to find one flaw, while a defender needs to close all of them. AI is the only tool that makes that defense possible. Cybersecurity is an arms race, and the teams working on security at Proton have been some of the earliest adopters of AI, because the safety of your data depends on winning that race.

But that argument doesn’t really address the objection. The current controversy isn’t about whether Proton should use AI to find vulnerabilities; it’s about whether pressure for “AI velocity” can override the judgment of engineers responsible for keeping its products secure.

Proton says it uses AI to review code changes, identify vulnerabilities through continuous security reviews, and monitor an attack surface that has “grown far beyond what unaided humans could monitor.” The company uses its own models alongside non-public cyber models from OpenAI and Anthropic.

The modern software development landscape is torn by two opposing forces. On one side, you have AI-based tools that are routinely finding nightmarish vulnerabilities in existing codebases and then exploiting them immediately. On the other side, you have a global movement that’s skeptical of the benefits of AI and outright opposed to construction of the data centers where they run.

Much of Proton’s growth over the past few years has been the direct result of people trying to escape big tech. So it shouldn’t be a surprise that many of Proton’s customers — at least those who are passionate enough to visit a Reddit forum — are deeply skeptical of anything related to AI.

Also: Ring’s new drone patrols your home to keep an eye on things – even upstairs

In a traditional software company, that realization would have led management to cautiously roll out AI-based features and reveal its AI-centric security strategy more deliberately. That didn’t happen here, obviously. Those blunt remarks from the CEO exposed a management culture that many employees and customers found troubling. It’s difficult to restore trust, both within the workforce and among customers, after that kind of public display of contempt.

Ironically, one of Yen’s comments from the original 404 Media story describes the company’s current dilemma with devastating accuracy.

In a Slack message, Yen told a Proton engineer, “perception is more important than truth, the truth doesn’t matter if you don’t win on perception.” The implication was that he was urging the employee to lie, or at least shade the truth. In fact, as Yen himself told a random Reddit commenter:

I do not believe perception should be more important than truth. I am stating that unfortunately it often ends up being the case. If you place it into the context in which it was said, it can be understood as, “it doesn’t matter that the truth is that Proton’s PQC implementation is better, this truth is irrelevant as long as it is not perceived to be this way, and we therefore need to correct that perception”

That’s Proton’s challenge now, distilled to its essence. It takes seconds to destroy a reputation. It can take months or years to recover from the perception that the company and its management can no longer be trusted.

Personally, I will continue to use Proton Pass and Proton VPN, both of which are solid, reliable products. But I’ve moved my secondary email accounts (which I had migrated from Gmail to Proton Mail); they’re now running on Fastmail. I had been considering making the switch for a long time, primarily because Proton Mail’s performance has been too slow for my taste. Current events just hastened that switch.

So we do have a good profile that we believe that is relevant in the setting. And we continue to obviously watch the space to see what the dynamic looks like and sort of evaluate kind of what the opportunity is, how it may shift. But we're pleased with the data we have, and I think certainly have a good foundation.

Operator: Our next question comes from Salim Syed of Mizuho.

Salim Syed: Congrats on the progress. I guess I'll just follow on the MS front. Christian, so the trial was updated also in October from 18 patients to 24 patients on clinicaltrials.gov, and I know you noted that as well today. Just curious if there's anything about the additional 6 patients that you plan to have enrolled into the study. Is there anything different that you'd like to see in their baseline criteria? Or what exactly was the reason to also increase the size of [indiscernible]? Did you not think you'd be able to get the signal you wanted in the 18 patients that you originally had planned?

Christian Itin: Thanks, Salim. What we had indicated in the press release is that we've been using 2 types of preconditioning regimens in the study. We've used Flu/Cy as well as bendamustine. And we want to make sure that the data set we have is a reasonable size to give us a strong indication of the actual clinical impact that we're seeing. And we felt that the [ DLBCL ] patients actually is going to be helpful. 18 patients for safety look is fine to look at from an efficacy perspective is on the low end. And enrollment is going really well in that study.

So it was an easy thing to add on, and we felt that, that was the right thing to do.

Operator: And our next question will come from Yanan Zhu of Wells Fargo.

Unknown Analyst: This is [ Kwan ] on for Yanan and congrats on the quarter. So on SLE, your ACR poster showed the cell expansion data. And it looks like 50 million might be more persistent than 100 million, and we know it's small, but anything you can share with us there?

Christian Itin: So we did -- first of all, thanks for the question. It is correct, we did include pharmacokinetic data. I think what you do see is that we do see good expansion in all patients. We see the typical range of about 3 months of persistence of the product. And then afterwards, you start seeing as the CAR T cells actually gradually remove, you can then actually see the reconstitution of the B-cell compartment, which is obviously one of the key features you want to see to be able to sort of demonstrate not only the reset, but also the recovery in those patients. So we do see that.

There's some fluctuations that we have seen in terms of the expansion. I don't think that we can actually conclude anything from the dose levels as far as we -- when we look at the data, and we also look at the broader range of data we have, we don't believe there are actually variabilities there from a product perspective or dose perspective, but you do have certainly patient-to-patient variability. So we don't think there is a difference from a dosing perspective there. But clearly, the 50 million cell dose is highly active and performs extremely well.

Unknown Analyst: Got it. And a quick question on AUCATZYL sales. So based on your guidance, it looks like the 4Q number might be similar or in the same range as 2Q and 3Q. So can you talk about the dynamics there? And when do you expect the sales to return to growth?

Christian Itin: Thanks for the question. So when we look at last year's trajectory, you could see that in last year's trajectory, you had basically Q2, Q3, Q4 in similar levels of sales that we had throughout the year. So it's not unexpected to see somewhat of that dynamic during the course of the year. What we do see is certainly this year is very positive impact from the real-world experience. There is significant updates that we're going to expect at ASH and [ ASTC ] coming up in the next 2, 3 months. And we believe that, that will have a significant impact and setting us up for a really good 2027 as well.

Operator: Our next question is from Roger Song of Jefferies.

Unknown Analyst: This is [ Fiona ] on for Roger. Congrats on all the progress. Just on the AUCATZYL sales, with another ROCCA data coming out in December, do you expect it to have another significant lift on the sales into '27? Or because this is not the first time you think the impact will be more moderate?

Christian Itin: I think -- first of all, thanks for the question, Fiona. I think when you look at sales curves, obviously, we're having a very significant step-up year 1 to year 2. What you typically see with the sales curves is that obviously the increase in year 3 and year 4 tend to obviously be smaller than what you see between year 1 and year 2. So there is clearly -- we would expect the curve to actually have a similar shape as you would know or what you've seen with other products.

We do believe that the continued work that's done at the ROCCA Consortium and collecting a large amount of data is a really powerful information because it's, in essence, a peer-to-peer communication of the treating physicians to their colleagues of what their actual experience is. And I think that is very valuable. And that's certainly what we've seen this year. We expect that to continue to have a significant impact. But I also would expect that as we sort of general look at the general sales curve that we would have a similar trajectory as you would normally see with product adoptions as well.

So I think that's kind of in terms of color at this point, I think, that we can provide.

Unknown Analyst: And if I may, just with respect to MS, would you still collect data and see the earlier biomarker data at -- before 12 months?

Christian Itin: Sure. You look at all the correlations. So you look at -- you want to have both the clinical outcome and the correlated pharmacodynamic markers that we're seeing. And that is important to actually see those parameters as well as imaging parameters as well. But in terms to actually assess the actual clinical scores as a clinical score, you do actually require a longer follow-up, and that was loud and clear, I think, from the KOLs in the field that they thought the data that was shown to date in the field was just premature.

Operator: Our next question comes from Matthew Phipps of William Blair.

Matthew Phipps: Just wondering how enrollment has been going across your autoimmune trials, both lupus and MS. You mentioned some robust enrollment in MS, but other companies have talked about maybe a slight slowdown over the end of the summer as there was kind of broader safety concerns for CAR T and autoimmune. And then for AUTO8, the abstract at ASH, I think just shows a couple of patients treated with the BCMA CAR construct alone with 2 achieving MRD negativity. At ASH, we also see patients that got kind of the dual BCMA and obe-cel constructs and then some follow-up on those patients.

Christian Itin: Okay. Matt, thanks for joining. On recruitment, we actually didn't feel that or didn't see an impact in the second half of the year. On the progressive MS side, it's a population of patients that we see is quite remarkable in terms of their interest in joining clinical trials, quite at one end of the spectrum across the autoimmune space. I think the lupus patients in general are much less inclined to go in clinical trials, which is what we've seen in the last 30 years and across a wide variety of development programs. So I think that is consistent. I don't -- we haven't significant change across the board there.

But the news flow that we have for the second half of the year, at least from what we are seeing, does not seem to have impacted patient flow in a way that would be visible to us in our clinical trials. And then on AUTO8, we have initially the study similar as we did the original study in multi myeloma patients, starting with the BCMA component and adding the CD19 component on top. Obviously, the abstract was done with an earlier data set. There's more data collected now, and we're going to have early patients also with both vectors included, so both the BCMA and the CD19 targeting component included.

And of course, also longer follow-up on the BCMA patients as well.

Operator: Our next question is from Douglas Tsao of H.C. Wainwright.

Douglas Tsao: Christian, I'm just curious on the MS side, it totally makes sense why you would wait to present the data to 12 months. I'm just curious what you think or how you think this might ultimately impact the time line in terms of development and sort of moving ahead to potentially registrational studies, et cetera.

Christian Itin: Thanks, Douglas. Really good question. So it doesn't change the decision-making process around the program. We had indicated that we would need longer-term follow-up to be able to assess actually the clinical outcome. I had indicated that actually for a while. And that is, I think, is unchanged in that sense. So you want to have that longer follow-up with the patients and based on that, then actually make your decisions around the clinical trial design and also the time lines associated with the pivotal program.

So that is unchanged from our perspective, which is also why we're going into the fall meeting because, frankly, the data at the March meeting, we stated that would not have been actionable from a development perspective or development decision perspective.

Douglas Tsao: Okay. Great. And also, if you could just maybe touch on, I think conceptually, we all get why you would try the preconditioning with bendamustine. But I'm just curious exactly what you might see and how significant could it be? And maybe some KOL feedback that you've gotten in terms of how much more tolerable that could ultimately be for patients.

Christian Itin: Yes, very good question. So the preconditioning regimens also have been developed for originally for stem cell transplants, and this is where the Flu/Cy conditioning is coming from. It's been very well optimized for that type of an application, and it is very well characterized and shown to be the most active way of preconditioning for lymphoma and leukemia patients. So that's where that's coming from, where we have an awful lot of data.

What Flu/Cy conditioning does is it leads to a temporary neutropenia in patients, which you see in a lot of the curves that you might have seen over time, including our own data, where you see an early kind of a drop in cell counts and then also recovery over time, which is typical for Flu/Cy conditioning. Bendamustine is known to actually have much less of an impact on this type of hematological toxicity. It also is known certainly in the case of leukemia and lymphoma to be somewhat less effective as a preconditioning agent compared to Flu/Cy. And so we're looking at this as an option for the autoimmune patients.

And this is what we're exploring in the current study and believe that's a relevant question to ask, obviously, in the context of the overall benefit risk profile that you have in autoimmune patients.

Operator: Our next question is from Mathijs Geerts Danau of KBC Securities.

Mathijs Geerts Danau: Congrats on the quarter. I was just wondering whether you expect to see some impact over the holiday period in the fourth quarter with the guidance increase now.

Christian Itin: Thanks, Mathijs. Good question. The fourth quarter certainly has an element of impact because you typically have a slow week around Thanksgiving. And you also tend to obviously have a slowdown, particularly on the dosing side from Christmas to New Year. So there's certainly impact in December that we would expect. And have seen in last year in the first year of commercialization, but we've also seen it when we look at clinical trial performance and conduct as well across the December period -- end of November and into the December period. So that's typical what you would expect. So there's going to be somewhat of an impact, but the impact certainly last year was limited.

Operator: Our next question comes from Rajan Sharma of Goldman Sachs.

Rajan Sharma: One on gross margin. Now that you've sort of had 3 quarters of positive gross margin, should we assume that's going to be a consistent sequential margin improvement until you get to that peak guidance of 65% to 70%? And then secondly, related to that, how are you thinking about time lines to reaching that now that you've obviously made some improvements on cost efficiencies? And then just on center onboarding, you've obviously delivered sort of more quickly relative to your expectations at the beginning of the year. Could you maybe just talk to the drivers of that? Is it a case that maybe you are underestimating the number of centers?

And could you maybe talk about where you think that goes next year?

Christian Itin: Yes. Very good question, Rajan. Thanks. So on the gross margin side, I think what we've been seeing is obviously a significant impact of, on the one hand, increased volume that we see come through the facility. But we've also made significant changes in the operating model, and there's a lot of operational excellence work that we've done to really look at any unit of operation and are optimizing that. There were some big changes or improvements we could implement in the Q2 time frame, and you saw that then reflected in the Q2 numbers, and you see that continue also Q3 as well. So that gives us sort of a new level and a new foundation.

And we continue to actually drive systematically through efficiencies in the manufacturing facility. So we expect that to continue to improve. We don't expect over the upcoming period step change, but a continuous improvement over time and are -- certainly been very pleased with the dynamic that we've seen this year, and we also already see that projected also into the fourth quarter as well.

So when we look into the kind of getting to the place where we get to what we believe is sort of the upper range of what is on the ALL side for the ALL business alone, we expect that we're approaching kind of that upper end of the range in 2028, but that will not stop us to continue to push forward as well beyond that. But I think 2028 is probably a good way of thinking about the range that we indicated in the presentation today as well.

When we look at center onboarding, I think where we're at is -- once you reach about, give or take, 80 centers in the U.S., which are obviously the largest centers across the country, you do actually have access to approximately 80% of the patients. So that's sort of the ballpark that you get to.

Now when you look at the chart that is visible on AutolusAssist, where you can see where the centers are distributed across the country, you do see that they kind of follow the major population density that we have across the U.S., which also means that if you get more towards the central part of the country that the distances between centers actually get increased, and that also creates opportunities. So when we look now in terms of the centers we're looking to onboard, that has, on the one hand, has certainly considerations about patient access and driving distances or travel distances for patients to reduce those.

But there is also another dynamic, which certainly has been very interesting to see, and that is that a lot of the physicians in the field are younger. It's a newer technology. They've grown up with the technology. And we see now some of those physicians kind of move out from their current academic settings into new centers and setting up CAR T therapy at those new centers. And what we also are looking to do is actually follow those physicians to the new centers that are setting up, and with that, have a very targeted approach towards center expansion and center addition.

But the same dynamics that we're seeing also as we get more information about nonacademic centers and patient flows where we have identified certainly a few centers that have a surprisingly good flow of ALL patients that I think normal market research would not have predicted. So those are kind of the areas. So a lot of it is very targeted and it's community-driven.

Operator: This does conclude the question-and-answer session. I would now like to turn it back to Christian Itin for closing remarks.

Christian Itin: Thank you very much, everybody, for joining today. And I would say, I've had a great quarter, looking forward to a great end of the year. And obviously, with the various conferences coming up, I think plenty of opportunity to also interact in person. So with that, looking forward to seeing you, and we'll keep you updated. Thank you very much.

Operator: Thank you for your participation in today's conference. This does conclude the program. You may now disconnect.

Expanded Gemini Intelligence, HiLight and more

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Google just announced its November Pixel Drop, which adds a slew of new features for Pixel phones and watches. Plus, the Pixel Tag officially goes on sale today (look out for our review here).

There's a ton of stuff in the drop, but some highlights include expanded Gemini Intelligence, a new Create My Widget feature and step-by-step workouts on Pixel Watch 3 and newer.

The company also announced its new Google Fi "Super Network." We've got more details about how it works here.

Let's dive into what's available and which devices support these new features.

For the most part, the big features are only coming to the Pixel 10 and Pixel 11 series phones in this update. Some smaller tools are available on Pixel 6 and later phones. Surprise, most of it is AI-related.

Starting with AI, Gemini Intelligence is now available on Pixel 10 phones, including the new Rambler feature, which automatically removes filler words and can format your spoken words into "clean, coherent" text. It also adds automations for specified apps, including grocery ordering, ridesharing and booking reservations.

Create My Widgets enables you to build custom widgets using AI by describing the type of tool you need. Google is also offering curated recommendations.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Gemini Call Screen is on Pixel 11 phones and screens calls on demand. For Pixel 10 and 11 phones, Gemini can make calls for you, doing things like checking inventory, putting items on hold, or making/changing reservations.

Pixel 11 phones are getting Pixel Solver, which uses generative AI to create custom templates and "conversational, multi-step problem solving for everyday" math.

Pixel 9 and above phones are getting Notification Summaries that will recap long conversations, giving you context at a glance.

The highlight feature, pun intended, is HiLight, announced at the Made By Google event in August. When your phone is face down, HiLight will glow to let you know if a favorite contact has sent you a message.

Otherwise, for 6a and above, there's a new Custom Icons style, which uses Nano Banana to generate. Transit Mode 2.0 triggers automatically based on phone sensors.

Pixel Search Updates lets you find content across your apps, web and settings using natural language search directly from the All Apps screen.

Unit Conversion is a module to help you skip toggling between the browser and the calculator. Pixel 6 and above phones are also getting Live Location Sharing for Pixel VIPs.

Finally, Pixel 10 phones are getting Extreme Charging Mode that quickly charges your phones to full.

Your Pixel Watch isn't getting as many features as the phones, but the big one is "Step-by-Step Workouts." Basically, your watch will give you step-by-step instructions for each exercise in your routine. It will also log reps, weights and track metrics from your Watch, or your phone.

This is available on Pixel Watch 3 and newer models.

Google announced that Create My Widgets, Gemini call Screen and Notification Summaries, outlined above, are "coming soon"; no specific date was provided.

Phone to Watch Unlock is also coming soon to Pixel Watch 3 and new models. This feature will let you unlock your watch with a nearby paired phone. No date was provided here either.
