#3101. We’ve Folded the iPhone Duo Almost 400,000 Times. How Much More Can It Take?

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Our Fold-a-Phone machine folds Apple's iPhone Duo 900 times every hour to test the durability of its hinge.

We’re now a third of the way through November, and the machine in CNET’s lab continues to work overtime testing Apple’s first folding phone, the $1,999 iPhone Duo. We purchased this poor phone more than two weeks ago, and since then its only job has been to bend and flatten, bend and flatten, until it breaks.

So how many times can we fold the iPhone Duo? As of 3 p.m. on Tuesday, Nov. 10, we’re at 390,000 folds, and by tomorrow we’ll reach 400,000 folds.

I oversee hardware and software testing as director of lab operations in our lab in Louisville, Kentucky. Over the last week, I’ve seen a lot of chatter about the sturdiness of the Duo’s folding hinge and its potential to fail or crack. I’ve periodically examined the Duo we’re testing in our machine, and so far, I haven’t seen any signs of damage. And the crease isn’t any more visible than it was when we took it out of the box. If that changes, I’ll let you know here and on our livestream.

In the meantime, let me explain what we’re doing. My team and I designed and built a proprietary machine to test foldable phones like Apple’s and its Samsung rival, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 (which we’ve also started testing). I’ve worked on the methodology and build of this testing rig for months in anticipation of Apple’s long-rumored foldable iPhone.

We even named our machine to match its purpose: Meet the Fold-a-Phone.

Now, my team of engineers and testing experts will watch the iPhone Duo open and close, open and close, to rigorously and systematically monitor the durability of Apple’s hinge and two screens.

After all, repeatedly folding a phone with bare hands can only get you so far in understanding the complex forces at play between the magnetics that snap the screen shut and the all-critical hinge.

CNET’s Senior Technology Reporter, Abrar Al-Heeti, has done a beautiful job capturing the iPhone Duo’s pros and cons in her smart, thorough review. Our Fold-a-Phone machine will add a deep data foundation to complement her real-world experience.

Since Apple hasn’t publicly shared claims of the iPhone Duo’s foldable lifespan, CNET’s Fold-a-Phone machine is poised to provide a wealth of valuable data about Apple’s first foldable phone and competing models in the foldable market.

And yes, you’d better believe we will use our treasure trove of in-house data to share status updates and comparisons during our ongoing testing window with the Duo.

Join CNET’s iPhone Duo livestream on YouTube weekdays from 1 p.m. to 5 p.m. ET, where you can follow along live and watch the Fold-a-Phone do its thing to a Duo.

The importance of this moment is hard to overstate. Apple’s appearance on the foldable smartfold frontier lags Samsung by seven years (the first Galaxy Fold went on sale in the US in September 2019). Motorola and other phone-makers have long experimented with foldable phones in every shape and size, including a trifold accordion foldable phone we first demoed in 2019.

CNET’s mobile experts, including Al-Heeti and Editor at Large Andrew Lanxon, have discussed the legitimizing effect of the iPhone Duo’s existence on the entire foldable phone landscape, which has previously felt like a new-wave fantasy rather than a mainstream riptide.

In many ways, Apple’s newfound competition with existing foldable phones completes the portfolio. That is precisely why we’re building the Fold-a-Phone now, and why our proprietary machine, methodology and test data will enrich our collective understanding of the capabilities – and yes, limitations – of foldable phones as our true next-generation mobile device.

Most current foldable phones are rated for 200,000 to 500,000 folds. As such, we knew we needed to create a robust and adaptable machine that could accommodate book- and flip-style foldable phones of any size, dimension and hinge orientation. (Note: The Fold-a-Phone was not built for trifold phones, which present a unique element to the engineering challenge.)

Moreover, we wanted to test the phone the way people would actually use it. No one just sits around opening and closing their foldable phone at top speed all day. Rather, you open it naturally, spend a few minutes watching a video, browsing a web page, or using an app, close it, and then put it in your pocket. This may happen dozens of times per day.

Mimicking this usage on the Fold-a-Phone limits undue stress on the phone hinge and avoids generating excess heat compared to a test built for speed.

We determined that a cadence of roughly 4 seconds could sidestep technical hurdles while also being reasonably fast. The foldable phone takes 1 second to open, 1 second to fully open, 1 second to close and 1 second to fully close. This cycle counts as a single completed fold. Then, the cycle repeats until either the hinge or the screen gives out.

In conceptualizing and building the Fold-a-Phone, our team has used standard, off-the-shelf components to simplify the machine’s development. The essential design consists of two armatures, distinctly designed to perform the opening and closing movements with both force and grace.

An industrial-grade stepper motor drives each armature, with the host software (running on a connected computer) deterministically adjusting the torque to complete each step of the process while also protecting the phone. If any of the several proximity sensors fail to detect the armature in the correct position, the machine stops immediately.

We also monitor the motors’ power usage to track how well the foldable phone opens and closes over time. We have set up cameras to capture images and video of the test from multiple angles, and we will analyze regular status updates from the computer to determine the current status of the phone and the test.

To ensure we never miss a major development, the entire rig is connected to an EcoFlow Delta 3 Plus power station to guard against electricity outages, and all the output data is saved to multiple locations.

To secure each phone to the machine, we use our CNET Lab Test-winning 3D printer, the Prusa Core One, to 3D-print a custom “sled” that matches each phone’s exact dimensions. We secure the phone to the sled with heavy-duty double-sided tape (yes, it works!) and then screw the sled onto the machine.

There’s always room for improvement. We’re constantly looking for ways to make the machine run more smoothly and quietly without disrupting the folding rhythm.

Apple’s presence is already changing the game and could very well spur innovation in ways we can’t predict today. But until then, our Fold-a-Phone machine will continue to test the iPhone Duo and its competitors, and CNET’s writers will report on how well these individual hinged devices stand up to the challenge – or fold under pressure.

#3098. Apple’s iPod Turns 25: Here’s the Song Catalog That Rode Wit You

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

On this day in 2001, Apple's iconic MP3 player was released. And now, an Apple Music easter egg lets you experience the nostalgic sound and scroll of the gadget's click wheel.

Back in 2001, some of the top songs included Nelly’s Ride Wit Me, Fallin’ by Alicia Keys and Ms. Jackson by Outkast. When people wanted to listen to those songs but weren’t near a car stereo or their home audio equipment, most carried music with them on skip-prone portable CD players, boomboxes or maybe even a homemade mix cassette.

Sure, some early adopters were already carrying a small collection of songs on a portable MP3 player (MP3s: the new-new thing!) like the Diamond Rio or Creative’s Nomad Jukebox. But these weren’t common, and you didn’t see them that often. There was no ubiquitous sign yet that the times were changing musically in a digital direction.

Enter Apple in November 2001 with its original iPod, a small hard drive encased in smooth white plastic that could stash between 1,000 and 2,000 songs, a sum that seemed godly at the time.

Who would ever need to listen to 1,000 songs (or have access to that many) at their fingertips? What mortal would dare?

The iPod, which was announced on Oct. 23, 2001, and released on Nov. 10, 2001, had a starting price of $400. It heralded the smartphone era before smartphones were a thing, making portable electronics more tactile, user-friendly and information-forward. The white earbuds that were bundled with the device were the beacon of that era. Before long, it seemed everyone had white cables coming out of their ears.

For the 25th anniversary of Apple’s game-changing music player, the device’s creators are getting nostalgic about its silver anniversary. On Apple Music’s website, you can find at its 404 Not Found page a playful mockup of the OG iPod with its pleasing-to-use scroll wheel and a selection of songs you might have had in your iPod at some time or another.

CNET writers and editors had a good time playing around with the fully functional iPod online, sharing favorite hits from its music library and enjoying some nostalgia ASMR.

We also looked back at CNET’s earlier write-ups, including one from CNET’s former Editor-in-Chief Connie Guglielmo, explaining what it was like to watch Steve Jobs introduce the iPod. There’s also a great 2021 piece by CNET’s Scott Stein on the iPod’s evolution, and a commentary by CNET’s Ty Pendlebury on how the iPod captured and held the throne for so long, surviving music streaming and rival players.

Read more: iPhone Duo Review: Late to the Foldable Party, but It Steals the Show

If the iPod can be primarily credited to one person — leading a team of many — it’s widely acknowledged to be Tony Fadell, who came to Apple as a contractor and went on to head one of its most successful product divisions. These days, Fadell is thinking a lot about the future of AI assistant devices, but he took time on his LinkedIn to acknowledge the iPod anniversary this week.

“We took it from approval to shipping in less than eight months,” he wrote. “There wasn’t time for endless refinements. We had to make decisions, trust our experience and stay focused on one clear promise: 1,000 songs in your pocket.”

While Fadell says that the iPod took a few generations to really take off and eventually come in iterations like the Nano and the Touch, some music fans who still love the original iPod design have been using the device for decades. If you have any hard drive-based gadget that lasts that long, count yourself lucky.

In addition to those old enough to remember what a Hoobastank is, iPods are also getting popular again with younger generations on a nostalgia kick, many of whom would rather carry around a separate physical device for their music than stream their Spotify accounts on their phone for the millionth time. Axios reports that iPods and MP3s are back in a big way in a trend called “friction-maxxing.” You don’t have to use that term to indulge, we promise.

Getting into the hobby isn’t cheap: Working iPod models can cost several hundred dollars on eBay. And one that’s never been opened? Try $25,000 to $60,000.

A cheaper route may be to keep the familiar outside trappings but replace the guts with a new motherboard. A group called Crowd Supply promises in a YouTube video a new way to bring nonworking iPods back to life. It hasn’t launched yet, but you can keep an eye on the project at Crowd Supply’s website. Other tinkerers have had years and years to work up hundreds of iPod hacks; you can find many of them on Hackaday.

Alternatively, it may be the function that a modern MP3 enthusiast seeks, not necessarily the Apple branding or hardware. Other companies, such as Fosi Audio, have their own takes on the modern music player, like the $80 DAP Neo. CNET has a list of the best MP3 players of 2026, with devices like the Shanling M0s and the Android-based HiBy R4 coming out on top.

Lastly, if you want to relive the iPod glory days, you don’t necessarily need new (or old) hardware at all; your phone can do it with iOS apps such as RetroPod, My Classic – Retro Console or, if you’re feeling saucy on Android, ClassiPod.

#3097. Why GeneDx Holdings Stock Just Dropped 16.6%

GeneDx met Wall Street's revenue target but missed on test volume and trimmed its volume growth outlook, and a stock priced on growth is paying for it.

GeneDx Holdings (WGS -16.57%) stock fell 16.6% on Tuesday, Nov. 10, after the biotech company lowered its growth targets for the year.

The S&P 500 and the Nasdaq Composite dropped 0.4% and 0.7%, respectively.

The genetic testing company GeneDx reported Q3 results on Monday after the bell. Sales jumped 5% to $123.1 million -- in line with what Wall Street was looking for -- and margins improved slightly. Unfortunately, testing volume lagged expectations. The company delivered 32,134 exome and genome results -- the DNA tests that are its core business -- up 25%. This is a good example of why expectations are everything in the stock market. The company is still growing, but not as quickly as expected. With two downward growth revisions this year now, I understand why investors are pricing in a third.

#3096. These Xiaomi phones are no longer getting support with the latest HyperOS 4 update

Xiaomi's new software has started rolling out in China, but older phones are being left behind.

Owners of a Xiaomi 17 in China are now receiving the latest HyperOS 4 update, which gives Xiaomi's software a new see-through look that's drawn plenty of comparisons to Apple's Liquid Glass. It began rolling out to the company's newest phones and tablets on October 15, 2026, but owners of the Xiaomi 12T and Redmi Note 12 are missing out. The update isn't coming to those models, which are already at, or are about to reach, the end of software support.

According to Xiaomi's official rollout schedule, the first batch of HyperOS 4 updates covers the Xiaomi 17 series, Redmi K100 and K90 series and the Xiaomi Pad 8, with more models following in waves through January 2027. Unfortunately, phones that are reaching the end of support this year, including the Xiaomi 12 and 12T, aren't on that schedule. Firmware trackers have also spotted a handful of cheaper models that, while still within their support windows, haven't been tested with HyperOS 4 at all. Xiaomi hasn't confirmed whether they'll miss out, though, and the rollout is only in China for now.

Xiaomi's schedule for its China firmware rollout lists 57 phones and 15 tablets in total. Following the first batch in mid-October 2026, the Xiaomi 17 Max, 17T and 17T Pro, Redmi K90 Max and Redmi Turbo 5 series were due by October 31, followed by the Xiaomi 15 series, MIX Flip 2, Civi 5 Pro and Redmi K80 series by November 15. The Redmi Note 17 and Note 15 lines come next, by November 30. December's batch is the biggest, taking in the Xiaomi 14 and 13 series, MIX Fold 3 and 4, Redmi K70 series and Redmi Note 14 Pro and 14 5G, while January 2027 is reserved for TVs and wearables.

A global beta opened in September 2026 for the Xiaomi 17, 17 Ultra and the Leica Leitzphone, followed by the 17T, 17T Pro, 15 and 15 Ultra, but Xiaomi hasn't yet provided a date for the global release. Beebom reported on October 11 that Xiaomi still hasn't confirmed a timeline for India or any other market, and Poco phones, which aren't sold in China, don't appear on the schedule at all.

Xiaomi publishes end-of-support dates on its security center site. Gizmochina has counted 19 devices due to drop off in 2026. The Xiaomi 12 and 12 Pro, Redmi Note 12 5G, Redmi 12C and Redmi A2 and A2+ lost support in March, and the Poco F5 and F5 Pro in May. The Xiaomi 12T and 12T Pro reached the end of the line in October, followed by the Redmi 13C and Poco C65 in November. Once a model winds up on that list, it stops receiving OS upgrades and security patches entirely, so it's worth knowing how to check if your Android phone is still getting security updates. Xiaomi's promises have gotten longer since, with the Xiaomi 15 getting four OS updates and six years of security patches, but that's still short of the seven years Samsung and Google now offer on their flagships.

Ximitime, which tracks Xiaomi's firmware, said there were no signs of HyperOS 4 test builds for any phone capped at Android 16. It named six models that hadn't entered testing: the Redmi Note 13 Pro 4G, Redmi Note 14S, Redmi A5 4G, Poco C71, Poco M6 Pro 4G and Poco X6 5G. Xiaomi hasn't confirmed that these phones are excluded, and some still have years of security updates left. If they are included, they'll stay on HyperOS 3.

Interestingly, the Xiaomi 13 series is on December's list, even though Xiaomi promised it three major Android updates, ending at Android 16, back in 2023. However, Xiaomi hasn't said whether its 13 series is getting Android 17 or a version of HyperOS 4 built on Android 16. With four years of security patches promised from its early 2023 global launch, the Xiaomi 13 is also now one of many popular smartphones in their last year of software support.

Xiaomi calls the new design Soft Light Glass, a translucent material that it says adjusts its transparency based on the colors and content behind it. The lock screen's clock can now be resized, moved and restyled, much like the iPhones running iOS 26. Per Xiaomi, the full effect will only run on phones sporting a Snapdragon 8 Elite, Dimensity 9500 or Xiaomi's own XRING O1 chip or newer; older phones on the list get a simplified version.

Xiaomi also claims that HyperOS 4 leaves 27.2 percent more memory free after eight hours of use and opens apps 17.5 percent faster after long sessions. Meanwhile, its voice assistant, Super XiaoAI 2.0, now runs on Xiaomi's own MiMo AI model and adds an Expert Mode that can carry out multi-step tasks across apps, though most of the AI features are limited to China for now. HyperOS 4 is reportedly based on Android 17, but Xiaomi's newest phones already got Android 17 in July 2026 through an interim release called HyperOS 3.3.

Onboard camera capability includes a 148-degree field of view and 360-degree rotation with a 2K video resolution. Two LED lights also activate in low-light conditions to help illuminate the scene for the drone video camera.

However, the drone is limited to just 8 minutes of flight time when operating on a “new, fully-charged battery under controlled conditions” according to the product description. It comes with a docking station for charging.

Another caveat in the product description is that the Ring Drone Cam may experience degraded performance when navigating in environments with reflective surfaces such as “polished marble or wet tile,” blank matte walls without any features, or transparent surfaces like frameless glass and mirrors.

Still, Amazon touts the drone as providing an “autonomous way to check on your home that has never existed before,” whether the customer is away or at home. The Ring Drone can be controlled directly from the Alexa Home Map interactive map that shows all of a customer’s Amazon-linked devices.

Meanwhile, Amazon has pitched the Ring Rover Cam priced at $1,000 as “an autonomous security robot designed for business.” This product is already available for preorder for those so inclined and scheduled to start shipping to customers on December 16, 2026.

The company described the Ring Rover as being inspired by customer feedback involving another invite-only beta product, the Amazon Astro robot designed for home monitoring.

The Ring Rover can livestream and record in up to 4K video resolution when patrolling or while doing a 360-degree scan at a designated location. Videos triggered by doorbell rings, motion events and “Live View” events are stored in the cloud for sharing and replaying for up to 180 days.

Like the Ring Drone, the Ring Rover can automatically respond to alerts from connected Ring devices by following its preprogrammed patrol points. But the wheeled robot is only designed to operate within a single-floor, indoor environment because it lacks stair-climbing capability.

Amazon’s product description also warns that the Rover is not compatible with “curved edges, sunken areas, flooring transitions greater than 1.375 inches (3.5 centimeters), and black glossy floors.”

To help compensate for its ground-based view, the Ring Rover comes with an automatically adjustable mast to peer over counters, shelving and other obstacles. It can supposedly cover up to 5,000 square feet (465 square meters), according to Amazon’s product description.

The Ring Rover also comes with additional security-related features such as a siren and light tower to loudly announce its presence, along with a microphone for two-way audio communication if the customer wants to address someone near the robot.

Ring was previously charged in a 2023 Federal Trade Commission investigation with allowing employees and contractors to watch Ring video recordings of customers’ private spaces. The FTC also described Ring as having lackluster safeguards that allowed hackers to access 55,000 US customers’ accounts.

Videos taken by the new Ring Drone and Ring Rover will be protected with Ring’s Throw Away the Key Encryption that was introduced in September 2026, according to Amazon’s announcement. The digital rights nonprofit Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF) has described this as an improvement over Ring’s former default settings, but still well short of end-to-end encryption.

There is currently no mention of the new Ring Robotics products implementing facial recognition or similar AI-powered technologies for identifying people. But starting in December 2025, Ring has allowed owners of fixed Ring doorbell cameras to turn on a “Familiar Faces” feature that uses facial recognition technology on visitors—and that is already the subject of a class action lawsuit.

#3092. Crypto Market Today, Nov. 10: Bitcoin Slides Below $74,000 as Hot Inflation Data Sends Crypto Markets Tumbling

Crypto markets extended losses as hotter-than-expected inflation hit Wall Street, raising fresh concerns about interest rates and the outlook for risk assets.

Cryptocurrency markets took another hit on Tuesday, November 10, as hotter-than-expected inflation data weighed on investor sentiment and fueled concerns about higher interest rates. As of early evening, Bitcoin (BTC -1.94%) fell 1.83% to $73,874.38, while Ethereum (ETH -3.91%) declined 3.43% to $2,059.16 and Solana (SOL -4.55%) dropped 3.69% to $83.37. The broad-based sell-off reflected weakening risk appetite as investors reassessed the outlook for Federal Reserve monetary policy.

Tuesday's inflation surprise triggered a sharp sell-off in U.S. government bonds, pushing Treasury yields higher as investors priced in more aggressive monetary tightening. The benchmark 10-year Treasury yield briefly surpassed 5%, while the more policy-sensitive two-year yield climbed toward 4.75%. Higher yields make fixed-income investments more attractive relative to speculative assets, creating additional headwinds for cryptocurrencies.

The U.S. dollar also strengthened, with the dollar index gaining approximately 0.5%. A stronger dollar can weigh on dollar-denominated assets like Bitcoin by tightening global financial conditions and reducing purchasing power for overseas investors.

Meanwhile, markets increasingly expect the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates in December, with some traders considering the possibility of a larger 50-basis-point increase. Together, rising bond yields, a stronger dollar, and tighter monetary policy expectations are creating an increasingly challenging backdrop for digital assets.

Spot Bitcoin ETFs traded lower, with iShares Bitcoin Trust ETF (IBIT -1.51%) down 1.51% and Fidelity Wise Origin Bitcoin Fund (FBTC -1.49%) down 1.49%. Spot Ether funds also weakened, as iShares Ethereum Trust ETF (ETHA -3.27%) fell 3.27%.

Bitcoin's struggle to hold $74,000 raises concerns about the strength of underlying demand. U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs have recorded approximately $1.5 billion in net outflows since November 2, removing an important source of buying pressure.

Derivatives markets also reflect growing caution. Bitcoin options traders are paying a premium for downside protection, while relatively subdued futures positioning suggests limited appetite for aggressively buying the dip. A recovery in ETF inflows, accompanied by stronger spot buying, would provide a more convincing signal that market conditions are improving.

Altcoins face an even more challenging outlook. Ethereum is approaching the psychologically important $2,000 level, while Solana is testing support near $80. Both could face additional selling pressure if Bitcoin weakens further, particularly as tighter liquidity tends to hit more volatile digital assets hardest.

For now, investors should watch whether Bitcoin can reclaim $75,000 and whether institutional flows begin to stabilize. Without renewed demand, any near-term rebound could prove difficult to sustain.

#3091. The US military seems to be getting nervous about the launch supply crunch

“Launch is extremely constrained and that is exactly the situation we predicted.”

The US military is taking a new approach to prop up commercial launch companies as SpaceX looks to wind down its Falcon rocket program, suggesting defense officials see the workhorse rocket’s retirement as a potential national security risk.

The Pentagon’s Office of Strategic Capital has twice in the last two weeks announced it was sending cash to two of SpaceX’s competitors in the launch business. First, on October 26, the office announced a $150 million conditional loan commitment to Stoke Space. Military officials revealed a second $150 million Pentagon loan Tuesday for Rocket Lab.

Stoke Space and Rocket Lab are the first two launch companies to receive significant support from the Office of Strategic Capital (OSC), an organization established in 2022 to infuse companies developing “vital” national security technologies with capital. OSC has been on a loan spree in recent weeks, committing hundreds of millions of dollars to companies specializing in batteries, drones, and semiconductors. In the space sector, the office also provided a $150 million loan to LeoLabs, a commercial satellite tracking company, for production and deployment of radar units.

SpaceX, the Pentagon’s leading launch provider, has stopped taking commercial orders for Falcon 9 launches after 2028 as the company shifts its focus to the next-generation, super-heavy-lift Starship rocket. Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy launches for government customers, including NASA and the US Space Force, are expected to continue a while longer. The Space Force’s launch contract with SpaceX allows the military to place Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy orders through 2029, with the actual launches extending through 2033.

Then, if Starship is fulfilling its promise, SpaceX plans to retire Falcon for good. Starship may eventually be capable of launching national security payloads, but SpaceX’s near-term priority is using the rocket’s massive cargo capacity for its own Starlink Internet satellites and Starmind orbital data centers.

Military space officials have held to a policy of assured access to space since the 1990s, with the Pentagon paying to support at least two US rocket programs capable of launching national security satellites. The support previously came in the form of direct subsidies, development funding, and launch contracts at premium prices to give the government technical and financial insight into their launch providers, schedule priority on their launch manifests, and, in some cases, to simply keep them in business.

The Space Force’s mix of launch providers today consists of SpaceX’s Falcon family and United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket, which has been grounded twice in the last two years by problems with its solid rocket boosters. ULA’s woes with Vulcan forced the Space Force to shift several national security missions to SpaceX.

Other launch providers aim to compete for their own slices of the growing pie of Space Force launch contracts. Space Systems Command, which oversees launch procurement for the Space Force, now forecasts the military will require up to 249 medium-to-heavy-lift launches through the early 2030s from its roster of launch contractors, more than double the command’s expectation just two years ago.

Alongside SpaceX and ULA, Space Systems Command has tapped Blue Origin, Rocket Lab, Stoke Space, Relativity Space, and Impulse Space for eligibility to compete for some of those national security launches. Blue Origin is the only company that has flown a rocket that could meet the Space Force’s requirements. Rocket Lab, Stoke Space, and Relativity Space are developing their own medium- and heavy-lift launch vehicles, while Impulse Space is working on in-space propulsion.

The loans from the Pentagon’s Office of Strategic Capital aim to get new medium-class rockets from Stoke Space and Rocket Lab ready to meet the military’s needs.

Stoke Space’s loan is tailored to support the buildout of the company’s second launch pad at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Florida. The second launch site would support flights of Stoke Space’s Nova Block 2 rocket, an upgraded version of the company’s fully reusable Nova Pathfinder, which is set to debut sometime next year.

“By supporting the construction of additional launch infrastructure, this commitment would enhance the overall capacity and resilience of the commercial space industrial base,” said Jordan Sebold, senior managing director of investments at OSC.

The loan to Rocket Lab will support the company’s efforts to increase the flight rate of its partially reusable Neutron rocket, which Rocket Lab says is also scheduled to make its first launch next year.

“The proposed loan would support faster vehicle delivery and processing and allow Rocket Lab to expand its fleet of maritime vessels with additional equipment for Neutron recovery and transport,” OSC said in a statement. “It would also enable manufacturing upgrades to increase the production of composite structures and engines, and support infrastructure that would reduce turnaround time between launches once the reusable rocket makes its operational debut.”

Both conditional loans are subject to “various financial, legal, technical, investment, due diligence, and other requirements,” OSC said.

Adam Spice, Rocket Lab’s chief financial officer, said Monday the Pentagon loan is on “very attractive terms” and “underscores the importance” of the military’s appetite for launch capacity.

“We always take it when we can get it,” Spice said in a quarterly earnings call. “It gives us additional capital to scale key parts of our business, Neutron in particular … I think this is a helpful indicator, a very positive indicator, about where everyone sees the demand constraint and how it can be unlocked, and capital is certainly a part of that.”

Rocket Lab also unveiled new pricing for the Neutron rocket—an increase from $55 million to $70 million per launch—in response to what the company said was a surge in bookings for the still-unproven launch vehicle. Rocket Lab said it now has a backlog of 117 launches on contract, including orders for Neutron missions and the company’s smaller Electron rocket.

“Launch is extremely constrained, and that is exactly the situation we predicted,” said Peter Beck, Rocket Lab’s founder and CEO.

#3090. This Janus Henderson fund manager owns CoreWeave debt — here's why he's sticking with it

CoreWeave can overcome the market's skepticism about its debt.

That isn't the consensus view — some Coreweave debt remains deeply distressed with yields above 15%. But Coreweave should power through this tough stretch, according to John Lloyd, global head of multi-sector and corporate credit at Janus Henderson.

"It's a little bit of overreacting," Lloyd tells CNBC, referring to the sell-off in Coreweave bonds, which have tanked along with its equity.

Lloyd owns Coreweave 9.75% bonds due in 2031 in the firm's Multi-Sector Income Fund. The yield to maturity on the debt is now 15.97%, a more than 70% jump since its issuance in April. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.

"Bond prices are lower, spreads are wider, yields are wider, and I don't see a huge fundamental change in the ecosystem right now that would warrant that, other than their higher cost of financing, which I think they can get creative with," Lloyd added.

CoreWeave has taken on a massive amount of debt to fund its data center buildout. The company has roughly $51.6 billion in total debt, including about $35 billion in notes, bonds and loans.

The market is getting nervous about how CoreWeave will be able to keep financing its data centers, and at what cost. Its stock has tumbled 20% over the past week, while the spread on its five-year credit default swaps is nearly 1,081 basis points — lower than earlier in the session but up 13% week over week. Spreads of 1,000 basis points and above are generally a sign of credit distress.

CoreWeave shares moved roughly 2% higher on Tuesday, after tumbling over the past several days and hitting a 52-week low earlier in the session. Its bond yields and spreads remain highly elevated.

Lloyd believes the selloff is a bump in the road for the neocloud company.

The market has been spooked by the jump in Treasury rates, which pushes up funding costs for companies, he explained. The focus largely turned to companies like CoreWeave that have refinance risk when rates move higher, he said.

CoreWeave leverage is high with a debt-to-equity ratio of 702%, up from 290% a year ago. Moreover, CoreWeave will spend an estimated $36.4 billion on capital expenditures this year against Ebitda of $7.5 billion, according to consensus estimates.

Revenue and Ebitda will ramp up next year, hitting $26.5 billion and $16.7 billion respectively, analysts estimate. But capex will hit $47.9 billion, indicating the company may need to finance its data center buildout with more equity issuance and/or debt.

Lloyd isn't necessarily worried about CoreWeave's ability to finance its capital expenditures, despite the fact that its capex outweighs its free-cash flow.

"Next year … they're going to be generating operating free-cash flow that'll support some of that capex need," he said.

The company can also turn to other methods of funding, like more GPU financing, which will allow it to borrow against its graphics processing units or rental contracts, he noted. In addition, CoreWeave could ask its biggest customers — including Microsoft, Meta Platforms and OpenAI — to increase their prepayments, he added.

"They can probably get creative enough where they don't even need to come to the high-yield market," Lloyd said.

The company also doesn't have any near-term maturities, which means it isn't facing a refinancing risk anytime soon, he added.

Meanwhile the supply/demand dynamic should remain tight across the AI compute landscape. Overall adoption rates within the ecosystem are running above consensus demand curves, he said. Add to that a bottleneck in supply, with chips and memory power sold out, and it's a nice set up for CoreWeave.

"All data point to the business model functioning very, very well," Lloyd said. "CoreWeave is one of the best-in-class at getting data centers up and actually running them," he added, noting that CoreWeave's financials have been improving throughout the year.

Another turning point could come if Anthropic goes forth with an IPO, expected in November, followed by OpenAI. Successful IPOs for the frontier labs could soothe market nerves and help support the neocloud operators.

"You just need more of those data points where people become more comfortable with the AI demand side," Lloyd said.

CoreWeave still needs to convince markets it can handle higher market rates and get through the financing bottlenecks.

Lloyd sees the company making it, albeit with some bumps along the way. The bonds should recover, he says, "just not in that straight line."

#3089. Gaining Financial Control Requires More Than Just a High Income

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site. This compensation helps us provide tools and services - like free credit score access and monitoring. With the exception of mortgage, home equity and other home-lending products or services, partner compensation is one of several factors that may affect which products we highlight and where they appear on our site. Other factors include your credit profile, product availability and proprietary website methodologies.

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

Income is one factor to feeling financially in control, but your approach to managing your money is crucial, too.

Earning more money can boost your feeling of financial control.

Nearly 9 in 10 (89%) Americans with a household income of $100k-plus say they feel in control of their day-to-day finances compared with 62% of Americans with a household income of less than $50k, according to NerdWallet’s October 2026 Financial Resilience Index survey conducted by The Harris Poll.

But getting a raise or a higher-paying job isn’t a surefire way to feel in control. Pairing your paycheck with good financial habits is a more robust approach.

Nearly 4 in 5 (78%) Americans feel in control of their day-to-day finances, according to the survey. That’s up from 73% in September.

There’s no single external measure for what makes someone feel in control of their finances. If you swap financial positions with someone else who feels in control, for example, there’s no guarantee you would feel the same way.

That said, a person who lives comfortably with what they have and who has the ability to withstand unexpected expenses has a good chance of feeling in control.

Americans with lower household incomes are much more likely to feel a lack of control in their day-to-day finances compared with those with higher household incomes.

That may seem intuitive. Someone with a high income is more likely to be able to cut back on luxuries, such as dining or vacations, when the costs of groceries and healthcare rise. Someone whose income is lower might not have expenses to cut.

However, that narrative is an overgeneralization.

If feeling in control of your finances depended entirely on having a high income, you might expect to see a much higher share of Americans with low incomes who feel they aren’t in control of their day-to-day finances.

But in fact, the majority (62%) of Americans with a household income of less than $50k do feel in control of their day-to-day finances. At the other end of the income spectrum, it’s clear that money doesn’t automatically result in feeling in control: About 1 in 10 Americans (11%) with a household income of $100k+ say they don’t feel this.

A high income alone won’t offset spending more than you earn, and it isn’t a substitute for an emergency fund. Good financial habits are an important component of financial control, too. They may look like:

Preparing for an emergency: Car repairs, medical bills, broken appliances: There are plenty of expensive emergencies that can pop up, even if you’re doing everything right. One-third (33%) of Americans don’t have enough cash on hand to cover an unexpected $1,000 expense if it popped up this month. Those who have an emergency fund can avoid relying on credit.

Managing debt: Monthly expenses that exceed income indicate a shaky financial footing — not great for developing a feeling of control. Nearly 2 in 5 Americans (38%) say they’ll have to rely on credit to manage expenses in October. Managing debt goes beyond paying your credit card bill each month. For example, if you get the maximum car loan or mortgage that lenders approve, a large portion of your paycheck is committed to debt payments. Keeping your overall debt load low gives you flexibility if your situation changes in the future.

Avoiding expensive mistakes: Saving money takes time. Spending it can happen quickly. A separate recent NerdWallet study found that 3 in 5 Americans (60%) say they’ve spent money on something expensive and later regretted it. Luxury items, gambling and vehicles topped the list of regrettable purchases. Pump the brakes on avoidable expensive purchases. For any big buy, take a day or two to mull over your options, especially if you have outstanding debt or if your emergency fund is low. Considering spending decisions carefully is another way to feel more in control.

The feeling of control is likely to emerge over time. Build momentum by making progress on one tangible financial goal — saving money or paying down debt, for example — before adding another.

Yes, Americans across a range of incomes report feeling in control financially. But it would be glib to suggest that this demonstrates that the feeling of financial control can be flicked on like a light switch, if only people tried harder.

There are plenty of reasons why the road to feeling in control can be arduous. Family obligations, medical concerns, affordability issues and limited opportunities can all present real obstacles, even for those who strive to practice sound financial habits along the way.

Production ramp-up and deferred deliveries define its near-term outlook.

Ur-Energy Inc. (URG -16.10%) reported its transition to a multiasset production profile following the launch of operations at Shirley Basin and the first resin shipment to its Lost Creek processing hub. Management indicated that the company is currently focused on a production ramp-up across its Wyoming assets while advancing a district-scale expansion strategy. The company reported significant year-over-year increases in uranium sales and capture rates as it optimizes wellfield flow and processing capacity. Operational initiatives include the implementation of sand filtration systems and the construction of a permanent wastewater treatment facility to support higher throughput levels. Additionally, the company is progressing exploration at Lost Creek South and North Hadsell while preparing a technical report for the potential development of Lost Soldier as a satellite mine.

Matthew Gili: Thank you, Alex, and thanks to all of you who joined us today. The market backdrop supports Ur-Energy's disciplined development of a domestic district scale ISR platform. During the quarter, we delivered 190,000 pounds of U3O8 under long-term contracts, generating $12.3 million in revenue. Year-to-date sales increased 67.3% compared to the same period last year. Pounds captured increased 26.4% year-to-date, while pounds drummed 341,058 through the first 9 months, an increase of approximately 18% year-over-year.

Our third quarter cash cost was $40.40 per produced pound with year-to-date cash costs declining 7.6% compared with the same period in 2025. We ended the quarter with 233,378 pounds of finished inventory at the conversion facility. And in-process and plant inventory increased from 19,496 pounds to 85,708 pounds, including inventory adjustments. While our production ramp-up continues, these year-over-year improvements reflect the progress we're making as we optimize our operations and build production capacity across both assets. Lost Creek continues to advance production growth through operational improvements, infrastructure investment and expansion of wellfield capacity. At Lost Creek, we drummed 341,058 pounds through the first 9 months of 2026, an increase of 18.2% from the prior year period.

A sand filtration system was brought online in July to increase flow rates while a new wastewater treatment facility is being constructed. The new facility is on schedule to be in operation in the second quarter of 2027 and is expected to fully optimize wastewater capacity. The sand filtration system has been effective in decreasing fine particles from the wellfield and increasing flow rates. And since the end of the quarter, we have implemented process and other measures to better manage wastewater, while advancing the permanent facility. Since the end of the quarter, we have also completed maintenance of the elution and ion exchange systems at the plant to increase processing and drumming of pounds.

In the wellfield at Lost Creek, we are advancing in Mine Unit 5. Wellfield construction is well underway with regulatory approval and the start of production targeted for the first quarter of 2027. Together, these initiatives are advancing our ramp-up and positioning Lost Creek for sustained production growth. We are building a district scale ISR operation and reestablishing Wyoming as the top uranium district in the U.S. We are achieving this through steady ramp-up of existing operations and by advancing multiple assets with potential as future satellite mines. The satellite model allows us to employ our capital more efficiently by our skilled, experienced team.

At Shirley Basin, we reached an important milestone in August when we made our first uranium shipment to Lost Creek for processing. This marked our transition to a multi-asset domestic uranium producer. We have captured 25,330 pounds of uranium year-to-date at Shirley Basin, including 14,697 pounds in the third quarter. Our team is improving wellfield operating parameters and plans to bring additional header houses online during the fourth quarter of 2026 and throughout 2027. We are also optimizing the operation's lixiviant chemistry. Optimization since the end of the quarter has produced positive results as we continue the production ramp-up. For now, Shirley Basin operates as a spoke of our Lost Creek hub, and we are pleased with the ramp-up progress.

However, it is important to note that Shirley Basin also retains the flexibility to become a stand-alone production hub as the Great Divide Basin develops. With ramp-up underway at our operating mines and processing hub, we are accelerating progress at a selection of other assets in Wyoming, paving the way for mine expansion and new satellite operations. Not many people realize that our Lost Creek property is 55 square miles, and we are producing on just a fraction of that land package. This is incredibly prospective land. That is why at Lost Creek South, where we have 3 major trends, we have commenced a 120-hole exploration program, testing 7 miles of composite trend.

We're testing mine expansion targets as well as regional targets with strong potential for hosting a new resource. At Lost Soldier, which is just 17 miles from Lost Creek, we are in the final stages of a technical report. We expect to release the report by year-end with a construction decision to follow. Its proximity to Lost Creek provides yet another opportunity for development as a satellite operation within our growing production platform. At North Hadsell, 13 of 33 widely spaced drill holes with spacing up to 1,000 feet intersected production-grade uranium in our drilling program that we completed earlier this year. Planning is underway to follow up this highly successful program.

Together, these projects demonstrate the depth of our organic growth pipeline and the opportunity to expand our district scale uranium production platform by leveraging our existing infrastructure and operating expertise. Our strategy combines near-term production growth, district scale expansion and disciplined capital allocation. To close, our growth strategy has 6 clear priorities. First, increase uranium production and cash flow as we continue to advance production ramp-up and operational optimization at both Lost Creek and Shirley Basin. Second, expand our district scale ISR production platform across Wyoming. Third, advance a pipeline of capital-efficient satellite mine opportunities to support long-term growth. Fourth, build upon our leading operating execution and maintain a competitive low-cost production profile.

Fifth, build on the growing strategic importance of a domestic U.S. uranium supply. And finally, remain disciplined in how we grow and allocate capital with the objective of delivering sustainable long-term value. That is how we intend to translate our operating assets and development pipeline into America's uranium powerhouse. Thank you. We look forward to your questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Your first question is coming from Soundarya Iyer with B. Riley.

Soundarya Iyer: So I'm just curious, like can you walk us through the path -- the production path to 2027, like specifically the timing of MU5 permit, how that feeds into '27, '28 production? And how you see that 1.4 million pounds 2027 deliveries being covered between inventory and new production?

Matthew Gili: Thank you for the question, Soundarya. I appreciate it. Expected a question from Soundarya. So look, I'm going to kind of answer it in 2 different ways, 2 different -- looking at each of the different properties. So when we talk about Lost Creek, we are laying the groundwork for a plant that can be expanded to progress the output of multiple mines as we go beyond the 2 that we currently have in production. This year continues our successful track record as we continue to see larger year-over-year increases in production and efficiency.

We talked about in the call, some of the things we're doing at Lost Creek to improve the flow rates and to improve our wastewater treatment capacity and to just continue the very successful ramp-up at Lost Creek. At Shirley Basin, we're in the early phases of ramp-up. And during this time, we've been optimizing our processes, including the resin transfer system, elution and ion exchange systems at Lost Creek, well performance in our first 2 header houses and lixiviant chemistry, and we have seen very positive results since the end of the quarter. So each of the properties were in ramp-up. We're continuing that ramp up. It's going very well. It's going very successful.

Steve, did you have any other color to add to that?

Steven Hatten: No, I think the main thing that what Matt and the rest of the team are doing is we are focusing on optimizing the main components of production, which are always flow and grade. And we work daily to increase those, and that's where we see ourselves going in '27.

Matthew Gili: Yes. It's really an exciting time. And I can't be more thrilled with the progress. When I look at Lost Creek, our flow rates have increased substantially. And like Steve said, it's flowing. The flow rates at Lost Creek are really coming up. They come up every single day this month. I couldn't be more thrilled. And at Shirley basin, that optimization of the lixiviant chemistry is absolutely demonstrating itself with significant improvements in the grade that we received from the wells. So both properties are advancing through start-up, advancing through ramp-up. I couldn't be more thrilled with the progress. And that's the color I've got there, Soundarya. Does that answer your question?

Soundarya Iyer: Yes, Matt. Just a follow-up on that, like on prioritizing development spending and the CapEx requirement for '27. So how are you looking at managing the liquidity next year? And what milestones do you see that you actually gets to that EBITDA inflection point somewhere in late '27, early '28 year time frame?

Matthew Gili: Absolutely. And so we're projected to spend another $26 million on the Lost Creek wastewater facility and another $8 million on Shirley Basin through next year. With our expected production and sales in the pipeline, together with our existing cash resources, this is our source of funding. And importantly, we also maintain financial flexibility, have a range of options available to support our ongoing operations and growth initiatives. We will continue to evaluate our capital requirements with a focus on accelerating our production ramp-up and advancing our organic growth pipeline.

Operator: Your next question is coming from Anthony Taglieri with Canaccord Genuity.

Anthony Taglieri: Maybe just to get a bit more granular at Lost Creek. So you guys indicated some of the lower grades that were realized in the quarter just given the decline from some of the older header houses. Is this something that can improve before Mine Unit 5 Phase 1 comes online early next year? Or is that sort of what we're waiting for to see some of those -- that grade profile improve? I guess what I'm getting at is I know you don't provide quarterly guidance, but given we're in Q4, you have some results that you've already been seeing this quarter, directionally, should we expect an improvement in finished production in Q4 or something similar to Q3?

Matthew Gili: Great question, Anthony. Ramp-up is not always straight line. The key driver of Lost Creek is the flow. So right now, we're in the grade environment that we're in. As we progress into Mine Unit 5, we'll get into a new environment with different grades. Really, the target of our initiatives at Lost Creek right now are the increase in flow and the flow is going up and production is flow times grade. So we have flow going up and grade holding constant, which implies an increase in production. Steve, any more color on Lost Creek and how we're progressing through the rest of this year?

Steven Hatten: Sure. Look, we continue on a daily basis to look for nuggets that we can assist in increasing that grade. As Matt said, our primary focus there has been grade and flow. And with respect to flow, we have seen the increases. We have seen productivity. We have seen optimization due to the sand filters that we installed, and we are very much looking forward to that wastewater facility coming on early next year. The areas that we're working on right now, we are going back pattern by pattern, trying to find areas, where we can make small increases in grade.

But your assertion that the grade is what it is for the remainder of this year is closer to the reality that we face in the later stages of mining in any pattern in any ISR facility.

Matthew Gili: Yes. And it's important to note that we have -- we've moved out of Mine Unit 2. We moved into the second phase of Mine Unit 1. So we've moved into the second phase of Mine Unit 1, and then we will then progress into Mine Unit 5. So we're always advancing through our mining units as we go. We're not -- we do not have any permitting delays. We're just advancing through our Mine Units. Right now, we're in a phase of lower grade, but grades can and do fluctuate in ISR.

The overall grade has exceeded our estimates, and we expect the end of the decline curve in Mine -- as we approach the end of the decline curve in Mine Unit 2, we are already in the process of transitioning to a new mine unit flow. That's what we focused on. It's -- Lost Creek is flow. And I couldn't -- I wish I couldn't be more thrilled with the progress we're making on maximizing flow and understanding how to operate the new filtration.

Anthony Taglieri: Okay. Great. That's super helpful. Maybe just a follow-up on the contracting front. So we saw one of your U.S. peers recently, they signed 2 market reference contracts with no floors and ceilings, so indexed 100% of the spot price at the time of delivery. Are you guys also seeing some of these contracts available? And would that be a preferred structure moving forward?

Matthew Gili: Anthony, it's my favorite question. All right. We absolutely. We all get the same interactions with the utilities. We're all in the same environment. And we are absolutely in a state of transition, in my opinion, in a state of transition with how uranium is contracted. What you are seeing -- I believe I'm being careful with my wording. What I believe you are seeing is absolutely a shift from pricing security to security of supply. Customers want security of supply. I know this because the term price is $10 more than the spot price. I don't have to read between the lines. I just read the line and it says the utilities are concerned about future supply.

I see this as an opportunity. And I see this absolutely as a chance. I don't want spot price. I want a premium spot price going forward. And I see we're poised for a real change in how this works and our interactions with our customers are becoming very different. And again, they're very much focused on surety of supply, and that implies a premium. Does that answer your question, Anthony?

Operator: Your next question is coming from Heiko Ihle with H.C. Wainwright.

Unknown Analyst: Matt, it's Kate filling in for Heiko here. Now that we're halfway through fourth quarter, would you be able to walk us through maybe the expected cash burn on the Shirley Basin ramp-up quarter-by-quarter over the next few?

Matthew Gili: Well, I'm not really -- okay. So when we talk about the cash burn at Shirley Basin, the spend -- we call it spend. The spend we do on development and operations remains constant. We're not -- as we advance Shirley Basin through mine development, we're not changing the amount of drills rigs and how we change the development going forward at Shirley Basin. So our cash spend is relatively constant at Shirley at Lost Creek as well. We don't operate under campaigns. We don't bring in groups of drills and drill a bunch of wells and then have them leave. We just maintain a steady production of 25 or so rigs across the company and march our development forward.

Our development is our mining, and we're always preparing for moving into the next environment. And we install 8 to 10 header houses at each mine each year, and we're just going to continue to do that for the next decade. So our cash burn is relatively consistent. We did touch on the finishing up the capital projects. Shirley Basin will finish off this year with another $8 million projected for next year to finish off the wastewater treatment plant there, and we're finalizing the wastewater treatment plant at Lost Creek. Does that give you color?

Unknown Analyst: No, absolutely. I appreciate the answer. And if I could just follow up with one more regarding Lost Soldier. Are there any other critical milestones you think we should be paying close attention to before a construction decision beyond the aquifer test and technical report, which I assume the latter is coming next month.

Matthew Gili: Yes. So look, the aquifer testing is done. We're now just compiling the technical report. The absolute catalyst, the milestone is going to be this publication of the technical report at the end of this year. Very excited about being able to share our analysis of Lost Soldier and then moving into a construction decision in 2027. The catalyst you're looking for is the publication of that technical report.

Operator: Your next question is coming from Jeff Grampp with Northland Capital Markets.

Jeffrey Grampp: At the risk of beating a dead horse at Lost Creek on the production front, it sounds like grade is steady. Flow is up quite a bit sequentially, but pounds were down a little bit. So was there just some downtime at the plant during the quarter or some other kind of interruptions that explain the lower production in Q3 versus Q2 given the other variables you talked about?

Matthew Gili: Thanks, Jeff. I'll pass over to Steve to give a little bit of color.

Steven Hatten: Jeff. I think during the end of the previous period, we had seen some activities related to bringing the sand filters online. Again, flow grade, right? I beat the same dead horse all the time as well. We know that grade is fairly constant at this phase of mining in the Mine Units that we have. So our whole focus was on flow.

And during the end of the previous quarter, we had some maintenance activities that drove a lot of that flow, and we are also really learning how to optimize the use of our sand filter system I can really say confidently that we have done a great job doing that, and we are seeing growth on a routine basis now.

Matthew Gili: Yes. Yes. Thanks, Steve. Yes, that's the color I've guided. It's about increasing flow at Lost Creek. As Steve pointed out, we did some maintenance to the ion exchange columns in the third quarter. That impacts your ability to take flow from the wellfield. And the sand filters have just completely changed the environment there and really pleased with their performance.

Jeffrey Grampp: All right. Great. I appreciate those details. And for my follow-up on North Hadsell, given the positive results earlier this year, can you update us on potential timing for additional work there? Is that something that could happen next year? Just any commentary on next steps would be great.

Matthew Gili: Thanks, Jeff. Look, we're very excited about North Hadsell. I mean, to get that kind of results from what is -- it's almost just greenfield exploration. Ryan, from a permitting standpoint, are we able to execute additional drilling in North Hadsell next year?

Ryan Schierman: Yes. So we've already submitted an expanded drill program to the BLM that would allow us to do larger scale drilling in North Hadsell. We're under that process right now. But yes, in all likelihood, it's indicative that we'll be able to go to North Hadsell.

Matthew Gili: And John Cooper, why are you as the Head of Geology, why are you excited about North Hadsell?

John Cooper: Well, excited because we had very little data to go on and just to go out and drill these wide spaced holes and encounter these types of grades and thicknesses. On wide spacing is pretty exciting.

Matthew Gili: Yes. So you can tell, Jeff, we're very excited about it. We have the permits in place. We have the desire, and we will pull together our plans as we go through the next couple of months for where we're going to execute our growth strategy in 2027.

Operator: Your next question is coming from Ali Mecklai with RBC Capital Markets.

Ali Mecklai: Stepping in for Andrew Wong, who can't make it today. It looks like there were some issues with transporting material from Shirley Basin to Lost Creek. Just curious what were the specific modifications needed at Lost Creek to unload Shirley Basin material? And do you expect those bottlenecks to persist through Q4?

Matthew Gili: Great question. Great. Steve, I'll hand it over to you. Transporting resin from Shirley to Lost Creek.

Steven Hatten: Transporting really wasn't a major issue. Any time you do something the first time, it takes time. So there is always -- we're going to call this granular ramp-up, okay? So when you start a new process, this was the first time for the new facility at Shirley to ship the product. So there was a learning curve there. And when we do the same thing receiving product at the Lost Creek facility, there was a learning curve there. We have since had multiple shipments and they've become much more streamlined. So initial steps, always the first time, much more careful. Our regulatory process is in place. New procedures are in place.

We have become much more comfortable with all those, and it's becoming much more routine.

Matthew Gili: Yes. That's the real message there is that we've become very routine in shipments of resin from Shirley Basin to Lost Creek.

Steven Hatten: I think it's clear. We've had issues not with transportation. That has gone smooth. It's on the receiving end of those vessels.

Matthew Gili: Yes. So things are going really well. I was there -- I was at Lost Creek on Thursday and we were doing a transfer of Shirley into the plant. It's going beautifully.

Ali Mecklai: Yes, definitely. Just one follow-up. It looks like pounds captured were up 50,000 pounds quarter-over-quarter. Pounds drummed were down roughly 35,000 pounds quarter-over-quarter. Can you just talk about which metric do you think is more important and why they might have differed in Q3?

Matthew Gili: Okay. Great question. You're very astute and you've looked at the data carefully. Look, they both matter because they both are really measuring the same things. We get paid on pounds drummed. So I tend to look at pounds drummed, but pounds captured just gives you an indication that there are -- there's pounds coming into the system. When you have -- when you're doing maintenance at the plant, sometimes you get into a position where you build up plant inventory.

At Shirley Basin, we're absolutely building up captured pounds of inventory is just as you build that dead load -- not the dead load, but the uranium load within your resin exchange columns, so it takes time, and we started up with 0% resin, and now we're building that up. And the other part of it, too, is that we just -- in the third quarter, did an inventory adjustment in that we were drumming significantly more pounds than we were capturing, which is not physically possible. And so it just indicated that we were underestimating our pounds captured. Pounds captured is a calculated number. Pounds drummed is measured, and that's gospel.

So we just adjusted our capture to reflect what we were showing in our drums.

Operator: Your next question is coming from Matthew Key with Texas Capital Securities.

Matthew Key: Most of my questions have been kind of touched on, but I wanted to talk a little bit about costs, came in a little bit higher in 3Q relative to the previous quarter. I imagine a lot of that is due to just fixed cost leverage. But I guess I wanted to ask you if you're seeing any additional inflationary pressures present in the business? And what are your kind of expectations over the coming quarters in regards to costs as output hopefully increases here in 4Q and into '27?

Matthew Gili: Yes. Thanks, Matthew. Thanks for the question. Jade, would you like to field this question for Matthew?

Jade Walle: Jade [ Walle ] here. Were you saying comps or cost -- or cost. We couldn't hear your sound, Matthew.

Matthew Key: Yes. It was regarding costs.

Unknown Executive: Are we talking cost of sales in terms of cost per pound? It's still part of that...

Unknown Executive: Or cost production cost side of things. During the quarter, we only sold 10,000 pounds of produced costs and the cost per pound of those was relatively static with what it was the previous quarter. We did sell 180,000 of non-produced pounds. And of course, they have a higher cost. So it changed the weighted average during the quarter increased the total average cost per pound sold because of those non-produced pounds that we sold during the quarter. That was just a function of the type of pounds that we sold during the quarter.

Matthew Gili: Yes. That makes sense. We had some pounds in inventory that we purchased previously. And so we just took this opportunity to get them out of the system. And so we have almost -- we have very little produced pounds left on purchased pounds left on inventory. You asked a question about inflation. We're not seeing inflationary pressures in that we don't -- our lixiviants that we use are oxygen and carbon dioxide and baking soda, and they just don't have the same sort of inflationary pressures that you might be getting from people that are using sulfuric acid or something like that. So we don't see that kind of pressure.

We see the normal pressures associated with employment in that Wyoming is a state with essentially no unemployment. But it's just a normal inflationary. There's no other drivers in Wyoming that are leading to an inflation on labor that's any different than just the overall inflation rate.

Operator: We have reached the end of the question-and-answer session. I would now like to invite the CEO, Matt Gili, to provide any closing remarks.

Matthew Gili: Thank you, operator. Very pleased with the ramp-up as it continues at Lost Creek and Shirley Basin and very energized by our growth strategy and the opportunities we see across our assets as we continue to build America's premier uranium powerhouse across the state of Wyoming. Thank you, everybody, for participating in today's call, and thank you to my team for all the hard work that you do every day. Thank you, operator.

Operator: Thank you, everyone. This does conclude today's conference call. You may disconnect your phone lines at this time, and have a wonderful day. Thank you for your participation.

TL;DR: Mortgage rates went up today, but they're still in a much better place than this time last month.

Mortgage rates are higher today, but only by a little. And they're still hovering below 7%, which is much better than what we saw around this time last month.

The average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage ticked up to 6.98% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. This is two basis points higher than Friday and five basis points higher than a week ago. (A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.)

Mortgage rates have more room to rise, as a stronger-than-expected jobs report reinforced expectations for a Federal Reserve rate hike in December.

Here are the average APRs we're seeing today, as well as movement over the past month for context:

As for what’s next: Tomorrow’s jobs report, showing October data, could potentially nudge mortgage rates in either direction. To understand the link between jobs data and mortgage rates, keep reading below the video.

» Take the next step: Compare mortgage rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

Mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to new inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

This week, the Nerds are watching the October Consumer Price Index, which comes out on Tuesday. CPI is one of two key measures of inflation, which the Federal Reserve aims to keep in check relative to the strength of the labor market. (The Fed looks more closely at a different inflation measure, the Personal Consumption Expenditures Index, which comes out Nov. 25.)

Right now, the labor market is looking pretty darn strong: The October jobs report, released Friday from the Bureau of Labor Statistics, showed U.S. employers added 165,000 jobs in October, far more than economists expected, and unemployment edged down to 4.1%.

Raising the federal funds rate is the Fed’s main tool for bringing inflation down, but rate hikes are only on the table when the labor market is strong enough to handle it. Considering Friday’s jobs data, it’s looking fairly likely that the Fed will approve a rate hike when the committee meets Dec. 8-9. The Fed doesn't set mortgage rates directly, but an anticipated rate hike can put upward pressure on mortgage rates, which respond to investors’ expectations for the economy and Fed policy.

Still, a jump in mortgage rates isn’t a sure thing, and market sentiment could shift over the next month. October’s inflation data will capture the effect of the Fed’s last rate hike, which came in the middle of September. If that worked as intended and inflation shows signs of slowing, mortgage rates might remain around 7%.

Refinancing might make sense if today’s rates are at least 0.5 to 0.75 of a percentage point lower than your current rate (and if you plan to stay in your home long enough to break even on closing costs).

With rates where they are right now, you may want to start considering a refi if your current rate is around 7.48% or higher.

Also consider your goals: Are you trying to lower your monthly payment, shorten your loan term or turn home equity into cash? For example, you might be more comfortable with paying a higher rate for a cash-out refinance than you would for a rate-and-term refinance, so long as the overall costs are lower than if you kept your original mortgage and added a HELOC or home equity loan.

If you're looking for a lower rate, use NerdWallet's refinance calculator to estimate savings and understand how long it would take to break even on the costs of refinancing.

There is no universal “right” time to start shopping — what matters is whether you can comfortably afford a mortgage now at today’s rates.

If the answer is yes, don’t get too hung up on whether you could be missing out on lower rates later; you can refinance down the road. Focus on getting preapproved, comparing lender offers, and understanding what monthly payment works for your budget.

NerdWallet’s affordability calculator can help you estimate your potential monthly payment. If a new home isn’t in the cards right now, there are still things you can do to strengthen your buyer profile. Take this time to pay down existing debts and build your down payment savings. Not only will this free up more cash flow for a future mortgage payment, it can also get you a better interest rate when you’re ready to buy.

If you already have a quote you’re happy with, you should consider locking your mortgage rate, especially if your lender offers a float-down option. A float-down lets you take advantage of a better rate if the market drops during your lock period.

Rate locks protect you from increases while your loan is processed, and with the market forever bouncing around, that peace of mind can be worth it.

#3085. The Overlooked AI Trade Hiding in a Beaten-Down Corner of the Market

Consulting stocks have slumped this year on fears that AI will replace them. But the newest jobs report shows companies hiring consultants at the fastest pace in nearly two years.

Investors have spent 2026 betting that artificial intelligence will put consultants out of work. Through Tuesday's close, Accenture (ACN +1.63%) was roughly flat this year, Cognizant (CTSH +2.20%) was down 20%, and Infosys (INFY +1.61%) was down 31%. Others have fallen just as hard: EPAM Systems (EPAM +4.67%) and research firm Gartner (IT -1.10%) are each down about 20%. Fueling the declines, investors have worried that if AI can write code and analyze data, companies will need fewer people to do it and fewer outside firms to manage it.

But recent jobs data tells a different story.

Employment in U.S. management and technical consulting rose by 17,300 in October to about 1.9 million, according to preliminary Bureau of Labor Statistics data. That was the largest monthly gain since December 2024, bringing the year-over-year increase to about 46,000 jobs, or 2.5%.

LPL Financial thinks AI is the reason. "Companies are not simply spending on chips, servers, and data centers, they are also hiring specialized workers who can help integrate new technology into existing workflows," it wrote in a market commentary this week. It compared the trend to the late 1990s, when consulting jobs grew at double-digit rates as businesses adopted the internet.

In other words, buying AI is the first step, but making it work inside a bank, hospital or factory takes people.

Accenture, the biggest name in the group, is still growing, just slowly. In its fiscal year ended Aug. 31, revenue rose 6% to $74.2 billion, and it set a record with 141 client bookings of $100 million or more. The company employs about 814,000 people, a reminder of how much of this business still runs on people. Fourth-quarter new bookings, a measure of future work, rose 4% to $22.2 billion, and the company expects revenue to grow 3% to 6% this fiscal year in local currencies, with earnings per share of $14.39 to $14.81, up 6% to 9%.

At nearly $260 a share, Accenture trades at roughly 18 times the midpoint of this year's earnings forecast, a modest price for a business that still grows and returns so much cash.

Still, the company is honest about the risk. In the same release, it warns that AI "could harm the company's business, including by reducing demand for our services." And the middle of its growth forecast, about 4.5%, would be slower than last year's 5% in local currencies, a sign that clients haven't rushed into big new AI projects yet.

The market and the jobs data are pointing in opposite directions, and one month of hiring doesn't settle the debate. But if LPL is right that the next phase of AI is about putting it to work, today's beaten-down consulting stocks could be the overlooked winners. Investors who want AI stocks beyond chipmakers may want to start with Accenture and watch whether its bookings keep climbing.
